A short textbook with computed figures

Fundamental Ideas from First Principles

Fifteen ideas worth thinking about for years, each one an equation that several fields discovered on their own

Preface

Claude wrote this book at Jai Sharma's direction in October 2026. Separate Claude agents audited its mathematics and checked its citations, and every figure computes its idea in the page.

This book is about one kind of idea: a single equation that physics, statistics, machine learning, control, economics, or pure mathematics found independently and named differently. Each name comes with tools the other fields lacked, so an idea with many names repays years of study. Diffusion is the model case. It generates images, it samples actions for reinforcement learning, and it simulates physical systems, and the same equation sits under all three.

Chapter 1 treats diffusion itself. Chapters 2 to 15 take one idea each, in an order where every chapter uses the ones before it, and the early chapters reach furthest into research on generative models and reinforcement learning. Every chapter has the same parts, in the order a seminal paper uses: the motivation (the problem that forced the idea), the intuition (the idea in one sentence and one computed picture), the statement, a derivation, figures, four ways to see the idea joined by short derivations, where it breaks and what is open, exercises, derivations to redo from a blank page, and notes for further reading. A line under each chapter's opening names the earlier chapters and the prerequisites it uses, and Appendix A states those prerequisites.

Every figure computes its idea in the page on a small problem, and the numbers in its caption come from that computation at the settings the caption names. The figure under "Where it breaks" computes the failure itself. The exercises come from a practice deck: each states a problem with numbers, and its answer, checked by a short computation, is folded under it. The derivations after the exercises each ask for a result of the chapter from a blank page, with a solution folded under it.

Introduction: ideas with many names

Diffusion passes three tests. It fits on a napkin: add noise with \(dx = g\,dW\), then run it backward with the score. Several fields found it on their own. Physicists call it Brownian motion and the heat equation, statisticians know its denoising step as Tweedie's formula, finance knows it as Black-Scholes, and machine learning calls it a diffusion model. Each name brings a tool the others lacked: the heat equation brings Fourier analysis, Tweedie brings empirical Bayes, and Langevin brings sampling.

The test can be applied to any idea: count the fields that have their own name for it. An idea with one name is a technique. An idea with five names is a place to stay for years, because every field that named it has already built tools to borrow. The table counts names for the fifteen ideas of this book.

Fields and ideas

Optimization and measure theory are fields, and each takes years. The kind of idea this book is about is one equation inside a field. Optimization's is convex duality: a convex function is described as well by its tangent lines as by its points. Chapter 2 applies it to \(\log \mathbb E[e^{f}]\) and KL. Measure theory's is the change of measure: an expectation under one distribution rewritten under another with a density, which on paths is Girsanov's theorem (Chapter 3). Most of measure theory exists to make statements like these two precise, so the statements come first here and the formalism is picked up when a proof needs it.

Chapter 1

Diffusion

Physics, statistics, and generative modeling

Add noise to data until nothing is left, and the density spreads by the heat equation. The score \(\nabla \log p_t\), the direction in which the noisy density rises, is all it takes to run the process backward, and it equals a denoiser, so it can be learned from data.

Uses Appendix A.1 and A.4.

1.1Motivation

Generative modeling asks for new samples from a distribution known only through examples. Writing its density down is hopeless in high dimension, because the normalizing constant is an integral over every possible image. Earlier approaches paid to avoid it: adversarial networks trained a sampler against a discriminator and were unstable, and normalizing flows restricted their architectures to keep the density tractable. The score \(\nabla \log p\) does not depend on the normalizing constant, it can be learned by regression on noisy copies of the data, and it is enough to run noise backward into data.

PAPERA document that moved capital

The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities

Price an option by the hedge that replicates it, and the price stops depending on anyone's appetite for risk.

Fischer Black and Myron Scholes, 1973 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

Traders adopted the formula almost at once, the Chicago Board Options Exchange opened the same year, and the formula became the basis of the listed-options and derivatives markets.

The link to this chapter: a change to log-price and rescaled time turns the paper's pricing equation into what it calls "the heat-transfer equation of physics" (p. 644, its equation 10), which is (1.1) here, whose solution is the heat kernel. The stock's expected return drops out of the price, which Chapter 3 reads as a change of measure.

1.2Intuition

Noise blurs data the way heat spreads, and at every level of blur the score is an arrow pointing back toward the data.

Figure 1.1The noised density as a surface

The noised density p_t(x) is a surface over position and time, and paths of the probability-flow ODE dx/dt = −½·∂x log p_t(x), run backward from draws of p_3, follow it from the wide noise at t = 3 into the data's three modes at t = 0.

Drag the surface, or slide turn, to see it from the side: the three peaks of p_0 at the back merge into one hump by t = 3 at the front. Of 2000 ODE paths started from draws of p_3, fractions 0.295, 0.497, and 0.207 end in the three modes, against weights of 0.3, 0.5, and 0.2, and the reverse SDE gives 0.303, 0.494, and 0.203. Switch to SDE paths: they jitter and cross on the way and land in the same proportions. Press resample: over five seeds every share stays within 0.027 of its weight. The flow carries each quantile of p_3 onto the same quantile of p_0, within 4.2e−8 on 200 quantiles, and both edges of the surface hold mass 1.0000.

1.3Statement

Theorem 1.1 (forward and backward)

Let \(dX_t = g(t)\,dW_t\) with \(X_0 \sim p_0\), and let \(p_t\) be the law of \(X_t\). Then \(p_t\) solves the heat equation, and the same marginals are produced backward in time by a stochastic and by a deterministic process:

\[ \partial_t p_t = \tfrac12 g(t)^2\, \Delta p_t, \tag{1.1} \]
\[ dX_t = -g(t)^2\, \nabla \log p_t(X_t)\, dt + g(t)\, d\bar W_t \quad \text{(reverse SDE, time running down)}, \tag{1.2} \]
\[ \frac{dX_t}{dt} = -\tfrac12\, g(t)^2\, \nabla \log p_t(X_t) \quad \text{(probability-flow ODE)}. \tag{1.3} \]

Theorem 1.2 (Tweedie's formula)

If \(X_\sigma = X_0 + \sigma Z\) with \(Z\) standard normal and independent of \(X_0\), then

\[ \mathbb E[X_0 \mid X_\sigma = x] = x + \sigma^2\, \nabla \log p_\sigma(x). \tag{1.4} \]

1.4Derivation

Heat equation. Over a short step \(h\), \(X_{t+h} = X_t + g\sqrt{h}\,Z\). For a smooth test function \(\varphi\), a second-order Taylor expansion gives

\[ \mathbb E\,\varphi(X_{t+h}) = \mathbb E\,\varphi(X_t) + \tfrac12 g^2 h\, \mathbb E\, \Delta\varphi(X_t) + o(h) \]

Writing both sides as integrals against \(p_t\) and moving the Laplacian onto \(p_t\) by integrating by parts twice gives (1.1).

Probability-flow ODE. Since \(\tfrac12 g^2 \Delta p = \nabla \cdot \big(\tfrac12 g^2\, p\, \nabla \log p\big)\), equation (1.1) is the continuity equation \(\partial_t p = -\nabla\cdot(p\, v)\) for the velocity \(v = -\tfrac12 g^2 \nabla \log p\). Particles that move with \(v\) therefore have marginals \(p_t\), in either direction of time, which is (1.3).

Reverse SDE. In reversed time \(s = T - t\), the density \(q_s = p_{T-s}\) satisfies \(\partial_s q = -\tfrac12 g^2 \Delta q\). A process with drift \(b\) and noise \(g\) has \(\partial_s q = -\nabla\cdot(q\, b) + \tfrac12 g^2 \Delta q\). Matching the two requires \(\nabla\cdot(q\,b) = g^2 \Delta q = \nabla\cdot(g^2 q \nabla\log q)\), and the gradient solution \(b = g^2 \nabla \log q\) is (1.2), Anderson's reverse drift. Noise added on the way back must be paid for with twice the ODE's drift.

Tweedie. Write \(p_\sigma(x) = \int p_0(x_0)\, \mathcal N(x; x_0, \sigma^2)\, dx_0\) and differentiate under the integral: \(\nabla p_\sigma(x) = \int p_0(x_0)\, \mathcal N(x; x_0, \sigma^2)\, \frac{x_0 - x}{\sigma^2}\, dx_0\). Dividing by \(p_\sigma(x)\) turns the integral into a posterior expectation, \(\sigma^2 \nabla \log p_\sigma(x) = \mathbb E[X_0 \mid X_\sigma = x] - x\). ∎

Consequence. The posterior mean minimizes \(\mathbb E\,\|D(X_\sigma) - X_0\|^2\) over denoisers \(D\), so a network trained to denoise at every noise level is, by (1.4), a network that knows the score. This is denoising score matching, and it is why diffusion models train by regression.

1.5Figures

Figure 1.2One noised mixture, four pictures

The same p_σ is a cloud of Brownian paths, a solution of the heat equation in τ = σ², a score field, and a denoiser, and Tweedie's formula E[x₀ | x] = x + σ²·∂x log p_σ(x) reads the denoiser off the score.

Slide σ from 0.05 to 3: p_σ keeps three modes until σ = 0.62 and two until 0.92, the score flattens, and the denoiser bends from the identity toward the data mean. At every σ the Bayes posterior mean and Tweedie's formula agree to within 1.6e−14, and p_σ solves ∂p/∂τ = ½∂²p/∂x² with a relative finite-difference residual of at most 1.4e−6. Press run: 200 particles start on the quantiles of p_3, follow dx/dσ = −σ·∂x log p_σ, and land 0.300, 0.500, and 0.200 in the three modes, each within 2.6e−9 of its quantile of p_0.05.

Figure 1.3Running the noise backward, two ways

The score alone runs the noise backward, as the reverse SDE dx = −∂x log p_σ d(σ²) + dW̄ or as the probability-flow ODE dx/d(σ²) = −½·∂x log p_σ, and both carry a Gaussian at σ = 3 onto the three-mode data.

Slide N from 10 to 400. At N = 10 both sets land too wide, the SDE more (variance 3.133 and 2.965 against the data's 2.732), and the SDE puts 0.443 of its particles in the middle mode against a weight of 0.5. As N grows both W1 distances to the data fall to the level of 2000 exact draws (median 0.039): the SDE's from 0.152 to 0.042, and the ODE's from 0.098 to 0.014, below that level because this seed's starting points happen to be lucky. Both sets of mode shares come within 0.011 of 0.3, 0.5, and 0.2. At large N the gap between the two is within seed-to-seed noise. Its paths are smooth and keep their order, and the SDE's jitter and cross.

1.6Four ways to see it

The same process is a cloud of particles, a spreading density, a vector field, and a denoiser (Figure 1.2). Each picture follows from the one before it.

  1. 1Particlesphysics

    Each particle takes independent Gaussian kicks, \(dX_t = g(t)\, dW_t\). Einstein used this picture of Brownian motion to count molecules, and a sampler simulates it.

  2. 1 → 2Average a test function over the particles. A second-order Taylor step gives \(\tfrac{d}{dt}\mathbb E\,\varphi(X_t) = \tfrac12 g^2\, \mathbb E\, \Delta\varphi(X_t)\) (Appendix A.1), and integrating by parts against \(p_t\) moves the Laplacian onto the density, which is (1.1).

  3. 2A densityanalysis

    The density solves the heat equation, so it is the data convolved with a Gaussian of variance \(\int_0^t g^2\). Fourier analysis applies: each frequency decays on its own (Chapter 7), and the surface \(p(x, t)\) flattens as \(t\) grows (Figure 1.1).

  4. 2 → 3Write the Laplacian as a divergence, \(\tfrac12 g^2 \Delta p = \nabla\cdot\big(\tfrac12 g^2\, p\, \nabla\log p\big)\). The heat equation becomes the continuity equation (Appendix A.4) with velocity \(v = -\tfrac12 g^2 \nabla \log p_t\), so the whole density moves along one vector field built from the score.

  5. 3A vector fielddynamical systems

    The score \(\nabla\log p_t\) points where the noised density rises. Following \(-\tfrac12 g^2 \nabla\log p_t\) forward in time spreads the data, and following it backward from noise gathers the data again (1.3).

  6. 3 → 4Differentiate the Gaussian convolution under the integral (Theorem 1.2): \(\sigma^2 \nabla \log p_\sigma(x) = \mathbb E[X_0 \mid X_\sigma = x] - x\). The score is the step from a noisy point to its best guess of the clean one, divided by the noise variance.

  7. 4A denoiserstatistics

    The posterior mean minimizes squared error, so a network trained to denoise at every noise level has learned the score. Statisticians know the identity as Tweedie's formula and use it for empirical Bayes, and machine learning uses it to train diffusion models by regression.

1.7Where it breaks and what is open

Theorem 1.1 holds for every starting distribution, including the empirical distribution of a training set. The noised density is then a mixture of Gaussians centered on the training points, its score has a closed form, and the reverse process run with that exact score returns the training points themselves, however many there are (Figure 1.4). A network that minimized the denoising loss perfectly would do the same. Trained networks make new samples because they fit the score imperfectly, in ways their architecture decides, and the largest of them still reproduce some training images (Carlini et al.). A second limit is cost: every sample takes tens of sequential network calls, and taking fewer steps adds discretization error (Figure 1.3).

Figure 1.4The exact score of a training set returns copies

With the exact score of a finite training set, the score of (1/n)·Σ N(x_i, t·I), the probability-flow ODE carries noise back onto copies of the training points, while the score of the density they came from spreads the same noise over the whole ring.

At the default n = 16 and σ = 0.01, 100.0% of the 1000 samples from the training-set score land within 0.05 of a training point, at a median distance of 0.012. From the same starting noise, the true-density score puts 2.8% there, at a median distance of 0.243. Slide n to 64: the copy rate stays at 100.0%, and only the true-density rate rises, to 11.2%, because 64 points cover more of the ring. Slide the stopping level up to σ = 0.1: the copies blur into small clouds and the rate falls to 14.4%.

  1. Why trained denoisers generalize. Two accounts compete. Networks are biased toward bases adapted to the geometry of images (Kadkhodaie et al.), and denoisers that are local and shift-equivariant create new images as mosaics of training patches (Kamb and Ganguli, and Chapter 7). Which mechanism dominates in large models, and how the balance shifts with the size of the training set, is open.
  2. Few steps without distillation. Sampling is sequential in the number of steps. Speculative decoding suggests guessing the trajectory and checking it in parallel. Chapter 4 gives the theory and its limits.
  3. Unmasking several tokens at once. Masked diffusion language models unmask several tokens per step and sample each from its own marginal. Given the tokens already revealed, the error of one such step is the total correlation of the tokens unmasked together, \(\mathrm{KL}\big(p(x_S \mid x_{\text{seen}}) \,\|\, \prod_{i \in S} p(x_i \mid x_{\text{seen}})\big)\). Mutual-information samplers measure the pairwise part of this quantity, and a bound on generation quality in terms of it is open.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 1.1Tweedie's formula

    With \(X_\sigma = X_0 + \sigma Z\), derive \(\mathbb E[X_0 \mid X_\sigma = x] = x + \sigma^2 \nabla\log p_\sigma(x)\). Then show that the posterior mean minimizes \(\mathbb E\,\|D(X_\sigma) - X_0\|^2\) over denoisers \(D\).

    Solution

    \(p_\sigma(x) = \int p_0(x_0)\, \mathcal N(x; x_0, \sigma^2 I)\, dx_0\), and \(\nabla_x \mathcal N(x; x_0, \sigma^2 I) = \mathcal N(x; x_0, \sigma^2 I)\, (x_0 - x)/\sigma^2\). Differentiating under the integral and dividing by \(p_\sigma(x)\),

    \[ \nabla\log p_\sigma(x) = \int \frac{p_0(x_0)\, \mathcal N(x; x_0, \sigma^2 I)}{p_\sigma(x)}\, \frac{x_0 - x}{\sigma^2}\, dx_0 = \frac{\mathbb E[X_0 \mid X_\sigma = x] - x}{\sigma^2}, \]

    because the fraction is the posterior density of \(X_0\) given \(X_\sigma = x\). For the second part, condition on \(X_\sigma\) and let \(m\) be the posterior mean:

    \[ \mathbb E\big[\|D - X_0\|^2 \mid X_\sigma\big] = \|D - m\|^2 + \mathbb E\big[\|X_0 - m\|^2 \mid X_\sigma\big], \]

    which is smallest at \(D = m\).

  2. Derivation 1.2The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process

    For \(dX_t = -X_t\, dt + \sqrt 2\, dW_t\) on the line, derive the Fokker-Planck equation, show that \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) is stationary, and find the law of \(X_t\) given \(X_0 = x_0\).

    Solution

    Itô's lemma gives the generator \(\mathcal L\varphi = -x\varphi' + \varphi''\) (Appendix A.1). Integrating by parts in \(\tfrac{d}{dt}\mathbb E\varphi(X_t) = \mathbb E\,\mathcal L\varphi(X_t)\) gives \(\partial_t p = \partial_x(x p) + \partial_x^2 p = \partial_x\big(x p + \partial_x p\big)\).

    For \(p \propto e^{-x^2/2}\), \(\partial_x p = -x p\), so the flux \(xp + \partial_x p\) vanishes and \(p\) is stationary. Solving the linear equation, \(X_t = x_0 e^{-t} + \sqrt 2 \int_0^t e^{-(t - s)}\, dW_s\), a Gaussian with mean \(x_0 e^{-t}\) and variance \(2\int_0^t e^{-2(t-s)} ds = 1 - e^{-2t}\).

Then Lipman et al., Flow Matching Guide and Code (2024), arXiv:2412.06264, with its library facebookresearch/flow_matching, whose discrete flow matching part covers masked diffusion. Chan and Lipman et al. do not derive the reverse SDE, so Section 1.4 is the derivation to keep.

Chapter 2

The tilt

Convex duality, from optimization

Multiply a distribution by \(e^{f}\) and renormalize. The result is the best trade between expected \(f\) and KL from the starting distribution, and the log of the normalizer is the value of that trade.

Uses Appendix A.2 and A.5.

2.1Motivation

Many problems ask for a distribution that scores well without straying far from a reference: a language model fine-tuned on human preferences that still writes like the pretrained model, a posterior that respects both a prior and the data, a physical system held at a temperature. Optimizing the score alone collapses onto its maximum and forgets the reference, and staying at the reference ignores the score. The tilt answers the trade in closed form, and its value, \(\log Z\), prices it.

PAPERA document that moved capital

DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning

Reinforcement learning on checkable answers can teach a language model to reason, at a fraction of frontier cost.

DeepSeek-AI, 2025 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

Its release in January 2025 set off a one-day sell-off in AI stocks of roughly a trillion dollars, led by NVIDIA, because it suggested that reasoning could be bought cheaply.

The link to this chapter: its GRPO objective (equation 1) maximizes a clipped advantage term minus \(\beta\, \mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}})\) with \(\beta = 0.001\), so the policy it aims at is the tilt \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\, e^{r/\beta}/Z\) of Theorem 2.1. The clipping only approximates that objective, and the reference is reset from time to time, so training runs a sequence of tilts.

2.2Intuition

Multiply the reference by \(e^{f}\) and renormalize, and you get the best compromise between chasing \(f\) and staying close to where you started.

Figure 2.1The tilt attains log Z

Among all densities q, the objective E_q[βf] − KL(q‖p) peaks at q* ∝ p·e^{βf}, where it equals log E_p[e^{βf}], and any other q falls short by exactly KL(q‖q*).

At the default β = 4 and δ = 0.3, q falls short of log Z = 1.5410 by 0.162245, and KL(q‖q*) is the same 0.162245. Slide δ to 0: J(q) reaches log Z and the gap closes. Slide β to 12: q* puts 0.980 of its mass on the taller bump and E_q*[f] climbs to 0.945, while at β = 0 the tilt does nothing and q* = p.

2.3Statement

Theorem 2.1 (Gibbs variational principle)

For a distribution \(p\) and a function \(f\) with \(Z = \mathbb E_p[e^{f}] \lt \infty\) and \(\mathbb E_p\big[|f|\, e^{f}\big] \lt \infty\), with the maximum over distributions \(q\) with \(\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) \lt \infty\),

\[ \log \mathbb E_p\big[e^{f}\big] = \max_{q}\, \Big\{ \mathbb E_q[f] - \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) \Big\}. \tag{2.1} \]

The maximum is attained only at the tilt \(q^*(x) = p(x)\, e^{f(x)} / Z\), and every other \(q\) falls short by exactly \(\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, q^*)\).

2.4Derivation

Since \(\log (q^*/p) = f - \log Z\),

\[ \mathbb E_q[f] - \mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p) = \mathbb E_q\Big[\log \frac{q^*}{p} + \log Z\Big] - \mathbb E_q\Big[\log \frac{q}{p}\Big] = \log Z - \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, q^*). \]

KL is nonnegative and vanishes only when \(q = q^*\). ∎

Read as convex duality, (2.1) says that \(f \mapsto \log \mathbb E_p[e^f]\) is the Legendre transform of \(q \mapsto \mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p)\). Both are convex and lower semicontinuous, so by the Fenchel-Moreau theorem the transform also runs the other way, which is the Donsker-Varadhan formula below. Each familiar result below is (2.1) with a particular \(f\).

  • Maximum entropy. With \(p\) uniform and \(f = \lambda\, T(x)\), the tilt is the exponential family \(q^* \propto e^{\lambda T}\), the Boltzmann distribution when \(T\) is minus an energy. The multiplier \(\lambda\) is the dual variable of the constraint \(\mathbb E[T] = t\).
  • KL-regularized RL. Maximizing \(\mathbb E_\pi[r] - \beta\, \mathrm{KL}(\pi\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}})\) is (2.1) with \(f = r/\beta\), so \(\pi^* \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}\, e^{r/\beta}\). Inverting, \(r = \beta \log (\pi^*/\pi_{\text{ref}}) + \beta \log Z\), which is DPO's implicit reward.
  • Bayes. With \(f(x) = \log p(y \mid x)\), the tilt of the prior is the posterior, the maximum is \(\log p(y)\), and the objective is the ELBO.
  • Temperature. Replacing \(f\) by \(f/\tau\) and multiplying by \(\tau\), the value tends to \(\operatorname{ess\,sup}_p f\), the largest value of \(f\) that \(p\) can produce, as \(\tau \to 0\). Log-sum-exp becomes max, the forward algorithm becomes Viterbi, and soft Bellman backups become hard ones.
  • Estimating KL. The dual statement \(\mathrm{KL}(p\,\|\,q) = \sup_T \{\mathbb E_p[T] - \log \mathbb E_q[e^{T}]\}\) (Donsker-Varadhan) is attained at \(T = \log (dp/dq)\), and MINE, a neural estimator of mutual information, maximizes it.

2.5Figures

Figure 2.2The tilt is a tangent line

A(β) = log E_p[e^{βf}] is convex, every distribution q gives the line β·E_q[f] − KL(q‖p) under it by (2.1), and the tilt q_β₀ ∝ p·e^{β₀f} gives the line that touches it at β₀, with slope E_q_β₀[f] and intercept −KL(q_β₀‖p).

At the default β₀ = 1.2 the tangent's slope by finite difference is 0.571489, and the tilt's mean reward computed directly is the same 0.571489. The tangent meets the A axis at −0.044586, which is −KL(q_β₀‖p) computed directly. The 20 random lines stay under the curve, the closest by 0.0146. Slide β₀ to 4: the slope climbs to 0.715304, the intercept falls to −0.404999, and q_β₀ piles onto the high-reward answers. At β₀ = 0 the tangent passes through the origin with slope E_p[f] = 0.496656, because q_0 = p.

Figure 2.3One dial from shortest path to sum over paths

The soft-min recursion V(cell) = c(cell) − τ·log Σ_next e^{−V(next)/τ} computes −τ·log Σ_paths e^{−cost/τ}, the tilt over all 924 paths, so it is the shortest path (Dijkstra, Viterbi) as τ → 0 and the forward algorithm at τ = 1.

At τ = 1 the recursion and the sum over all 924 paths both give 37.1698, inside 31.17 ≤ V_τ ≤ 38, and the Gibbs law spreads over 6.5 effective paths. Slide τ down to 0.02: the shading collapses onto the hard path and V_τ = 38.0000, the shortest-path cost. Slide τ up to 5: 422.9 effective paths and V_τ = 18.8822. Soft Q-learning runs this recursion at a fixed τ, and attention weights its keys by the same Gibbs rule.

Figure 2.4The same duality, read backward

KL(p‖q) = sup over T of E_p[T] − log E_q[e^T], and a critic T falls short by exactly KL(p‖q·e^T/Z), so the bound touches the true KL when T = log dp/dq up to a constant.

At a = 0.8 and b = 0 the bound is 0.48000, short of KL(p‖q) = 0.6017 by 0.12167, the same number as KL(p‖q·e^T/Z) on a grid. Slide a to 1: the best linear critic still misses by 0.1017, because log dp/dq is quadratic. Set a = 2.04 and b = −0.52: the critic lies on log dp/dq and the bound reaches 0.60167, short by 4e−8. MINE trains a neural T on this bound.

2.6Four ways to see it

The tilt is a statement about convex functions, a statement about Bayes' rule, a statement about heat, and a statement about rare events. All four are (2.1).

  1. 1Convex dualityoptimization

    Let \(A(\beta) = \log \mathbb E_p[e^{\beta f}]\). Every distribution \(q\) gives a line \(\beta \mapsto \beta\, \mathbb E_q[f] - \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p)\) that stays below \(A\), by (2.1) applied to \(\beta f\). The tilt \(q_\beta\) gives the line that touches \(A\) at \(\beta\): its slope is \(\mathbb E_{q_\beta}[f]\) and its intercept is \(-\mathrm{KL}(q_\beta \,\|\, p)\), so a convex curve is the upper envelope of its tangents (Figure 2.2).

  2. 1 → 2Put \(\beta = 1\) and \(f(x) = \log p(y \mid x)\) for an observation \(y\). Then \(Z = \int p(x)\, p(y \mid x)\, dx = p(y)\), the tilt \(p(x)\, p(y \mid x)/p(y)\) is the posterior, and (2.1) reads

    \[ \log p(y) = \max_q \Big\{ \mathbb E_q[\log p(y \mid x)] - \mathrm{KL}\big(q \,\|\, p\big) \Big\}. \]

  3. 2Bayes and the ELBOstatistics and machine learning

    The bracket is the evidence lower bound. Maximizing it over a family of \(q\) is variational inference, the gap is \(\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, \text{posterior})\), and a VAE maximizes it over an encoder and a decoder at once.

  4. 1 → 3Put \(p\) uniform on \(N\) states and \(f = -E/T\) for an energy \(E\) and a temperature \(T\). Then \(\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) = \log N - H(q)\) and \(\mathbb E_p[e^f] = Z/N\) with \(Z = \sum_x e^{-E(x)/T}\). Multiplying (2.1) by \(-T\),

    \[ -T \log Z = \min_q \Big\{ \mathbb E_q[E] - T\, H(q) \Big\}. \]

  5. 3Free energyphysics

    The bracket is the Helmholtz free energy \(U - TS\), and the Boltzmann distribution \(e^{-E/T}/Z\) minimizes it. A system in contact with a heat bath trades energy against entropy at the rate the temperature sets, and \(-T\log Z\) is the value of that trade.

  6. 1 → 4Draw \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) from \(p\). By Sanov's theorem their empirical distribution lands near \(q\) with probability about \(e^{-n\, \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p)}\). Given the rare event that the sample mean of \(f\) is near \(a \gt \mathbb E_p f\), it lands near the \(q\) with \(\mathbb E_q f = a\) that is closest to \(p\) in KL. A multiplier \(\lambda\) for the constraint gives \(q \propto p\, e^{\lambda f}\), and

    \[ -\frac1n \log P\Big(\tfrac1n \textstyle\sum_i f(X_i) \approx a\Big) \to \min_{\mathbb E_q f = a} \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) = \sup_\lambda \big\{ \lambda a - A(\lambda) \big\}. \]

  7. 4Gibbs conditioningprobability

    Condition many independent samples on a rare average, and each one looks like a draw from the tilt. The cost of the rare event is the Legendre transform of \(A\) (Cramér's theorem). The tilt appears for this reason in large deviations, in importance sampling for rare events, and in the proof of Hoeffding's inequality (Appendix A.6).

2.7Where it breaks and what is open

The tilt needs \(Z = \mathbb E_p[e^f] \lt \infty\). When \(f\) grows faster than the tails of \(p\) fall, there is no tilt: for \(p = \mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(f = \beta x^2/2\), \(Z = (1 - \beta)^{-1/2}\) for \(\beta \lt 1\) and \(Z = \infty\) for \(\beta \ge 1\). A Monte Carlo estimate of \(\log Z\) from samples of \(p\) always returns a finite number. The weights \(e^f\) have infinite variance from \(\beta = \tfrac12\), since \(\mathbb E_p[e^{2f}] = \infty\) there, so they pile onto a few samples in the tail and the estimate is wrong well before \(\beta = 1\) (Figure 2.5). A milder form of the same failure sits under reward overoptimization: a learned reward that is too large where the reference has little mass drags the tilt there, and the true reward falls as the KL from the reference grows (Gao, Schulman, and Hilton).

Figure 2.5An infinite normalizer, estimated as a finite one

When f grows faster than p's tails fall, E_p[e^f] is infinite and there is no tilt, and a Monte Carlo estimate of log Z from draws of p still reports a finite number.

At the default β = 0.8 the exact log Z is 0.8047 and the estimate from 1000 draws reads 0.7127, short by 0.0920, and the self-normalized weights have an effective sample size of 143.2 of 1000. The draws stop at |x| = 3.38, and the tilt N(0, 5) still has mass beyond. The gap opens before Z diverges because the weights have infinite variance from β = ½ on, where E_p[e^{2f}] = ∞. Slide β to 0.95: the gap grows to 0.4937 and the effective sample size falls to 56.7. Past β = 1 the true log Z is infinite and no tilt exists, and the estimate still reads 1.1215 at β = 1 and 2.0659 at β = 1.3.

  1. Choosing \(\beta\) when the reward is learned. The tilt's KL from the reference is a known function of \(\beta\) (Derivation 2.2), and along that curve the true reward rises and then falls. Predicting the turning point from the reward model's uncertainty, for example with earlier checkpoints as references, is open.
  2. Estimating large information from samples. Any lower bound on mutual information computed from \(n\) samples without assumptions on the distribution, Donsker-Varadhan's included, stays below about \(\log n\) (McAllester and Stratos). Pairwise information between tokens is small enough to stay under this ceiling. Estimating large information, such as that between a prompt and a long response, is open.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 2.1The tilt from a Lagrange multiplier

    Maximize \(\mathbb E_q[f] - \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p)\) over densities \(q\) with \(\int q = 1\) using a multiplier for the constraint (Appendix A.5), and recover the tilt and the value \(\log Z\).

    Solution

    The Lagrangian is \(\int q f - \int q \log(q/p) + \lambda(\int q - 1)\). Setting its derivative in \(q(x)\) to zero gives \(f(x) - \log(q(x)/p(x)) - 1 + \lambda = 0\), so \(q = p\, e^{f}\, e^{\lambda - 1}\), and normalizing gives \(e^{1 - \lambda} = Z\). The objective is concave in \(q\), so this is the maximum, and its value is \(\mathbb E_q[f] - \mathbb E_q[f - \log Z] = \log Z\).

  2. Derivation 2.2The tangent of \(\log Z\)

    Let \(A(\beta) = \log \mathbb E_p[e^{\beta f}]\) and \(q_\beta \propto p\, e^{\beta f}\). Show \(A'(\beta) = \mathbb E_{q_\beta}[f]\), \(A''(\beta) = \mathrm{Var}_{q_\beta}(f) \ge 0\), and \(\mathrm{KL}(q_\beta \,\|\, p) = \beta A'(\beta) - A(\beta)\). Read the last identity off the tangent line of \(A\) at \(\beta\).

    Solution

    \(A'(\beta) = \mathbb E_p[f e^{\beta f}] / \mathbb E_p[e^{\beta f}] = \mathbb E_{q_\beta}[f]\), and differentiating again gives \(\mathbb E_{q_\beta}[f^2] - (\mathbb E_{q_\beta} f)^2\). Since \(\log(q_\beta/p) = \beta f - A(\beta)\), \(\mathrm{KL}(q_\beta \,\|\, p) = \beta\, \mathbb E_{q_\beta} f - A(\beta) = \beta A'(\beta) - A(\beta)\).

    The tangent at \(\beta\) is \(b \mapsto A(\beta) + A'(\beta)(b - \beta)\). At \(b = 0\) it equals \(A(\beta) - \beta A'(\beta) = -\mathrm{KL}(q_\beta \,\|\, p)\).

Chapter 3

Change of measure

The core of measure theory

An expectation under one distribution equals an expectation under another, weighted by the ratio of their densities. On paths that ratio is Girsanov's, its cost is the energy of the drift that turns one process into the other, and the best drift for a terminal reward is the gradient of \(\log h\), a log-probability when the reward is an indicator. Control becomes inference.

Uses Chapter 2 and Appendix A.1 and A.3.

3.1Motivation

Some expectations are hard to compute under the distribution that defines them: the probability of a rare event, the price of an option whose real-world drift nobody knows, the value of a new policy estimated from data an old one collected. Sampling from the defining distribution wastes almost every sample, or cannot be done at all. A change of measure moves the expectation to a distribution that is easy to sample or easy to know, and pays with a weight, the density ratio. On paths that weight is a drift, which made pricing, conditioning, and control one computation.

3.2Intuition

Weighting paths by how likely they are under another law is the same as pushing them with a drift, with the same noise.

Figure 3.1Conditioning is a drift

Conditioning Brownian motion on landing in a window A adds the drift ∂x log h, with h(t, x) = P(B₁ ∈ A | B_t = x), and the energy E[½∫u² dt] that drift spends is the KL of the conditioned paths from the free ones, −log P(A).

At the default window [1, 1.5], P(A) = 0.0918: 14 of 200 free paths land in it, and 99.9% of 800 steered paths do. The energy the controller spends equals the surprise of the event: the steered paths spend ½∫u² dt = 2.43 ± 0.08 on average, against −log P(A) = 2.388. Slide c to 2.5 and w to 0.1: the surprise rises to 6.344 and the energy to 6.41 ± 0.13, and 98.8% of steered paths still land.

3.3Statement

Theorem 3.1 (change of measure)

If \(p\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(q\), then for every integrable \(g\)

\[ \mathbb E_p[g] = \mathbb E_q\Big[g \cdot \frac{dp}{dq}\Big]. \tag{3.1} \]

Theorem 3.2 (Girsanov, in KL form)

Let \(P\) be the law of \(dX_t = b_t\, dt + \sigma\, dW_t\) and \(Q\) the law of \(dX_t = \sigma\, dW_t\) on \([0, T]\), from the same start, where the drift \(b_t = b(t, X_{[0, t]})\) depends only on the path so far and \(\mathbb E_P \int_0^T |b_t|^2\, dt \lt \infty\). Then

\[ \log \frac{dP}{dQ} = \int_0^T \frac{b_t}{\sigma^2}\, dX_t - \frac12 \int_0^T \frac{|b_t|^2}{\sigma^2}\, dt, \qquad \mathrm{KL}(P \,\|\, Q) = \frac12\, \mathbb E_P \int_0^T \frac{|b_t|^2}{\sigma^2}\, dt. \tag{3.2} \]

Theorem 3.3 (Doob's h-transform and Cole-Hopf)

Under \(dX_t = dW_t\), let \(h(t, x) = \mathbb E\big[e^{r(X_T)} \mid X_t = x\big]\). Tilting the path measure by \(e^{r(X_T)}\) gives the process \(dX_t = \nabla \log h(t, X_t)\, dt + dW_t\), and its drift solves the control problem

\[ \min_u\; \mathbb E\Big[\tfrac12 \int_0^T |u_t|^2\, dt - r(X_T)\Big] \quad \text{for } dX_t = u_t\, dt + dW_t, \quad \text{with value } -\log h(0, x_0). \tag{3.3} \]

3.4Derivation

(3.1). \(\int g\, p = \int g\, \frac{p}{q}\, q\).

(3.2). Discretize time with step \(h\). Under \(P\) an increment is \(\mathcal N(b\,h, \sigma^2 h)\) and under \(Q\) it is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 h)\), so one step contributes \((b\,\Delta X - \tfrac12 b^2 h)/\sigma^2\) to the log ratio. Summing gives the integrals. Under \(P\), \(\Delta X = b\,h + \sigma\,\Delta W\) and the \(\Delta W\) terms have mean zero, so the expected log ratio is \(\sum \tfrac12 b^2 h / \sigma^2\).

(3.3). The function \(h\) solves the backward Kolmogorov equation \(\partial_t h + \tfrac12 \Delta h = 0\) with \(h(T, x) = e^{r(x)}\). Substituting \(V = -\log h\) gives \(\partial_t V + \tfrac12 \Delta V - \tfrac12 |\nabla V|^2 = 0\), and since \(\min_u \{ u \cdot \nabla V + \tfrac12 |u|^2 \} = -\tfrac12 |\nabla V|^2\) at \(u = -\nabla V\), this is the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation of (3.3) with terminal cost \(-r\). The optimal control is \(u = -\nabla V = \nabla \log h\), and the optimal cost is \(V(0, x_0) = -\log h(0, x_0)\). ∎

Two readings. By (3.2) the controller's energy \(\tfrac12 \mathbb E \int |u|^2\) is the KL of the controlled path measure from the free one, so (3.3) is Theorem 2.1 on path space: the free process tilted by \(e^{r(X_T)}\). Conditioning on an event \(A\) is the case \(r = \log \mathbf 1_A\), where the energy spent equals the surprise, \(-\log P(A)\).

3.5Figures

Figure 3.2A reward on the endpoint is a drift on the path

Tilting Brownian motion by a terminal reward, dQ/dP = exp(r(X₁))/Z, is the drift ∂x log h with h(t, x) = E[exp(r(X₁)) | X_t = x], and its KL from the free process is both E_Q[½∫u² dt] and E_Q[r(X₁)] − log Z.

At the defaults (the right bump at 2 with weight 0.6), log Z = −2.372. The steered paths spend ½∫u² dt = 1.161 ± 0.027, their endpoints give E_Q[r] − log Z = 1.175, and the exact KL is 1.162. Of the 1,000 endpoints, 40.9% land right of 0.25, against 40.8% under the exact tilt. Slide the bump to 3 and its weight to 0.95: the KL grows to 2.16. Tilting the endpoint distribution is a drift change, which is what reward fine-tuning of a diffusion model learns (adjoint matching).

3.6Four ways to see it

A change of measure reweights samples, adds a drift to a process, conditions on an event, and prices an asset. On paths these are one operation.

  1. 1Reweightingstatistics

    Sample from \(q\), weight each sample by \(dp/dq\), and averages estimate expectations under \(p\) (3.1). Statisticians call it importance sampling, and off-policy RL and PPO's ratio apply it to actions.

  2. 1 → 2On paths the weight is Girsanov's (3.2). Weighting the paths of the driftless process \(Q\) by \(\exp\big(\int b/\sigma^2\, dX - \tfrac12 \int |b|^2/\sigma^2\, dt\big)\) gives the same expectations as sampling the process with drift \(b\). Under the reweighted measure, \(W_t - \int_0^t b_s/\sigma\, ds\) is a Brownian motion, so the same paths read as noise plus the drift \(b\).

  3. 2A driftstochastic calculus

    Reweighting paths and adding a drift are the same act. The weight's log is linear in the path, and its expected value under the drifted process is the drift's energy, so the KL between the two processes is the energy a controller spends.

  4. 2 → 3Conditioning on \(X_T \in A\) reweights paths by \(\mathbf 1_A(X_T)/P(A)\). Its expectation given the path up to \(t\) is \(h(t, X_t)/h(0, x_0)\) with \(h(t, x) = P(X_T \in A \mid X_t = x)\). With \(\sigma = 1\), Itô's lemma and the backward equation \(\partial_t h + \tfrac12\Delta h = 0\) (Appendix A.1) give

    \[ d \log h(t, X_t) = \nabla \log h \cdot dX_t - \tfrac12\, |\nabla \log h|^2\, dt, \]

    the Girsanov exponent (3.2) with \(b = \nabla\log h\). Conditioning is the drift \(\nabla \log h\).

  5. 3Conditioningprobability

    Doob's h-transform turns a process conditioned on its future into a process with an extra drift (Figure 3.1). A terminal reward \(e^{r(X_T)}\) in place of an indicator gives Theorem 3.3, and guidance in diffusion models is the same drift with \(h(t, x) = p(y \mid X_t = x)\).

  6. 1 → 4Under the real-world measure a stock follows \(dS = \mu S\, dt + \sigma S\, dW\). Reweight by \(Z_T = e^{-\theta W_T - \theta^2 T/2}\) with \(\theta = (\mu - r)/\sigma\). By Girsanov, \(\tilde W_t = W_t + \theta t\) is a Brownian motion under the new measure \(Q\), and

    \[ dS = \mu S\, dt + \sigma S\, (d\tilde W - \theta\, dt) = r S\, dt + \sigma S\, d\tilde W. \]

  7. 4Pricingfinance

    Under \(Q\) every asset grows at the risk-free rate on average, and the price of a payoff \(H\) at time \(T\) is \(e^{-rT}\mathbb E_Q[H] = \mathbb E_P[e^{-rT} Z_T H]\). The state-price density \(e^{-rT} Z_T\) is the Radon-Nikodym weight, and Black-Scholes is this expectation for a call.

3.7Where it breaks and what is open

Equation (3.1) is exact whenever \(p\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(q\), and the estimator built on it is not. Importance sampling needs at least about \(e^{\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q)}\) samples before its averages settle, and that many suffice only when the log weights concentrate (Chatterjee and Diaconis). In \(d\) dimensions small mismatches add up: shifting each coordinate of a standard Gaussian by \(a\) costs \(\mathrm{KL} = d a^2/2\), and the effective sample size falls like \(n e^{-d a^2}\). Past the point where it should drop below one sample, the measured effective sample size stays high while the weighted averages are wrong, so the diagnostic hides its own failure (Figure 3.3). On paths, (3.2) makes that KL the energy of the missing drift, so reweighting paths from a poor controller costs samples exponential in the energy it failed to supply. Sampling methods learn the control for this reason instead of reweighting.

Figure 3.3Importance weights collapse with dimension

When p and q differ by a shift of a in each of d coordinates, KL(p‖q) = d a²/2 grows with d, the sample size importance sampling needs grows like e^KL, and the weights of a fixed sample pile onto a few draws.

Slide d up at a = 0.2. At the default d = 50, KL(p‖q) = 1: the measured effective sample size (ESS) is 322 of 2,000 against the large-n value of 271, the largest weight holds 1.6% of the total, and the mean weight is 0.960 where (3.1) promises 1. At d = 200 the large-n ESS is 0.671 draws, while the measured ESS still reads 49.1 and the mean weight falls to 0.486. The draws never reach the rare large weights that set E_q[w²], so the measured ESS overstates the sample. Push a to 0.5 as well: the largest weight holds 49.4% of the total, the mean weight is 2.05e−5, the estimate of a = 0.5 comes out 0.200, and e^KL = 7.20e10 draws are needed against the 2,000 drawn.

  1. Learning the control so the weights stay near 1. ASBS and adjoint matching learn a drift whose paths need almost no reweighting. A sampler that uses a learned \(-Q\) as its energy will chase that function's errors. How the variance of the weights grows from Pendulum to Hopper, and whether the bridge from the behavior policy keeps it small, is open.
  2. Twisted sampling for language. Twisted sequential Monte Carlo learns h-functions, called twists, for language models (Zhao et al.), which is Theorem 3.3 on token sequences. Using it to sample prompts conditioned on a target response, the task of Diffusion Investigator Agents, is open.
  3. Guidance without a trained classifier. Training-free guidance replaces \(h(t, x) = \mathbb E[p(y \mid X_0) \mid X_t = x]\) by \(p(y \mid \mathbb E[X_0 \mid X_t = x])\), moving the expectation inside. How large the resulting error is, and when it matters for jailbreak search, is open.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 3.1Girsanov's KL for a constant drift

    For a constant drift \(b\) on \([0, T]\) with \(N\) steps of size \(h\), compute the KL between the laws of the increments under \(P\) and \(Q\), and take \(N \to \infty\). Compare with the KL between the endpoint laws \(\mathcal N(bT, \sigma^2 T)\) and \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 T)\), and explain why they agree.

    Solution

    The increments are independent, so the path KL is \(N\) times \(\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathcal N(bh, \sigma^2 h) \,\|\, \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 h)\big) = \frac{b^2 h^2}{2\sigma^2 h}\), which totals \(\frac{b^2 T}{2 \sigma^2}\) for every \(N\). The endpoint KL is \(\frac{(bT)^2}{2\sigma^2 T} = \frac{b^2 T}{2\sigma^2}\), the same.

    Under both laws the path given its endpoint is the same Brownian bridge, so the endpoint carries all the information that separates them. In general the data-processing inequality makes the path KL at least the endpoint KL, with equality exactly when the paths given their endpoint have the same law under both measures. The h-transform drifts of Theorem 3.3 have this property, and a drift that varies in time without depending on the endpoint does not.

  2. Derivation 3.2The Brownian bridge as an h-transform

    Condition Brownian motion started at 0 to be at \(y\) at time \(T\). Using \(h(t, x) = p_{T-t}(y - x)\), with \(p_s\) the \(\mathcal N(0, s)\) density, derive the drift of the conditioned process and check that it pulls the path to \(y\).

    Solution

    \(\log h(t, x) = -\frac{(y - x)^2}{2(T - t)} + \text{const}\), so \(\nabla\log h = \frac{y - x}{T - t}\) and \(dX_t = \frac{y - X_t}{T - t}\, dt + dW_t\).

    The pull grows without bound as \(t \to T\). Solving the linear equation gives mean \(\frac{t}{T} y\) and variance \(\frac{t(T - t)}{T}\), which vanishes at \(t = T\), so the path ends at \(y\).

Chapter 4

Fixed points

Contraction, from analysis

A map on a complete space that shrinks every distance by a fixed factor \(\gamma \lt 1\) has exactly one fixed point, and iterating the map reaches it geometrically fast. A step-by-step computation is the fixed point of a map on its whole sequence, so it can be solved in parallel rounds.

Uses Chapter 1.

4.1Motivation

Many quantities are defined by an equation they must satisfy instead of a formula: the value of a policy, the stationary distribution of a chain, the importance of a web page, the trajectory of an ODE. Solving such an equation directly means inverting a large system or running a long sequential loop. Contraction gives a third way: apply the defining map again and again from any start, and the error shrinks by a fixed factor each time. The same view turns a sequential computation into a map on its whole trajectory, which can be iterated in parallel.

PAPERA document that moved capital

The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine

Rank a page by the ranks of the pages that link to it, and let the link structure of the web do the judging.

Sergey Brin and Lawrence Page, 1998 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

PageRank was the core of Google's search, which outranked keyword matching and built the company.

The link to this chapter: the paper defines \(\mathrm{PR}(A) = (1 - d) + d \sum_i \mathrm{PR}(T_i)/C(T_i)\) with \(d = 0.85\) and computes it by "a simple iterative algorithm" (Section 2.1.1). Each iteration is a contraction with factor \(d\), so the error shrinks by 0.85 per sweep (Theorem 4.1, and the PageRank exercise). As printed, with \(1 - d\) where \((1 - d)/N\) would make the ranks sum to one, they sum to the number of pages.

4.2Intuition

A map that shrinks every distance by a fixed factor, applied again and again, walks every starting point into its one fixed point.

Figure 4.1A cobweb into the fixed point

Iterating a map whose slope at its fixed point is under 1 in size walks a cobweb into the fixed point, and near it the error shrinks by that slope at every step.

The map is T(x) = 2 + s·sin(x − 2). Its slope at x* = 2 is s, and its Lipschitz constant on the whole line is γ = |s|, so (4.1) applies whenever |s| < 1. At the default s = 0.6 the cobweb climbs a staircase into x*, the error ratio over the last four steps is 0.6000, equal to |T′(x*)|, and at k = 10 the error is 5.5e−3 under Banach's bound of 1.5e−2. Slide s to −0.6: the staircase becomes a spiral with the same ratio. At s = 0.9 the ratio is 0.8984, and the bound loosens to 2.44 against an actual error of 0.229. Past 1 in size the fixed point repels: at s = 1.3 the cobweb settles on another fixed point at 0.7785, and at s = −1.3 on a 2-cycle between 0.7785 and 3.2215.

4.3Statement

Theorem 4.1 (Banach)

If \(T\) maps a complete metric space to itself and \(d(Tx, Ty) \le \gamma\, d(x, y)\) with \(\gamma \lt 1\), then \(T\) has exactly one fixed point \(x^*\), and the iterates \(x_{k+1} = T x_k\) satisfy

\[ d(x_k, x^*) \le \frac{\gamma^k}{1 - \gamma}\, d(x_1, x_0). \tag{4.1} \]

Theorem 4.2 (the Bellman operator contracts)

\[ (\mathcal T V)(s) = \max_a \Big[ r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\, V(s') \Big] \quad\text{satisfies}\quad \|\mathcal T V - \mathcal T W\|_\infty \le \gamma\, \|V - W\|_\infty. \tag{4.2} \]

Proposition 4.3 (a sequence, solved in parallel)

The Euler trajectory \(x_{i+1} = x_i + h\, f(x_i)\), \(i \lt N\), is the fixed point of the map \(\Phi(x)_i = x_0 + h \sum_{j \lt i} f(x_j)\) on the whole sequence. Iterating \(\Phi\) makes the first \(k\) steps exact after \(k\) rounds. If \(f\) has Lipschitz constant \(L\) and \(T = Nh\), the error after \(k\) rounds is at most

\[ \frac{(L T)^k}{k!}\, \max_i |e_{0, i}|. \tag{4.3} \]

4.4Derivation

(4.1). By induction \(d(x_{k+1}, x_k) \le \gamma^k d(x_1, x_0)\), so for \(m \gt k\) the triangle inequality and a geometric sum give \(d(x_m, x_k) \le \frac{\gamma^k}{1-\gamma} d(x_1, x_0)\). The sequence is Cauchy, its limit \(x^*\) satisfies \(T x^* = x^*\) because \(T\) is continuous, and letting \(m \to \infty\) gives (4.1). Two fixed points would satisfy \(d(x^*, y^*) = d(Tx^*, Ty^*) \le \gamma\, d(x^*, y^*)\), so they coincide.

(4.2). For any two functions of the action, and because the weights \(P(s' \mid s, a)\) sum to one,

\[ \big|\max_a f(a) - \max_a g(a)\big| \le \max_a |f(a) - g(a)|, \qquad \Big|\gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\,(V - W)(s')\Big| \le \gamma\, \|V - W\|_\infty. \]

Together they give (4.2).

(4.3). Entry \(i\) of \(\Phi^k(x)\) depends only on entries before it, and entry 0 is given, so exactness spreads one entry per round. The error \(e_{k, i} = |x^{(k)}_i - x_i|\) after \(k\) rounds obeys \(e_{k+1, i} \le hL \sum_{j \lt i} e_{k, j}\). Induction with \(\sum_{j \lt i} \binom{j}{k} = \binom{i}{k+1}\) gives \(e_{k, i} \le (hL)^k \binom{i}{k} \max_j e_{0, j} \le \frac{(L\, ih)^k}{k!} \max_j e_{0, j}\), and \(ih \le T\). ∎

Linear recurrences. When each step is affine, \(x_{i+1} = a_i x_i + b_i\), composing two steps gives another affine step, \((a_1, b_1)\) then \((a_2, b_2)\) is \((a_1 a_2,\; a_2 b_1 + b_2)\), and this composition is associative. A prefix scan therefore computes every \(x_i\) in \(\log_2 N\) parallel rounds with no iteration at all, and Newton's method reduces a nonlinear recurrence to a few such scans.

4.5Figures

Figure 4.2Value iteration contracts by γ

The Bellman backup is a γ-contraction in the max norm, so value iteration from any start reaches the one fixed point V* with ‖V_k − V*‖∞ ≤ γ^k ‖V_0 − V*‖∞.

Every move costs 0.04, slips sideways with probability 0.2, and the goal pays +1 and ends the episode. Press play: value spreads out from the goal one cell per sweep. At γ = 0.9 the largest measured ratio is 0.880 and the error reaches 1e−6 in 37 sweeps, where γ^k alone guarantees it by sweep 131. Slide γ to 0.99: the ratio rises to 0.981, still below γ, and 44 sweeps suffice against a guarantee of 1,369. For the first 13 sweeps, while value spreads, the error shrinks by 0.85 to 0.88 per sweep at γ = 0.9. Once value reaches every cell, it shrinks by about 0.55.

Figure 4.3A sampler's steps, solved in parallel rounds

N Euler steps of an ODE are the fixed point of a map on the whole trajectory, x_i = x_0 + h·Σ f(x_j, t_j) over j < i, so Picard rounds that update all N states at once reach the sequential answer in far fewer than N rounds when the drift is smooth.

Press play: after round k the first k steps are exact, yet the whole trajectory settles long before k reaches N. At N = 100 the largest change drops below 1e−4 in 13 rounds (7.7 steps per round), and the error is 2.7 at the default k = 3, 0.26 at k = 6, and 3.4e−6 at k = 13. Slide N from 10 to 400: the rounds go from 9 to 13 while the sequential steps grow 40-fold, so each round does the work of 30.8 steps at N = 400. This is the mechanism behind parallel sampling of diffusion models (ParaDiGMS).

Figure 4.4A linear recurrence in log₂ T rounds

Each step h ↦ a(t)·h + b(t) is an affine map, and composing affine maps is associative, so a prefix scan computes every h(t) of h(t) = a(t)·h(t−1) + b(t) in log₂ T parallel rounds.

Slide r from 0 to 4 at T = 16: the positions that match the loop double each round, 1, 2, 4, 8, then all 16, and the final scan differs from the loop by 4.4e−16. Switch T to 32: one more round, five in all, against 32 sequential steps. Mamba trains its selective recurrence with this scan, and linear attention is the case a = 1.

4.6Four ways to see it

A fixed point is where a cobweb ends, where gradient descent stops, where a parallel solver agrees with a sequential one, and where no player wants to move. The first three use contraction, and the fourth shows what is left without it.

  1. 1A contractionanalysis

    Iterate a map whose slope is below 1 in size and the iterates walk a cobweb into the fixed point, shrinking the error by the slope each step (Theorem 4.1, Figure 4.1). Value iteration is this picture with the max norm (Theorem 4.2).

  2. 1 → 2Gradient descent is the map \(T(x) = x - \eta \nabla f(x)\), whose fixed points are the stationary points of \(f\). Its Jacobian is \(I - \eta \nabla^2 f\), so if \(\mu I \preceq \nabla^2 f \preceq L I\),

    \[ \|T x - T y\| \le \max\big(|1 - \eta\mu|,\, |1 - \eta L|\big)\, \|x - y\|, \]

    a contraction for \(0 \lt \eta \lt 2/L\), with the smallest factor \((\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)\), \(\kappa = L/\mu\), at \(\eta = 2/(\mu + L)\).

  3. 2Gradient descentoptimization

    Convergence rates of first-order methods are contraction factors, and the condition number \(\kappa\) sets them. Chapter 9 keeps the same argument when \(f\) is not convex, with \(f\) itself as the quantity that shrinks.

  4. 1 → 3The whole-trajectory map of Proposition 4.3 is no contraction in the max norm, and it becomes one in a weighted norm. With \(\|e\|_\lambda = \max_i e^{-\lambda i h} |e_i|\),

    \[ e^{-\lambda i h}\, |\Phi(x)_i - \Phi(y)_i| \le e^{-\lambda i h}\, hL \sum_{j \lt i} e^{\lambda j h}\, \|x - y\|_\lambda \le \frac{hL}{e^{\lambda h} - 1}\, \|x - y\|_\lambda \le \frac{L}{\lambda}\, \|x - y\|_\lambda, \]

    so \(\lambda = 2L\) gives the factor \(\tfrac12\).

  5. 3A sequence solved in parallelnumerical analysis

    A sequential computation is the fixed point of a map on its whole trajectory, and every entry of an iterate can be computed at once (Figure 4.3). Jacobi decoding of language models, ParaDiGMS for diffusion, and DEER for recurrent networks iterate this map, and a prefix scan solves the affine case exactly (Figure 4.4).

  6. 1 → 4Drop contraction and keep only continuity on a compact convex set. Brouwer's theorem still gives a fixed point, with no uniqueness and no promise that iteration finds it. Nash applied it to the map that moves each player's mixed strategy \(\sigma_i\) toward the pure strategies \(k\) that beat it, with gains \(g_{ik} = \max\big(0,\, u_i(k, \sigma_{-i}) - u_i(\sigma)\big)\):

    \[ \sigma_{ik} \mapsto \frac{\sigma_{ik} + g_{ik}}{1 + \sum_{k'} g_{ik'}}. \]

    The map is continuous on a product of simplices, and its fixed points are exactly the equilibria.

  7. 4Equilibriumeconomics

    Every finite game has an equilibrium in mixed strategies (Nash, by Brouwer's theorem), and an exchange economy under mild conditions has prices that clear every market (Arrow and Debreu, through an existence theorem for generalized games that rests on a fixed-point theorem). Existence comes without an algorithm: iterating best responses can cycle (Chapter 8).

4.7Where it breaks and what is open

Proposition 4.3 bounds the error after \(k\) rounds by \((LT)^k/k!\), and the bound falls below a tolerance only once \(k\) passes about \(e \cdot LT\). A stiff drift has a large \(L\), and once \(LT\) is comparable to the number of steps \(N\), the rounds needed approach \(N\) and parallel rounds buy nothing over sequential steps (Figure 4.5). Chaotic dynamics fail the same way, because errors grow along the trajectory. Newton's method on the whole trajectory converges in far fewer rounds (DEER), at the price of a Jacobian per step and an instability that damping repairs (Gonzalez et al.).

Figure 4.5A stiff drift needs as many rounds as steps

Picard rounds on a whole trajectory shrink the error like (LT)^k/k!, which starts to fall only once k passes LT, so a stiff drift with a large L needs nearly as many rounds as there are sequential steps, and the parallel speedup disappears.

The drift has Lipschitz constant L = λ on [0, T] with T = 1, and the map is the one in Proposition 4.3. At the default λ = 4 the error first grows, to 3.87 at round 3, then falls below 1e−6 at round 17, a speedup of 3.76 over the 64 sequential steps, and (4.3) guarantees it by round 20. Slide λ to 60, still a stable Euler step with λh = 0.9375: the error peaks at 1.2e17 at round 30, the bound promises nothing before round 64, and the iterate matches the sequential trajectory only at round 64, when the exact prefix covers every step, a speedup of 1.00. At λ = 0.5, 6 rounds suffice.

  1. An acceptance rule for parallel sampling. A rule that stops where the parallel guesses disagree is closer to speculative decoding's acceptance test than to ParaDiGMS's fixed tolerance. Whether it keeps the samples' distribution exact, and how many model calls it saves on a flow-matching image model, is open. The project below measures it.
  2. Fixed points with no contraction. Equilibria of games, and the saddle points GAN training looks for, exist by Brouwer's theorem, and no known algorithm finds them fast in general: computing a Nash equilibrium of a two-player game is PPAD-complete. Which learning dynamics reach equilibrium in the games of machine learning, such as self-play and red-teaming, is open. Chapter 8 takes it up.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 4.1The Bellman contraction

    Prove (4.2). Then, with rewards in \([0, 1]\) and \(V_0 = 0\), find how many sweeps of value iteration guarantee \(\|V_k - V^*\|_\infty \le \varepsilon\).

    Solution

    For each state,

    \[ \big|\max_a F(a) - \max_a G(a)\big| \le \max_a |F(a) - G(a)|: \]

    if the left maximum is attained at \(a^*\) by \(F\), then \(\max F - \max G \le F(a^*) - G(a^*)\), and symmetrically. Apply it with \(F(a) = r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a) V(s')\) and \(G\) the same with \(W\). The rewards cancel, and \(|\gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)(V - W)(s')| \le \gamma \|V - W\|_\infty\) because the weights sum to 1.

    \(\|V^* - V_0\|_\infty \le 1/(1 - \gamma)\), so \(\|V_k - V^*\|_\infty \le \gamma^k/(1 - \gamma)\), which is at most \(\varepsilon\) once \(k \ge \log\big(1/(\varepsilon(1 - \gamma))\big) / \log(1/\gamma)\). For \(\gamma\) near 1 that is about \(\frac{1}{1 - \gamma} \log \frac{1}{\varepsilon(1 - \gamma)}\) sweeps.

  2. Derivation 4.2A scan, then Newton on the whole trajectory

    Show that composing affine steps \(x \mapsto a x + b\) is associative, and that a prefix scan computes every \(x_i\) of \(x_{i+1} = a_i x_i + b_i\) in \(\lceil \log_2 N \rceil\) rounds. Then write one Newton step for the nonlinear recurrence \(x_{i+1} = F(x_i)\) as an affine recurrence.

    Solution

    Composition is function composition, which is associative, and in coordinates \((a_1, b_1)\) then \((a_2, b_2)\) is \((a_2 a_1,\, a_2 b_1 + b_2)\). In round \(r\) every position \(i\) combines its partial result with the one \(2^r\) places earlier, so after round \(r\) position \(i\) holds the composition of the last \(\min(i, 2^{r+1})\) steps, and \(\lceil \log_2 N \rceil\) rounds cover every prefix.

    Linearize \(F\) at the current guess \(x^{(k)}\): \(x_{i+1} = F(x^{(k)}_i) + J_i\, (x_i - x^{(k)}_i)\) with \(J_i = F'(x^{(k)}_i)\). This is the affine recurrence with \(a_i = J_i\) and \(b_i = F(x^{(k)}_i) - J_i x^{(k)}_i\), solved by one scan per Newton step, as in DEER.

Chapter 5

Optimal transport

The geometry of distributions

Distributions form a space whose distance is the least cost of moving mass from one to the other. In that space the straight line between two distributions moves mass instead of fading it, diffusion is gradient descent on free energy, and adding entropy gives the Schrödinger bridge.

Uses Chapters 1, 2, and 4, and Appendix A.2, A.4, and A.5.

5.1Motivation

Comparing two distributions by how much their densities overlap fails when they barely overlap: KL is infinite and total variation is maximal for two point masses a millimeter apart, so a learning signal built on either gives no gradient. Monge asked in 1781 for the cheapest way to move a pile of earth into a hole, and Kantorovich relaxed the question to plans that may split mass. The distance that results grows smoothly as one distribution slides away from another, and it turns the space of distributions into a geometric space with straight lines and gradients.

5.2Intuition

Move mass along straight lines instead of fading it out in one place and in at another, and distributions acquire distances, midpoints, and gradients.

Figure 5.1Moving mass against fading it

The straight line between two distributions in W2 moves every quantile of p₀ along the monotone map T = F₁⁻¹∘F₀, so the distance from p₀ grows exactly like t.

Slide t. The displacement curve carries p₀'s two bumps toward each other until they merge into p₁, and its W2 from p₀ is exactly t times W2(p₀, p₁) = 4.023. The mixture keeps both of p₀'s bumps and grows p₁ in place, and at t = 0.5 it sits 0.549 of the way. Each particle travels straight from its quantile in p₀ to the same quantile in p₁.

5.3Statement

Definition 5.1 (the 2-Wasserstein distance, and its dual)

\[ W_2(p, q)^2 = \min_{\pi \in \Pi(p, q)} \mathbb E_{(X, Y) \sim \pi}\, |X - Y|^2, \tag{5.1} \]

where \(\Pi(p, q)\) is the set of couplings with marginals \(p\) and \(q\). By Kantorovich duality the same number is a maximum over prices,

\[ W_2(p, q)^2 = \max_{\varphi(x) + \psi(y) \le |x - y|^2} \Big\{ \mathbb E_p[\varphi] + \mathbb E_q[\psi] \Big\}, \]

and an optimal plan moves mass only between pairs where the prices are tight, \(\varphi(x) + \psi(y) = |x - y|^2\).

Theorem 5.2 (optimal maps and straight lines)

Let \(p\) and \(q\) have finite second moments. If \(p\) has no atoms, the optimal map on the line is the monotone one, \(T = F_q^{-1} \circ F_p\). In \(\mathbb R^d\), if \(p\) has a density, the optimal map exists, is unique, and is the gradient of a convex function (Brenier). The cost is the least kinetic energy of any flow between the two (Benamou-Brenier):

\[ W_2(p, q)^2 = \min_{\rho, v} \int_0^1 \!\! \int \rho_t\, |v_t|^2\, dx\, dt \quad \text{subject to}\quad \partial_t \rho + \nabla \cdot (\rho v) = 0,\; \rho_0 = p,\; \rho_1 = q. \tag{5.2} \]

Theorem 5.3 (Jordan, Kinderlehrer, and Otto)

The Fokker-Planck equation \(\partial_t \rho = \nabla \cdot (\rho \nabla V) + \Delta \rho\) is the gradient flow in \(W_2\) of the free energy \(F(\rho) = \int V \rho + \int \rho \log \rho\), and

\[ \frac{d}{dt} F(\rho_t) = -\int \rho_t\, \big|\nabla (V + \log \rho_t)\big|^2. \tag{5.3} \]

Proposition 5.4 (entropic transport)

With the entropy \(H(P) = -\sum_{ij} P_{ij} (\log P_{ij} - 1)\), the coupling that minimizes \(\langle C, P \rangle - \varepsilon H(P)\) with given marginals has the form

\[ P_\varepsilon = \mathrm{diag}(u)\; e^{-C/\varepsilon}\; \mathrm{diag}(v), \tag{5.4} \]

and Sinkhorn's algorithm finds \(u\) and \(v\) by fixing the row sums and the column sums in turn.

5.4Derivation

Duality. For any plan and any prices that satisfy the constraint, integrating \(\varphi(x) + \psi(y) \le |x - y|^2\) against the plan gives \(\mathbb E_p\varphi + \mathbb E_q\psi \le \mathbb E_\pi |X - Y|^2\), so every price pair bounds every plan from below, with equality exactly when the plan sits on tight pairs. For finitely many points the two optima are equal by linear-programming duality (Derivation 5.2 does the bookkeeping).

Monotone maps. For \(a \lt b\) and \(c \lt d\), crossing costs more:

\[ (a - d)^2 + (b - c)^2 - (a - c)^2 - (b - d)^2 = 2(b - a)(d - c) \gt 0. \]

Uncrossing any crossing pair lowers the cost, so the optimal plan on a line is monotone.

(5.3). One step of size \(\tau\) minimizes \(F(\rho) + W_2(\rho, \rho_k)^2 / 2\tau\). Its optimality condition moves mass with velocity \(v = -\nabla \tfrac{\delta F}{\delta \rho} = -\nabla (V + \log \rho)\), and as \(\tau \to 0\) the continuity equation with this \(v\) is

\[ \partial_t \rho = \nabla \cdot (\rho \nabla V) + \nabla \cdot (\rho \nabla \log \rho) = \nabla\cdot(\rho \nabla V) + \Delta \rho. \]

Along the flow, \(\frac{d}{dt}F = \int \frac{\delta F}{\delta \rho}\, \partial_t \rho = -\int \rho\, |v|^2\).

(5.4). With multipliers \(\alpha_i\) and \(\beta_j\) for the marginal constraints, stationarity of the Lagrangian reads \(C_{ij} + \varepsilon \log P_{ij} - \alpha_i - \beta_j = 0\), so \(P_{ij} = e^{\alpha_i/\varepsilon}\, e^{-C_{ij}/\varepsilon}\, e^{\beta_j/\varepsilon}\). ∎

Links. The free energy is \(F(\rho) = \mathrm{KL}(\rho \,\|\, \pi) - \log Z\) with \(\pi \propto e^{-V}\), so diffusion comes to rest at a tilt (Chapter 2). The entropic plan (5.4) also minimizes \(\langle C, P\rangle + \varepsilon\, \mathrm{KL}(P \,\|\, p \otimes q)\) over couplings. It is the independent coupling tilted by \(e^{(f_i + g_j - C_{ij})/\varepsilon}\), where the potentials \(f\) and \(g\) restore the marginals, and Sinkhorn is a fixed-point iteration that finds them (Chapter 4). The same construction on path measures is the Schrödinger bridge.

5.5Figures

Figure 5.2Prices that certify a plan

The cheapest transport plan and the best prices φ, ψ with φ(x) + ψ(y) ≤ (x − y)² reach the same total, and the plan only uses pairs where the prices are tight.

Slide the shift or draw new points. The primal cost and the dual value agree at every setting: at the default shift of +0.30 both are 0.1535, and the largest φᵢ + ψⱼ − Cᵢⱼ is 0 up to rounding. The plan's 7 pairs are tight, and 6 more pairs are tight but unused (dashed), 13 of the 49. The faint curves extend the prices to every point as φ(x) = minⱼ (x − yⱼ)² − ψⱼ and its mirror for ψ, and they pass through every stem. Tap a source: its slacks Cᵢⱼ − φᵢ − ψⱼ are 0 at its partner and never negative, so at these prices no other target is cheaper.

Figure 5.3The geodesic as a surface

Along the W2 geodesic every quantile of p₀ rides a straight line in (x, t), so the density surface slides its bumps across, while the straight line in density space fades one bump out and the other in.

Slide t and switch the path. On the geodesic W2(p₀, ρₜ) equals t·W2(p₀, p₁) at every t, 2.011 at t = 0.5, and every quantile path projects to a straight line on the (x, t) floor. On the mixture the same readout is 2.209 at t = 0.5, off the constant-speed line, and the variance swells to 5.269 because the mixture holds mass at both ends at once. The geodesic's variance falls from p₀'s 2.214 to p₁'s 0.563 and reads 1.223 at t = 0.5. Drag to turn the surface.

Figure 5.4Diffusion as gradient descent on free energy

In the W2 geometry the Fokker-Planck equation is steepest descent on F(ρ) = ∫Vρ + T∫ρ log ρ, so F falls at exactly the rate ∫ρ|∂x(V + T log ρ)|² and comes to rest at the Boltzmann density.

Press Play or slide t. At T = 0.4 and t = 0.5 the measured dF/dt is −0.1410 and the dissipation is −0.1412, a ratio of 0.999, and F − F_min = T·KL = 0.1874. Slide T down to 0.15: the mass fills the right well quickly and then waits at the barrier, so at t = 10 the gap is still 0.088, near T·log 2 = 0.104, the gap of a density that fills one well of two.

Figure 5.5Entropic transport by Sinkhorn

Adding ε times the plan's negative entropy to the transport cost makes the optimal plan diag(u)·exp(−C/ε)·diag(v), and Sinkhorn finds u and v by fixing the row sums and the column sums in turn.

Slide ε. At the default ε = 0.05 the error shrinks by a factor of 0.733 per iteration and the plan costs 0.3744 against the exact 0.3539. Slide ε down to 0.005 and the iterations up to 400: the plan approaches the exact matching, at cost 0.3548 after 400 iterations, and the decay slows to 0.997 per iteration, leaving an error of 2.1e−3. The plan is the independent coupling tilted by exp((f ⊕ g − C)/ε), where the potentials f and g restore the marginals (the tilt), and Sinkhorn is a fixed-point iteration (the fixed point).

5.6Four ways to see it

Optimal transport has four standard pictures. Each comes with tools of its own, and each follows from the one before it in a few lines.

  1. 1A linear programoperations research

    A plan is a nonnegative matrix with row sums \(p_i\) and column sums \(q_j\), and its cost is linear in the plan. With equal weights on \(n\) points each, the optimum is a permutation, and transport is the assignment problem.

    \[ \min_{\pi \ge 0}\; \sum_{ij} \pi_{ij} C_{ij} \quad \text{subject to} \quad \textstyle\sum_j \pi_{ij} = p_i,\; \sum_i \pi_{ij} = q_j. \]

  2. 1 → 2Attach a price \(\varphi_i\) to each row constraint and \(\psi_j\) to each column constraint. Linear-programming duality gives the same optimal value from the prices, and complementary slackness says the plan moves mass only between pairs where the prices are tight: \(\pi_{ij} \gt 0\) implies \(\varphi_i + \psi_j = C_{ij}\) (Figure 5.2).

  3. 2Priceseconomics

    A shipper charges \(\varphi(x)\) to collect at \(x\) and \(\psi(y)\) to deliver at \(y\), and no customer would rather move the mass directly as long as \(\varphi(x) + \psi(y) \le c(x, y)\). The best such prices earn exactly the transport cost.

    \[ \min_{\pi \in \Pi(p, q)} \mathbb E_\pi\, c(X, Y) = \max_{\varphi(x) + \psi(y) \le c(x, y)} \Big\{ \mathbb E_p[\varphi] + \mathbb E_q[\psi] \Big\}. \]

  4. 2 → 3Take \(c = \tfrac12 |x - y|^2\) and write \(u(x) = \tfrac12|x|^2 - \varphi(x)\). At the best prices \(u\) is convex, and at a tight pair the function \(x \mapsto \varphi(x) + \psi(y) - c(x, y)\) reaches its maximum of zero, so its gradient vanishes: \(\nabla\varphi(x) = x - y\), that is, \(y = \nabla u(x)\), Brenier's map. Moving each particle at constant speed along \(x \mapsto x + t(\nabla u(x) - x)\) gives a flow whose kinetic energy is the transport cost.

  5. 3A fluidphysics

    Mass flows with a velocity field, the continuity equation keeps it from appearing or vanishing, and the cost is the total kinetic energy (5.2). The cheapest flow moves every particle on a straight line at constant speed (Figure 5.3).

  6. 3 → 4Read (5.2) as a Riemannian metric on densities: a small change \(\partial_t \rho = -\nabla\cdot(\rho \nabla \phi)\) has squared length \(\int \rho\, |\nabla\phi|^2\). Along it, \(\tfrac{d}{dt} F = \int \rho\, \nabla \tfrac{\delta F}{\delta \rho} \cdot \nabla \phi\), and minimizing this plus half the squared length over \(\phi\) gives \(\nabla \phi = -\nabla \tfrac{\delta F}{\delta \rho}\), so steepest descent is

    \[ \partial_t \rho = \nabla \cdot \Big( \rho\, \nabla \frac{\delta F}{\delta \rho} \Big). \]

  7. 4A gradient flowpartial differential equations

    Many evolution equations are steepest descent of an energy in this metric. The heat equation descends \(\int \rho \log \rho\), Fokker-Planck descends the free energy (Theorem 5.3, Figure 5.4), and the porous-medium equation \(\partial_t \rho = \Delta \rho^m\) descends \(\tfrac{1}{m-1}\int \rho^m\). A time step of size \(\tau\) is the JKO step:

    \[ \rho_{k+1} = \arg\min_\rho \Big\{ F(\rho) + \frac{W_2(\rho, \rho_k)^2}{2\tau} \Big\}. \]

5.7Where it breaks and what is open

Every picture above is exact for the true distributions, and every method sees samples. Two samples of size \(n\) from the same distribution on \([0, 1]^d\) sit at transport distance of order \(n^{-1/d}\) for \(d \ge 3\) (Fournier and Guillin), so halving the error takes \(2^d\) times the data. A coupling computed on a minibatch carries this error, and in high dimension most of it is noise. Entropic regularization trades the error for bias: the Sinkhorn divergence converges at the rate \(n^{-1/2}\) in every dimension (Genevay et al.), and it measures a blurred cost.

Figure 5.6Empirical transport in high dimension

Two samples of n points from the same law sit at a transport distance that shrinks only like n^(−1/d), so in high dimension no feasible sample size makes empirical transport accurate.

Pick a dimension. The true distance is 0 for every d. At d = 1 the fitted slope is −0.498, the n^(−1/2) of the theory. At the default d = 20 it is −0.075 against the theory's −1/20: at n = 256 the two samples still sit 1.196 apart, the best matching costs 0.663 of a random pairing, and halving the distance would take about 10 000 times more points. The distance here is W1 with the Euclidean cost, and W2 shrinks at the same rate n^(−1/d) once d ≥ 5 (Weed and Bach 2019).

  1. Minibatch couplings for flow matching. Pairing noise and data by OT inside each minibatch straightens flow-matching paths (Tong et al.), and the pairing within a batch of \(n\) is a sample estimate with the error above. How the batch size should grow with the data's dimension, and whether the straighter paths still pay off at image scale, is open.
  2. Transport between data types never measured together. Translating between data types never measured together is transport with an unknown cost. Whether a few pairs can pin down the cost and let OT or a Schrödinger bridge carry the rest is open, and the project below measures it.
  3. Rates set by the data's own dimension. Empirical transport converges at a rate set by the intrinsic dimension of the data, below the ambient one (Weed and Bach). Which learned flows achieve rates of that kind is open.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 5.1The JKO velocity

    Start from \(F(\rho) = \int V\rho + \int \rho\log\rho\) and the continuity equation. Derive the velocity of steepest descent in \(W_2\), show that the resulting equation is Fokker-Planck, and derive the dissipation (5.3).

    Solution

    The first variation is \(\frac{\delta F}{\delta \rho} = V + \log \rho + 1\). For a change \(\partial_t \rho = -\nabla\cdot(\rho v)\), integrating by parts (the constant drops because mass is conserved) gives

    \[ \frac{d}{dt}F = -\int \Big(V + \log\rho\Big)\, \nabla\cdot(\rho v) = \int \rho\, v \cdot \nabla(V + \log \rho). \]

    Minimizing \(\frac{d}{dt}F + \tfrac12 \int \rho |v|^2\) pointwise in \(v\) gives \(v = -\nabla(V + \log\rho)\). Since \(\rho \nabla\log\rho = \nabla\rho\), the continuity equation becomes \(\partial_t\rho = \nabla\cdot(\rho\nabla V) + \Delta\rho\), and substituting \(v\) back gives \(\frac{d}{dt}F = -\int \rho\, |\nabla(V + \log\rho)|^2\).

  2. Derivation 5.2Tight prices never cross

    For a plan \(\pi\) with marginals \(p, q\) and prices with \(\varphi_i + \psi_j \le C_{ij}\), show that \(\sum_i p_i \varphi_i + \sum_j q_j \psi_j \le \sum_{ij} \pi_{ij} C_{ij}\), with equality exactly when \(\pi\) puts mass only on tight pairs. Then show that on a line with \(c = |x - y|^2\) two tight pairs carrying mass never cross.

    Solution

    Using the marginals,

    \[ \sum_i p_i\varphi_i + \sum_j q_j\psi_j = \sum_{ij}\pi_{ij}(\varphi_i + \psi_j) \le \sum_{ij}\pi_{ij} C_{ij}, \]

    and the gap is \(\sum_{ij} \pi_{ij}(C_{ij} - \varphi_i - \psi_j)\), a sum of nonnegative terms that vanishes exactly when every pair with mass is tight.

    Suppose \(a \lt b\), \(c \lt d\), and the pairs \((a, d)\) and \((b, c)\) are tight. The pairs \((a, c)\) and \((b, d)\) satisfy the constraint, so subtracting gives \(C(a, d) + C(b, c) \le C(a, c) + C(b, d)\). The crossing identity of Section 5.4 says the left side exceeds the right by \(2(b - a)(d - c) \gt 0\), a contradiction.
