Chapter 6

The geometry of a step

Information geometry

Steepest descent depends on how the length of a step is measured. Measure it in KL between the model before and after, and the step stops depending on the parametrization, and its size follows from a budget.

Uses Chapter 2 and Appendix A.2 and A.5.

6.1Motivation

Gradient descent assumes that a step of a given length means the same thing in every parameter. It does not. The same change to a standard deviation is tiny when the deviation is large and enormous when it is small, and reparametrizing a model changes the path that gradient descent takes. Practitioners compensate with tuned learning rates, warmups, and per-parameter scalings. Measuring a step by how much it changes the model's predictions, the KL between before and after, fixes the units once, so the step stops depending on the parametrization, to first order in its size, and its size can be computed from a budget.

6.2Intuition

A step's true size is how much it changes what the model predicts, and the set of models one small step away is an ellipse whose shape the Fisher information sets.

Figure 6.1KL balls are Fisher ellipses that shrink with σ

In the parameters (μ, σ) of a Gaussian, the models within KL ε of a center nearly fill the Fisher ellipse ½δᵀFδ = ε, and the ellipses shrink in proportion to σ, so one step in the parameters is a large step between distributions where σ is small.

Slide ε. Each ball is the ball at (0, 1) scaled by σ, so a step of 0.1 in μ costs a KL of 0.0016 at σ = 1.75 and 0.0247 at σ = 0.45. At the default ε = 0.05 the exact ball and the ellipse differ by at most 22.2% along any ray, most straight up in σ, where the ball reaches 0.2733 against the ellipse's 0.2236. At ε = 0.005 the gap is 6.2%, and at ε = 0.5 it is 113.7%. Switch to estimates: 300 maximum-likelihood fits from n = 50 draws give n·Var(μ̂) = 1.129 and n·Var(σ̂) = 0.486 against F⁻¹ = diag(1, 0.5), and 60.7% of them land inside δᵀFδ ≤ 2/n against 63.2% for the limiting normal law, within the 8.2% Monte Carlo error of 300 datasets.

6.3Statement

Proposition 6.1 (steepest descent under a norm)

For a gradient \(g\) and the norm \(\|\delta\|_M^2 = \delta^\top M \delta\), the step of length \(\varepsilon\) that decreases the loss fastest is

\[ \delta^* = \arg\min_{\|\delta\|_M \le \varepsilon} \langle g, \delta \rangle = -\varepsilon\, \frac{M^{-1} g}{\sqrt{g^\top M^{-1} g}}. \tag{6.1} \]

Theorem 6.2 (Fisher information is the curvature of KL)

\[ \mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \,\|\, p_{\theta + \delta}) = \tfrac12\, \delta^\top F(\theta)\, \delta + O(|\delta|^3), \qquad F(\theta) = \mathbb E\big[\nabla \log p_\theta\, \nabla \log p_\theta^\top\big]. \tag{6.2} \]

So the step whose KL is \(\varepsilon\) is \(\delta^* = -\sqrt{2\varepsilon / g^\top F^{-1} g}\; F^{-1} g\), the natural gradient with a computed size.

6.4Derivation

(6.1). Minimize \(g^\top \delta + \lambda (\delta^\top M \delta - \varepsilon^2)\). Stationarity gives \(\delta = -M^{-1} g / 2\lambda\), and the constraint fixes \(\lambda\).

(6.2). Expand \(\log p_{\theta + \delta}\) to second order inside \(\mathrm{KL} = \mathbb E_\theta[\log p_\theta - \log p_{\theta+\delta}]\). The first-order term is \(-\delta^\top \mathbb E[\nabla \log p_\theta] = 0\), and the second-order term is \(\tfrac12 \delta^\top (-\mathbb E\,\nabla^2 \log p_\theta)\, \delta = \tfrac12 \delta^\top F \delta\).

Invariance. If \(\theta = \varphi(\eta)\) with Jacobian \(J\), then \(g_\eta = J^\top g_\theta\) and \(F_\eta = J^\top F_\theta J\), so \(J\, F_\eta^{-1} g_\eta = F_\theta^{-1} g_\theta\): to first order both parametrizations take the same step in distribution space. ∎

  • Softmax policies. In the logits, \(F = \mathrm{diag}(\pi) - \pi\pi^\top\) and the gradient of \(\mathbb E_\pi[r]\) is \(F A\) with \(A\) the advantage. \(F\) is singular, because adding a constant to every logit leaves \(\pi\) unchanged, so the natural step uses the pseudo-inverse: \(F^{+} F A = A - \bar A\, \mathbf 1\) with \(\bar A\) the plain average of the entries of \(A\), and the step is \(\pi \leftarrow \pi\, e^{\eta A} / Z\). This is multiplicative weights (Chapter 8) and a tilt (Chapter 2).
  • Weight matrices. Under the spectral norm, \(\max_{\|\Delta\|_{\mathrm{op}} \le 1} \langle G, \Delta \rangle\) is the nuclear norm of \(G\), attained at \(U V^\top\) from the reduced SVD \(G = U \Sigma V^\top\) (uniquely when \(G\) has full rank). Muon applies this orthogonalization to its momentum. The Frobenius norm gives the normalized gradient \(G / \|G\|_F\), and the largest-entry norm gives the sign update.

6.5Figures

Figure 6.2One fit, two parametrizations

The natural gradient step −F⁻¹∇L is defined by the distributions it moves between, so to first order it takes the same path whether σ or log σ is the parameter, while plain gradient descent changes with the choice.

Slide the step size. At the default η = 0.5, plain gradient descent never settles in (μ, σ) and fits in 13 steps in (μ, log σ), while the natural steps fit in 13 steps in both charts, on paths that stay within 0.086 of each other. At η = 1 the natural steps fit in 5 and 6 steps, and plain descent takes 138 steps in one chart and never settles in the other. Switch to fixed KL per step: every path converges at every budget on the slider, and at KL 0.010 per step all four fit in 17 to 19 steps.

Figure 6.3Natural policy gradient is multiplicative weights

For a softmax policy the natural gradient of E_π[r] is the advantage itself, up to a constant shift of every logit, so the step is π ← π·exp(ηA)/Z, and it keeps moving where the vanilla gradient π⊙A vanishes.

Slide η. At η = 1 the natural steps reach π(arm 1) ≥ 0.95 in 17 steps and vanilla policy gradient needs 166. Near the corner π⊙A is tiny: the first vanilla step moves the policy by a KL of 8.6e−7 and the first natural step by 5.3e−3. The vanilla gradient vanishes near the boundary, while the natural step moves every logit by ηA whatever π is.

6.6Four ways to see it

The Fisher metric shows up in four places: as the length that defines steepest descent, as the limit on how precisely data can pin a parameter down, as the local shape of a Bregman divergence, and as the Gauss-Newton matrix of least squares.

  1. 1A metricoptimization

    Steepest descent is defined only once the length of a step is. In the length \(\|\delta\|_M\) it points along \(-M^{-1} g\) (6.1), and with \(M = F\) the length is the KL between the models before and after (6.2).

  2. 1 → 2By (6.2) the models within KL \(\varepsilon\) of \(\theta\) fill the ellipse \(\tfrac12 \delta^\top F \delta \le \varepsilon\). An unbiased estimate from \(n\) samples has covariance at least \(F^{-1}/n\), and maximum likelihood attains this as \(n\) grows, so its scatter fills the ellipse \(\delta^\top F \delta \lesssim d/n\) (Figure 6.1). Distance in the Fisher metric counts how many samples it takes to tell two models apart.

  3. 2The Cramér-Rao boundstatistics

    No unbiased estimator beats the inverse Fisher information:

    \[ \mathrm{Cov}\big(\hat\theta(X_1, \dots, X_n)\big) \succeq \frac1n\, F(\theta)^{-1}. \]

  4. 1 → 3Replace the quadratic \(\tfrac12 \|\delta\|_M^2\) by the Bregman divergence of a convex function \(\psi\),

    \[ D_\psi(x', x) = \psi(x') - \psi(x) - \langle \nabla\psi(x), x' - x\rangle. \]

    The step \(x_{k+1} = \arg\min_x \{\langle g, x\rangle + \tfrac1\eta D_\psi(x, x_k)\}\) satisfies \(\nabla\psi(x_{k+1}) = \nabla\psi(x_k) - \eta g\). Since \(D_\psi(x + \delta, x) = \tfrac12 \delta^\top \nabla^2\psi(x)\, \delta + O(|\delta|^3)\), small mirror steps are steepest descent in the metric \(\nabla^2 \psi\).

  5. 3Mirror descentconvex optimization

    For an exponential family with log-partition \(A\), \(\nabla^2 A = F\) and \(D_A(\theta', \theta) = \mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \,\|\, p_{\theta'})\). Mirror descent in the natural parameters with \(\psi = A\) moves the mean parameters \(\mu = \nabla A(\theta)\) by \(-\eta \nabla_\theta L\), the same move as a natural-gradient step in \(\mu\) (Raskutti and Mukherjee). On the simplex with \(\psi = \sum_i x_i \log x_i\), mirror descent is multiplicative weights (Chapter 8).

  6. 1 → 4Let a model predict a Gaussian mean, \(y \sim \mathcal N(f_\theta(x), I)\), and let \(J\) be the Jacobian of \(f_\theta(x)\). The score is \(J^\top (y - f_\theta(x))\), so

    \[ F = \mathbb E_x\, \mathbb E_y \big[ J^\top (y - f_\theta)(y - f_\theta)^\top J \big] = \mathbb E_x \big[ J^\top J \big], \]

    the Gauss-Newton matrix of the squared loss. For other exponential-family outputs, when the network outputs the natural parameters (a canonical link), the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix equals the Fisher (Martens).

  7. 4Gauss-Newtonnumerical analysis

    To fit residuals \(r(\theta) = f_\theta(x) - y\), linearize \(r\) and solve the least-squares problem in the step: \(\delta = -(J^\top J)^{-1} J^\top r\). With unit noise this is the natural-gradient step with \(\eta = 1\), and Levenberg-Marquardt's damping \(J^\top J + \lambda I\) is a trust region.

6.7Where it breaks and what is open

Every view needs \(F\) or \(\nabla^2 \psi\), a \(p \times p\) matrix. At \(10^8\) parameters it takes \(4 \cdot 10^{16}\) bytes in float32, and inverting it takes about \(10^{24}\) operations, so every practical method approximates it: Kronecker factors per layer (K-FAC, Shampoo), a diagonal (Adam divides by the square root of a running average of squared gradients, a rough diagonal of the empirical Fisher), or a norm whose steepest step has a closed form (Muon). The cheapest substitute, the empirical Fisher built from per-example gradients at the observed labels, is a different matrix. It vanishes at a perfect fit and distorts steps elsewhere (Kunstner et al.).

Figure 6.4The exact Fisher is too big, and its cheap stand-in points the wrong way

The exact Fisher matrix of a p-parameter model takes p² numbers to store and about p³ operations to invert, and its cheap stand-in, the empirical Fisher (the mean outer product of per-example gradients), can point a step away from the fit.

The data follow the model of Kunstner et al.'s Figure 1, y = 2 + 2x + ε with lognormal x and ε ~ N(0, 1), here with 100 points. For this model the true Fisher is the Hessian, so the natural step is Newton's. At the default η = 0.25, from start 1 the natural steps run straight to the fit in 28 steps and gradient descent takes 98. The empirical-Fisher step leaves at 99.6° from the natural one and takes 223 steps: far from the fit the residuals are large, so the empirical Fisher is large and its steps are short. Slide η to 1: the natural step lands in one step, gradient descent diverges (it is stable only below η = 0.623), and the empirical Fisher takes 54. Slide p: at 10⁸ parameters the exact Fisher takes 40 PB in float32 and 10²⁴ flops to invert, 31.7 years at 10¹⁵ flop/s, and it fits on one 80 GB GPU only up to p = 141,421.

  1. A metric worth its cost. Which approximation of the geometry buys the most loss per flop at scale is open: K-FAC, Shampoo, and SOAP keep curvature, and Muon keeps only a norm. A step can only be computed, rather than tuned, in a metric that is affordable.
  2. The KL budget for post-training. TRPO fixes a KL radius per step and PPO approximates it by clipping. Which reference to measure the distance from, and how large a total budget a run should spend, are open. One proposal uses training checkpoints as references, each weighted by the data it saw.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 6.1Fisher information is the curvature of KL

    Derive (6.2), including why the first-order term vanishes and why \(-\mathbb E\, \nabla^2 \log p_\theta = \mathbb E[\nabla \log p_\theta \nabla \log p_\theta^\top]\). Then compute \(F\) for \(\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) in the parameters \((\mu, \sigma)\) and in \((\mu, \log\sigma)\).

    Solution

    The score has mean zero: \(\mathbb E_\theta[\nabla \log p_\theta] = \int \nabla p_\theta = \nabla \int p_\theta = 0\). Differentiating \(\log p\) twice gives \(\nabla^2 \log p = \nabla^2 p / p - \nabla\log p\, \nabla\log p^\top\), and \(\mathbb E[\nabla^2 p / p] = \nabla^2 \int p = 0\). So the second-order term of \(\mathbb E_\theta[\log p_\theta - \log p_{\theta + \delta}]\) is \(-\tfrac12 \delta^\top \mathbb E[\nabla^2 \log p_\theta]\, \delta = \tfrac12 \delta^\top F \delta\).

    For the Gaussian, with \(z = (x - \mu)/\sigma\), the scores are \(\partial_\mu \log p = z/\sigma\) and \(\partial_\sigma \log p = (z^2 - 1)/\sigma\). Since \(\mathbb E z^2 = 1\), \(\mathbb E (z^2 - 1)^2 = 2\), and \(\mathbb E z(z^2 - 1) = 0\), \(F = \mathrm{diag}(1/\sigma^2,\, 2/\sigma^2)\). With \(s = \log\sigma\), \(\partial_s = \sigma\, \partial_\sigma\), so \(F = \mathrm{diag}(1/\sigma^2,\, 2)\).

  2. Derivation 6.2The Cramér-Rao bound in one dimension

    Let \(T(X)\) be an unbiased estimator of a scalar \(\theta\) from one sample. Show \(\mathrm{Var}\, T \ge 1 / F(\theta)\), and extend it to \(n\) independent samples.

    Solution

    Let \(s = \partial_\theta \log p_\theta(X)\), with mean zero and variance \(F\). Unbiasedness gives \(\mathbb E[T s] = \int T\, \partial_\theta p_\theta = \partial_\theta\, \mathbb E_\theta T = 1\), so \(\mathrm{Cov}(T, s) = 1\). By Cauchy-Schwarz, \(1 = \mathrm{Cov}(T, s)^2 \le \mathrm{Var}(T)\, \mathrm{Var}(s) = \mathrm{Var}(T)\, F\).

    The score of \(n\) independent samples is the sum of their scores, so its variance is \(nF\), and \(\mathrm{Var}\, T \ge 1/(nF)\).

Notes and further reading

Guides. Nielsen, An Elementary Introduction to Information Geometry (2020), the Fisher metric from definitions: arXiv:1808.08271. Then Martens, New Insights and Perspectives on the Natural Gradient Method (JMLR, 2020), the natural gradient as a second-order method: arXiv:1412.1193. For the Riemannian prerequisites, Sigmundur Gudmundsson's An Introduction to Riemannian Geometry (lecture notes), the chapters on metrics and geodesics. The Fisher metric of \(\mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) is twice the hyperbolic half-plane metric in the coordinates \((\mu/\sqrt 2, \sigma)\), with curvature \(-\tfrac12\), so the geodesics of the hyperbolic half-plane are the shortest paths between Gaussians.

Chapter 7

Symmetry

Fourier analysis and group representations

If a linear operation looks the same after a shift, complex exponentials are its eigenvectors, whatever its kernel is. A symmetry supplies the right basis, the right layers, and the quantities that stay fixed.

Uses Chapter 1 and Appendix A.7.

7.1Motivation

A fully connected layer on a 224 by 224 image keeps a separate weight for every pair of pixels and must learn separately that a cat in the corner is a cat in the center. Physics met the same redundancy earlier, in laws that are the same everywhere and at every time. A linear operation that commutes with shifts is determined by one kernel, is diagonal in the Fourier basis, and needs far fewer parameters and examples. A symmetry removes what should not matter.

PAPERA document that moved capital

ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks

A deep convolutional network trained on GPUs wins ImageNet by a wide margin, and deep learning takes over vision.

Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey E. Hinton, 2012 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

Its 2012 win started the modern deep-learning era and the demand for GPUs that followed.

The link to this chapter: its convolutional layers share weights across positions, which the paper justifies by the "stationarity of statistics and locality of pixel dependencies" (Section 1). A weight-shared convolution commutes with shifts, so Theorem 7.1 diagonalizes it, and training on translated and reflected images (Section 4.1) is group averaging on the data side.

PAPERA document that moved capital

Attention Is All You Need

Drop recurrence and convolution, and let attention alone relate every position to every other.

Ashish Vaswani et al., 2017 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

The Transformer became the architecture of large language models.

The link to this chapter: its positional encodings are sinusoids at geometrically spaced frequencies, and the paper notes that for any fixed offset \(k\), \(PE_{pos+k}\) is a linear function of \(PE_{pos}\) (Section 3.5). That linear map is a rotation of each frequency pair, the mechanism that rotary embeddings later built into attention itself. The paper offers it as a hypothesis about why relative positions are easy to learn.

7.2Intuition

If a linear operation does not care where it is applied, waves pass through it keeping their shape and frequency and change only in size and phase.

Figure 7.1Shift invariance diagonalizes a map

A linear map on a ring that commutes with shifts has every complex exponential φ_k as an eigenvector, whatever its kernel, and its eigenvalue on φ_k is λ_k = Σ_m c_m·e^{2πikm/N}.

At the default blur and k = 5, A·φ_5 ÷ φ_5 is λ_5 from (7.1), 0.2909, in every cell, and the largest residual over all 32 modes is round-off, below 1e−13. Pick Random: the eigenvalues turn complex and the residual stays below 1e−13. Pick Position gain: ‖SA − AS‖ jumps from 0 to 0.165, the largest residual to 0.354, the Fourier-basis matrix grows off-diagonal entries next to its diagonal, and A·φ_5 ÷ φ_5 reaches 0.4364 at cell 8.

7.3Statement

Theorem 7.1 (shift-invariant maps are diagonal in the Fourier basis)

Let \(S\) shift a vector on a ring of \(N\) cells, \((Sx)_n = x_{n+1}\), and let \(A_{ij} = c_{(j - i) \bmod N}\) be any circulant map. Then \(AS = SA\), and each Fourier mode \(\varphi_k(n) = e^{2\pi i k n / N}\) is an eigenvector,

\[ A\, \varphi_k = \lambda_k\, \varphi_k, \qquad \lambda_k = \sum_{m} c_m\, e^{2\pi i k m / N}, \tag{7.1} \]

so convolution becomes multiplication after a Fourier transform (\(\lambda_k\) is the kernel's DFT at \(-k\) in the usual sign convention). For the heat equation on the ring, each mode decays on its own:

\[ \hat u_k(t) = \hat u_k(0)\, e^{-4 \sin^2(\pi k / N)\, t}. \tag{7.2} \]

7.4Derivation

\(S \varphi_k = e^{2\pi i k / N} \varphi_k\), and these \(N\) eigenvalues are distinct, so each eigenspace of \(S\) is one-dimensional. Since \(S(A \varphi_k) = A S \varphi_k = e^{2\pi i k / N} A \varphi_k\), the vector \(A\varphi_k\) lies in the same eigenspace, so \(A \varphi_k = \lambda_k \varphi_k\). Reading off entry \(i\) gives \(\lambda_k\):

\[ (A\varphi_k)_i = \sum_j c_{j-i}\, e^{2\pi i k j/N} = e^{2\pi i k i/N} \sum_m c_m\, e^{2\pi i k m/N}. \]

The discrete Laplacian has \(c_0 = -2\) and \(c_{\pm 1} = 1\), so \(\lambda_k = 2\cos(2\pi k/N) - 2 = -4\sin^2(\pi k/N)\), and (7.2) follows. ∎

  • Characters. The modes are the characters of the cyclic group, and their orthogonality, \(\frac1N \sum_n e^{2\pi i k n/N} = \mathbf 1[N \mid k]\), turns counting problems into averages over roots of unity.
  • Rotary embeddings. Rotating a query at position \(m\) and a key at position \(n\) by \(R(m\theta)\) and \(R(n\theta)\) gives \(R(m\theta)^\top R(n\theta) = R((n - m)\theta)\), so attention logits depend on \(n - m\) alone.
  • Other groups. A layer \(f\) is equivariant when \(f(g \cdot x) = g \cdot f(x)\) for every group element \(g\). Rigid motions (SE(3)) give the equivariant layers of protein models, and by Noether's theorem every continuous symmetry of an action conserves a quantity along its solutions.

7.5Figures

Figure 7.2Heat flow removes fine detail first

Heat flow on a ring commutes with shifts, so each Fourier mode decays on its own by e^{−λ_k t} with λ_k = 4·sin²(πk/N), and high frequencies die first.

At the default t = 10, every frequency above k = 10.8 has lost more than half its amplitude, the texture at k = 48 has fallen from 0.110 to 4.8e−7, and the steps keep 0.871 of the variance. Slide to t = 1000: half survives only below k = 1.1, and 0.149 of the variance is left. The heat flow is computed in the cells by squaring the local rule, and its spectrum matches e^{−λ_k t} to within 1e−10 at every t. Run backward, the flow restores coarse structure before fine. Dieleman (2024) argues that Gaussian noise on natural images drowns frequencies in this same order, so diffusion models generate coarse to fine.

Figure 7.3Rotary embeddings see only the offset

RoPE rotates each pair of query coordinates by m·θ_i and each pair of key coordinates by n·θ_i, so the logit is Re Σ_i q_i·k̄_i·e^{i(m−n)θ_i} and depends on m − n alone.

At the default offset 3, every RoPE logit on the diagonal m − n = 3 equals Re Σ q_i·k̄_i·e^{3iθ_i} = 0.4461, and over n = 0 to 199 they spread by less than 1e−13. The additive sinusoidal embedding spreads by 11.297 on the same diagonal. Pick Absolute for the heatmap: its stripes break up, because q·p_n and p_m·k depend on each position separately.

Figure 7.4A layer that turns with its input

A layer that moves each point by Σ_j (x_i − x_j)·φ(|x_i − x_j|²) uses only differences and distances, so rotating the input rotates the output: f(Rx) = R·f(x) exactly, for any φ.

At the default 120°, the EGNN-style layer's output on the rotated chain lands on R·f(x) to within 1e−13, while the MLP misses by 1.109. Slide to 0°: both gaps are 0, since any function agrees with itself, and at 60° the MLP misses by 1.210. φ here is a fixed six-unit network of the squared distance, any other φ keeps the guarantee, and SE(3)-equivariant structure models for proteins build on the same construction.

Figure 7.5A symmetry conserves a quantity

The potential r²/2 + r⁴/4 looks the same after any rotation, so the angular momentum L = x·v_y − y·v_x is conserved, and a term ε·y²/2 that breaks the symmetry lets L drift while the energy, protected by the symmetry in time, stays fixed.

The particle starts at (1.2, 0) with velocity (0, 0.6), and leapfrog with step 0.005 runs it to t = 60. At the default ε = 0.15, L moves between 0.964 and 1.439 times its start, a range of 0.475 of L(0), while E stays within 1.1e−5 of its start. At t = 60 the torque −ε·x·y gives dL/dt = 0.0492, and the finite difference of L gives 0.0492 too. Slide ε to 0: the dashed curve becomes a circle and the range of L falls to 2.8e−14, which is round-off. Leapfrog's kicks point along the force, which is radial at ε = 0, so the integrator keeps L as exactly as the true flow does. Slide to 0.5: E still holds to 1.1e−5. Press New start for another orbit.

7.6Four ways to see it

A symmetry gives a basis in which the problem separates, a way to average away what should not matter, a quantity that never changes, and a model that needs fewer examples. Each picture follows from the first.

  1. 1Shared eigenvectorslinear algebra and signal processing

    A linear map that commutes with the shift shares its eigenvectors, the Fourier modes (Theorem 7.1). Convolutions, heat flow, and stationary covariances all become diagonal in the same basis.

  2. 1 → 2The projection onto mode \(k\) is a weighted average of the shifts,

    \[ P_k = \frac1N \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} e^{-2\pi i k n / N}\, S^n, \qquad P_k \varphi_j = \mathbf 1[j = k]\, \varphi_j, \]

    because \(S^n \varphi_j = e^{2\pi i j n/N} \varphi_j\) and the characters are orthogonal. For \(k = 0\) the weights are equal, and \(P_0\) averages a vector over all of its shifts, which projects it onto the shift-invariant vectors.

  3. 2Group averagingalgebra and statistics

    For a finite group \(G\) acting on inputs, the average \(\bar f(x) = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} f(g \cdot x)\) is invariant, and averaging is the projection onto invariant functions (the Reynolds operator). Data augmentation averages a loss over the group in the same way.

  4. 2 → 3Suppose the inputs \(X\) have a \(G\)-invariant distribution and the target \(h\) is invariant. Then \(f(gX) - h(X)\) has the law of \(f(X) - h(X)\), and Jensen's inequality gives

    \[ \mathbb E\, \big(\bar f(X) - h(X)\big)^2 \le \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g} \mathbb E\, \big(f(gX) - h(X)\big)^2 = \mathbb E\, \big(f(X) - h(X)\big)^2. \]

    Averaging never hurts, and it helps by the variance of \(f\) along each orbit, which an invariant model never has to learn.

  5. 3Sample efficiencylearning theory

    A model built to be invariant or equivariant spends no data learning the symmetry, and for equivariant models the gain in generalization is strict (Elesedy and Zaidi). Convolutions, rotary embeddings, and SE(3)-equivariant layers are this picture applied to images, positions, and molecules.

  6. 1 → 4A continuous symmetry is a one-parameter group, such as rotations \(e^{sJ}\) with \(J = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\). If \(V(e^{sJ}x) = V(x)\) for every \(s\), differentiating at \(s = 0\) gives \(\nabla V(x) \cdot Jx = 0\). For \(\ddot x = -\nabla V(x)\) and the angular momentum \(L = \langle Jx, \dot x\rangle\),

    \[ \frac{dL}{dt} = \langle J\dot x, \dot x\rangle + \langle Jx, -\nabla V(x)\rangle = 0, \]

    since \(J\) is skew, so the first term vanishes, and the symmetry kills the second.

  7. 4Conserved quantitiesphysics

    Noether's theorem: every continuous symmetry of an action conserves a quantity along its solutions. Symmetry in time conserves energy, in space momentum, and in rotation angular momentum (Figure 7.5). In quantum mechanics the conserved quantities are the operators that commute with the Hamiltonian, so they share its eigenvectors, which is view 1 again.

7.7Where it breaks and what is open

Theorem 7.1 assumes the symmetry holds exactly, and sampling breaks it twice. \(N\) samples cannot tell frequency \(k\) from \(k + N\), so content above \(N/2\) folds back as a low frequency. A layer that keeps every second output commutes only with shifts by two, so a network with strided layers is equivariant to a coarse grid, and its output changes when the input moves by one pixel (Azulay and Weiss). Blurring before subsampling restores most of the lost equivariance (Zhang).

Figure 7.6Aliasing breaks shift equivariance

Sixteen samples cannot tell frequency f from f ± 16, so a frequency above 8 reappears as |f − 16·round(f/16)|, and a stride-2 layer that keeps every other cell without smoothing lets these aliases break equivariance under a one-cell shift.

At the default f = 13, the samples are those of frequency 3: the DFT's largest coefficient sits at k = 3 as predicted, and the lowest-frequency sinusoid through them is cos(2π·3t − 0.6) to within 1e−14. Prediction and peak agree at every f from 0 to 16. Below, a shift by two cells moves the stride-2 output by exactly one cell, with error 0. A shift by one cell should move it by half a cell, to where the band-limited interpolant of the output points. The plain stride misses by 0.637 of the output's norm. Pick Blur then stride: averaging with weights (1, 4, 6, 4, 1)/16 first, as in Zhang (2019), cuts the error to 0.093. A signal with nothing above frequency 16 of 64 gives the plain stride an error below 1e−15, so the whole error is aliasing.

  1. Symmetries the data only has approximately. Real data is close to symmetric, and how much a model should respect a symmetry, or which group the data has, is usually chosen by hand. Learning it from data is open, and it matters for protein and robot models, where SE(3) is exact for physics and broken by gravity and grippers.
  2. Locality and equivariance as the source of new samples. A denoiser restricted to be local and shift-equivariant produces new images as mosaics of training patches (Kamb and Ganguli), which ties the memorization of Chapter 1 to this chapter. Whether this explains trained diffusion models, and what plays the part of locality for masked diffusion language models, is open.
  3. Positions beyond the trained context. RoPE's lowest frequencies turn by less than one full rotation over a typical training context, so positions past it are rotations the model never saw. Rescaling the frequencies extends the context (YaRN). A rule that ties context length to the frequency spectrum from first principles would serve the search for cheaper attention.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 7.1Commuting with the shift means circulant

    Show that a matrix commutes with the cyclic shift \((Sx)_n = x_{n+1}\) exactly when it is circulant, derive its eigenvalues (7.1), and derive the decay rate (7.2) of heat on a ring.

    Solution

    \(S_{ij} = \mathbf 1[j = i + 1]\), so \((AS)_{ij} = A_{i, j-1}\) and \((SA)_{ij} = A_{i+1, j}\), indices mod \(N\). They agree for all \(i, j\) exactly when \(A_{i+1, j+1} = A_{ij}\), so \(A_{ij}\) depends only on \(j - i\): \(A_{ij} = c_{j - i}\).

    Then

    \[ (A\varphi_k)_i = \sum_j c_{j-i}\, e^{2\pi i k j/N} = e^{2\pi i k i/N} \sum_m c_m e^{2\pi i k m/N}, \]

    which is (7.1). For heat, \(\dot u = A u\) with \(c_0 = -2\) and \(c_{\pm 1} = 1\), so

    \[ \lambda_k = e^{2\pi i k/N} + e^{-2\pi i k/N} - 2 = 2\cos(2\pi k/N) - 2 = -4\sin^2(\pi k/N), \]

    and each Fourier coefficient solves \(\dot{\hat u}_k = \lambda_k \hat u_k\).

  2. Derivation 7.2Noether for rotations and for time

    For \(\ddot x = -\nabla V(x)\) in the plane, show that \(L = x_1 \dot x_2 - x_2 \dot x_1\) is constant when \(V\) depends only on \(|x|\), and that \(E = \tfrac12 |\dot x|^2 + V(x)\) is constant for every \(V\). Which symmetry does each use?

    Solution

    Differentiating,

    \[ \dot L = \dot x_1 \dot x_2 + x_1 \ddot x_2 - \dot x_2 \dot x_1 - x_2 \ddot x_1 = -(x_1 \partial_2 V - x_2 \partial_1 V), \]

    which is the torque. If \(V = v(|x|)\), then \(\nabla V = v'(|x|)\, x/|x|\) is parallel to \(x\), and the torque is zero. This uses symmetry under rotation.

    \(\dot E = \dot x \cdot \ddot x + \nabla V \cdot \dot x = \dot x \cdot (\ddot x + \nabla V) = 0\). This uses symmetry under shifts in time: \(V\) does not depend on \(t\).

Chapter 8

No-regret dynamics

Online learning and games

Keep weights on the options proportional to \(e^{-\eta \cdot (\text{cumulative loss})}\). With \(\eta\) proportional to \(1/\sqrt T\), regret against the best option grows only like \(\sqrt T\), and when both players of a zero-sum game do this, their averages approach an equilibrium.

Uses Chapters 2 and 6 and Appendix A.6.

8.1Motivation

Decisions often have to be made with no model of what comes next: which forecaster to follow tomorrow, which detector to deploy against an attacker who adapts. Statistical learning assumes the data come from a fixed distribution, and an adversary breaks that assumption. Online learning drops it and scores a learner against the best fixed choice in hindsight. Multiplicative weights keeps that regret growing only like the square root of time against any sequence, and when two such learners play each other in a two-player zero-sum game, their averages approach an equilibrium.

8.2Intuition

Weight each option by \(e^{-\eta}\) raised to its losses so far, and no sequence of losses can make you much worse than the best option in hindsight.

Figure 8.1Self-play averages to the equilibrium

When both players of a zero-sum game run Hedge, their time-averaged strategies form an approximate equilibrium whose error is the regret divided by T, so the averages close in on the minimax equilibrium even while the current strategies spiral away from it.

Rock beating scissors pays 2 here, so the equilibrium is (¼, ½, ¼). Both players start at the uniform mix, so they play the same mix every round. At the default η = 0.05 and 1000 rounds, the current strategy circles the equilibrium on a widening spiral and ends with exploitability 0.393, while the time average sits at (0.258, 0.492, 0.251) with exploitability 0.0094. Each player's regret, 9.4, stays far below the fixed-η bound 122.0, and small regret over many rounds is what pulls the average in. Slide η to 0.15: the spiral reaches the edge of the simplex (current 1.916), and the average holds at 0.0203. Press Play to watch the spiral form.

8.3Statement

Theorem 8.1 (Hedge)

With losses \(\ell_t \in [0, 1]^n\) and weights \(p_{t, i} \propto e^{-\eta L_{t-1, i}}\), where \(L_{t,i}\) is expert \(i\)'s loss so far, the regret against the best expert satisfies

\[ \sum_{t=1}^T \langle p_t, \ell_t \rangle - \min_i L_{T, i} \le \frac{\ln n}{\eta} + \frac{\eta T}{8} = \sqrt{\tfrac12\, T \ln n} \quad \text{at } \eta = \sqrt{8 \ln n / T}. \tag{8.1} \]

Theorem 8.2 (minimax from no regret)

If both players of a zero-sum game with payoff matrix \(M\) have regret at most \(R_T = o(T)\) after \(T\) rounds, their time-averaged strategies form a \(2R_T/T\)-equilibrium, so every limit point of the averages is an equilibrium, and

\[ \max_p \min_q\, p^\top M q = \min_q \max_p\, p^\top M q. \tag{8.2} \]

8.4Derivation

(8.1). Let \(\Phi_t = \sum_i e^{-\eta L_{t, i}}\). By Hoeffding's lemma,

\[ \frac{\Phi_{t}}{\Phi_{t-1}} = \mathbb E_{i \sim p_t}\, e^{-\eta \ell_{t,i}} \le \exp\!\big(-\eta \langle p_t, \ell_t\rangle + \eta^2/8\big), \]

so \(\ln \Phi_T \le \ln n - \eta \sum_t \langle p_t, \ell_t\rangle + \eta^2 T/8\). Also \(\ln \Phi_T \ge -\eta \min_i L_{T,i}\). Combining the two and dividing by \(\eta\) gives (8.1).

(8.2). Let \(\bar p\) and \(\bar q\) be the averages and \(R\) a bound on both regrets. Then

\[ \begin{aligned} \min_q \max_p p^\top M q &\le \max_p p^\top M \bar q \le \frac1T \sum_t p_t^\top M q_t + \frac RT \\ &\le \min_q \bar p^\top M q + \frac{2R}T \le \max_p \min_q p^\top M q + \frac{2R}{T}. \end{aligned} \]

The reverse inequality always holds, and \(R/T \to 0\). The same chain shows that neither player can gain more than \(2R/T\) by deviating from \(\bar p\) or \(\bar q\). ∎

A tilt again. Hedge's weights solve \(\min_p \{\langle p, L \rangle + \tfrac1\eta \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, \text{uniform})\}\), which is Theorem 2.1 with \(f = -\eta L\). This is follow-the-regularized-leader with an entropy regularizer, and the natural policy gradient of Chapter 6 makes the same update.

8.5Figures

Figure 8.2Patching the latest jailbreak cycles

A defender who retrains only against the latest attack is a best response to the last move, and it cycles; a defender who learns from the whole history (fictitious play, which converges in zero-sum games by Robinson's theorem, or Hedge) converges to the game value.

Four attack families sit on a ring, and a detector trained on one family blocks it, partly blocks its two neighbors, and misses the opposite one. At the default 300 rounds, chasing the latest attack flips between detectors for families 1 and 3, the attacker answers with the family each one misses, and success stays at 0.85 to 0.91 every round. Training on all past attacks deploys the mix of every detector trained so far (fictitious play), and its worst-case success falls to 0.482 against the exact game value 0.479. Hedge's weights reach 0.497. At 1000 rounds they reach 0.481 and 0.487. The value comes from support enumeration and matches a 100,000-round Hedge self-play run (0.4790).

Figure 8.3Hedge in continuous time circles the equilibrium

As its step shrinks, Hedge becomes the replicator equation ṗ_i = p_i((Ap)_i − pᵀAp), and in zero-sum rock-paper-scissors KL(p*‖p) stays constant along its orbits, because d/dt KL(p*‖p) = −(p*ᵀAp − pᵀAp) and both terms vanish.

A win pays a and a loss costs 1, and every a has the equilibrium (⅓, ⅓, ⅓). At the default a = 1 the game is zero-sum, both terms of the rate vanish, and KL stays at 0.1688 from t = 0 to t = 40 on the middle orbit. The largest change on any of the three orbits is 9e−11, the error of RK4. Slide a to 1.2: the measured rate is −0.00309, the formula gives −0.00309, and KL falls to 0.0134 as the orbits spiral in. Slide to 0.8: KL climbs to 1.0878 and the orbits spiral out toward the edges. Hedge with step η = 0.001, run for 10,000 rounds, lands within 2e−4 of the replicator path at t = 10.

8.6Four ways to see it

Multiplicative weights is an algorithm for learning from losses, a proof of the minimax theorem, a regularized optimization step, and a model of evolution. The joins below are each a few lines.

  1. 1Online learningcomputer science

    Choose a mixture over \(n\) options each round, pay its expected loss, and compare with the best single option in hindsight. Hedge's regret is \(O(\sqrt{T \ln n})\) against any sequence of losses, chosen in advance or by an adversary (8.1).

  2. 1 → 2Let both players of a zero-sum game run Hedge. The chain of inequalities in the proof of Theorem 8.2 turns the two regret bounds into a duality gap of at most \(2R/T\) for the averaged strategies, so no-regret learning proves the minimax theorem and supplies an algorithm that computes the equilibrium (Freund and Schapire).

  3. 2Minimaxgame theory

    In a finite two-player zero-sum game, the order of play does not matter once players may randomize (8.2). The value is a linear program, and its dual is the other player's linear program.

  4. 1 → 3By Theorem 2.1 with \(f = -\eta L_{t-1}\), Hedge's weights solve

    \[ p_t = \arg\min_{p \in \Delta} \Big\{ \langle p, L_{t-1} \rangle + \frac1\eta \sum_i p_i \log p_i \Big\}. \]

    Follow-the-regularized-leader with the entropy as regularizer makes this choice. Written one round at a time, \(p_{t+1} \propto p_t\, e^{-\eta \ell_t}\), it is mirror descent with the mirror map \(\sum_i p_i \log p_i\), whose Bregman divergence is KL (Chapter 6).

  5. 3Regularized optimizationconvex optimization

    Changing the regularizer changes the algorithm: the squared norm gives projected online gradient descent, and the entropy gives Hedge. Every regret bound of this family adds two terms, the regularizer's range divided by \(\eta\) and how far each step moves, and the best \(\eta\) balances them.

  6. 3 → 4Write the payoffs as gains \(u = -\ell\). One Hedge step changes \(\log p_i\) by

    \[ \eta u_i - \log \sum_j p_j e^{\eta u_j} = \eta\, (u_i - \langle p, u\rangle) + O(\eta^2). \]

    Let \(\eta \to 0\) with time \(\tau = t\eta\), and the steps become

    \[ \frac{dp_i}{d\tau} = p_i \big( u_i - \langle p, u \rangle \big). \]

  7. 4Replicator dynamicsevolutionary biology and economics

    Read \(p_i\) as the share of a population playing type \(i\) and \(u_i\) as its fitness: types that beat the population average grow. In rock-paper-scissors, \(\mathrm{KL}(p^* \,\|\, p)\) stays constant along the orbits, so continuous-time Hedge circles the equilibrium forever (Figure 8.3).

8.7Where it breaks and what is open

Theorem 8.2 is about averages. The strategies actually played do not settle: in a zero-sum game with an interior equilibrium, the replicator flow conserves \(\mathrm{KL}(p^* \,\|\, p)\), each discrete Hedge step overshoots its closed orbit, and the iterates spiral out toward the boundary (Bailey and Piliouras). A deployed policy is the last iterate, and averaging the parameters of a sequence of networks does not average the policies. Optimistic Hedge, which counts the last loss twice, makes the last iterate converge in zero-sum games with a unique equilibrium (Daskalakis and Panageas). In games that are not zero-sum, no-regret averages reach only coarse correlated equilibria, a weaker notion than Nash's.

Figure 8.4The last iterate spirals out

When both players of matching pennies run Hedge, their averages converge to the equilibrium while KL(p*‖p_t) of their current strategies grows every round, and optimistic Hedge, which counts the last payoff twice, brings the current strategies in.

Player 1 wins on a match and player 2 on a mismatch, and both start at (0.7, 0.4), where KL from the equilibrium is 0.1076. At the default η = 0.1, Hedge's KL rises every round, passes 1 at round 373, and reaches 4.728 at round 2000, with player 1 pinned to tails. The average still closes in, to KL 4.3e−4, as Theorem 8.2 promises. Pick Optimistic Hedge: the weights use the cumulative payoff plus the last payoff once more, and the current strategies spiral in to KL 2.0e−10, with the average at 2.8e−6. Slide η up: at 0.5 Hedge's KL passes 1 at round 17 and ends at 30.050, its average ends at 3.3e−4, and optimistic Hedge reaches the equilibrium to round-off.

  1. Last iterates for language-model self-play. Nash learning from human feedback and other self-play methods for preferences deploy the current policy. Regularizing toward a reference makes the iterates converge to the equilibrium of a regularized game (Munos et al.), and how much regularization the true game can bear is open.
  2. The red-team loop with approximate responses. Theorem 8.2 assumes each player responds exactly. In a red-team loop between a jailbreak attacker and a detector, both are trained networks, each response is approximate, and whether training on the history keeps its guarantee is open. The project below measures it on jailbreak families.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 8.1Hedge's regret bound

    With losses in \([0, 1]\) and weights \(p_{t,i} \propto e^{-\eta L_{t-1, i}}\), derive (8.1) and the best fixed \(\eta\). Use Hoeffding's lemma (Appendix A.6).

    Solution

    Let \(\Phi_t = \sum_i e^{-\eta L_{t,i}}\), so \(\Phi_0 = n\). Then \(\Phi_t / \Phi_{t-1} = \sum_i p_{t,i}\, e^{-\eta \ell_{t,i}} = \mathbb E_{i \sim p_t} e^{-\eta \ell_{t,i}}\). Hoeffding's lemma for a variable in \([0, 1]\) gives \(\log \mathbb E\, e^{-\eta \ell} \le -\eta\, \mathbb E \ell + \eta^2/8\). Summing over \(t\),

    \[ -\eta \min_i L_{T,i} \le \ln \Phi_T \le \ln n - \eta \sum_t \langle p_t, \ell_t\rangle + \frac{\eta^2 T}{8}. \]

    Rearranging gives regret at most \(\ln n/\eta + \eta T/8\). The two terms are equal at \(\eta = \sqrt{8 \ln n / T}\), where the sum is \(\sqrt{T \ln n / 2}\).

  2. Derivation 8.2Replicator orbits conserve KL

    For the replicator equation \(\dot p_i = p_i((Ap)_i - p^\top A p)\) with \(A\) the rock-paper-scissors matrix (antisymmetric, with \(Ap^* = 0\) at \(p^* = (\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)\)), show that \(\mathrm{KL}(p^* \,\|\, p)\) is constant along solutions.

    Solution

    Differentiating,

    \[ \frac{d}{dt}\mathrm{KL}(p^* \,\|\, p) = -\sum_i p^*_i \frac{\dot p_i}{p_i} = -\sum_i p^*_i \big((Ap)_i - p^\top A p\big) = -p^{*\top} A p + p^\top A p. \]

    Antisymmetry gives \(p^\top A p = 0\) and \(p^{*\top} A p = -p^\top A p^* = 0\), so the derivative vanishes. The orbits are the level sets of \(\mathrm{KL}(p^* \,\|\, \cdot)\), closed curves around \(p^*\).

Chapter 9

Potential functions

Lyapunov's second method, from dynamics

Find a quantity that is bounded below and drops at every step by a measurable amount. The drops add up to at most its starting height, so the process cannot keep making large moves forever. Stability, the convergence of optimizers, regret bounds, the running time of algorithms, and the convergence of games all follow from one such quantity.

Uses Chapters 4, 5, and 8, and Appendix A.1.

9.1Motivation

Proving that an algorithm terminates, that a system settles, or that an optimizer converges seems to need a different argument each time. Lyapunov's 1892 thesis on the stability of motion found the argument for stability, which later proved termination and convergence too: exhibit a quantity that only decreases and is bounded below. The quantity need not be the process's own objective, and finding it is the creative step.

WHITEPAPERA document that moved capital

Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System

A chain of proof-of-work lets strangers agree on one ledger without a trusted intermediary.

Satoshi Nakamoto, 2008 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

It created Bitcoin and the cryptocurrency industry that grew from it.

The link to this chapter: Section 11 computes the chance that an attacker \(z\) blocks behind ever catches up as a gambler's ruin, \((q/p)^z\) when honest miners find the next block with probability \(p \gt q\). A potential gives it in one line: \((q/p)^{D_t}\) is a martingale for the attacker's deficit \(D_t\), and optional stopping turns that into the answer, as in the exercise on gambler's ruin.

9.2Intuition

Find a quantity that only goes down and is bounded below, and the process cannot keep making large moves.

Figure 9.1The energy of a damped pendulum only goes down

Along a damped pendulum's path the energy E = ½ω² + 1 − cos θ falls at the rate bω², so the level sets of E are fences that every path crosses only inward.

Three paths start at seeded points, and path 1 starts above the separatrix E = 2. At the default damping b = 0.3, the marked point on path 1 at t = 2 has dE/dt = −0.4479 by a finite difference of E and −0.4479 from −bω², and the two agree to 1.8e−4 everywhere on path 1. Path 1 swings over the top once, crosses the separatrix inward, and its energy falls from 3.775 to 4.5e−4 by t = 30. No step raises E on any path. Slide the damping to 0: each path keeps its energy, path 1 goes over the top 11 times, and the largest rise is 4.8e−10 of RK4 error. That is energy conservation, the law that time symmetry gives in Chapter 7. Press Play to move the point along path 1, or New starts for other paths.

9.3Statement

Theorem 9.1 (a quantity that only goes down)

Let \(V \ge V_{\min}\) along a sequence \(x_0, x_1, \dots\) with \(V(x_{k+1}) \le V(x_k) - c(x_k)\) and \(c \ge 0\). Then

\[ \sum_{k \lt K} c(x_k) \le V(x_0) - V_{\min}, \qquad \min_{k \lt K} c(x_k) \le \frac{V(x_0) - V_{\min}}{K}. \tag{9.1} \]

In particular, if every step that has not finished has \(c \ge c_0 \gt 0\), the process finishes within \((V(x_0) - V_{\min})/c_0\) steps.

Theorem 9.2 (Lyapunov)

Let \(\dot x = f(x)\) with \(f(x^*) = 0\), and let \(V\) be continuously differentiable with \(V(x^*) = 0\) and \(V(x) \gt 0\) for \(x \ne x^*\). If

\[ \dot V(x) = \nabla V(x) \cdot f(x) \le 0, \tag{9.2} \]

then \(x^*\) is stable. If moreover \(\dot V(x) \lt 0\) for \(x \ne x^*\) and \(V(x) \to \infty\) as \(|x| \to \infty\), every trajectory converges to \(x^*\). If only \(\dot V \le 0\) holds and the trajectory stays in a bounded set, it approaches the largest invariant set inside \(\{\dot V = 0\}\) (LaSalle's invariance principle).

Theorem 9.3 (the descent lemma)

If \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(f \ge f^*\), then

\[ f\big(x - \eta \nabla f(x)\big) \le f(x) - \eta\Big(1 - \frac{L\eta}{2}\Big)\, |\nabla f(x)|^2, \tag{9.3} \]

and gradient descent with \(\eta = 1/L\) satisfies

\[ \min_{k \lt K} |\nabla f(x_k)|^2 \le \frac{2L\,\big(f(x_0) - f^*\big)}{K}. \tag{9.4} \]

Proposition 9.4 (potential games)

A game in which players minimize costs is an exact potential game if some \(\Phi\) on strategy profiles satisfies

\[ c_i(s_i', s_{-i}) - c_i(s_i, s_{-i}) = \Phi(s_i', s_{-i}) - \Phi(s_i, s_{-i}) \]

for every player \(i\) and every change \(s_i \to s_i'\). In a finite exact potential game, every sequence of strictly improving moves is finite and ends at a pure Nash equilibrium. Congestion games are exact potential games with Rosenthal's potential \(\Phi = \sum_{e} \sum_{j=1}^{n_e} \ell_e(j)\), where \(n_e\) is the load on resource \(e\) and \(\ell_e\) its cost per user.

9.4Derivation

(9.1). Adding \(c(x_k) \le V(x_k) - V(x_{k+1})\) over \(k \lt K\) telescopes to \(V(x_0) - V(x_K) \le V(x_0) - V_{\min}\), and the minimum of \(K\) numbers is at most their mean.

(9.2). For \(\varepsilon \gt 0\) let \(m\) be the minimum of \(V\) on the sphere \(|x - x^*| = \varepsilon\), which is positive, and choose \(\delta\) with \(V \lt m\) on the ball of radius \(\delta\). A trajectory that starts in that ball has \(V \lt m\) forever, since \(V\) never increases, so it never reaches the sphere. For convergence, \(V(x(t))\) decreases to a limit \(v\). If \(v \gt 0\), the trajectory stays in the compact set \(\{v \le V \le V(x(0))\}\), where \(\dot V \le -c \lt 0\) for some \(c\), and \(V\) would fall below \(v\) in finite time. So \(v = 0\) and \(x(t) \to x^*\).

(9.3) and (9.4). Integrating \(\nabla f\) along the segment from \(x\) to \(y\) and using the Lipschitz bound gives \(f(y) \le f(x) + \nabla f(x)\cdot(y - x) + \tfrac L2 |y - x|^2\). Putting \(y = x - \eta\nabla f(x)\) gives (9.3). At \(\eta = 1/L\) each step lowers \(f\) by at least \(|\nabla f(x_k)|^2/2L\), and (9.1) with \(V = f\) gives (9.4).

Proposition 9.4. A strictly improving move lowers the mover's cost, so it lowers \(\Phi\) by the same amount. A finite game has finitely many profiles, so \(\Phi\) cannot fall forever, and the sequence ends at a profile where no player can improve, which is a pure Nash equilibrium. For a congestion game, a driver who leaves route \(e\) for route \(e'\) changes Rosenthal's sum by \(\ell_{e'}(n_{e'} + 1) - \ell_e(n_e)\), which is the change in that driver's cost. ∎

When the drop vanishes on a curve. A damped pendulum has energy \(E = \tfrac12 \omega^2 + (1 - \cos\theta)\) and \(\dot E = -b\omega^2\), which is zero all along the line \(\omega = 0\), so the strict form of Theorem 9.2 does not apply. A trajectory cannot stay on that line except at a rest point, because there \(\dot\omega = -\sin\theta \ne 0\). The largest invariant set inside \(\{\dot E = 0\}\) is the set of equilibria, and LaSalle's principle sends every trajectory to one of them.

Earlier chapters, read for their potential. Banach's proof uses the distance \(d(x_k, x^*)\), which shrinks by \(\gamma\) each step (Chapter 4). The free energy \(F(\rho_t)\) is a Lyapunov function for Fokker-Planck, and (5.3) is its rate of descent (Chapter 5). Hedge's regret proof bounds \(\ln \Phi_t = \ln \sum_i e^{-\eta L_{t,i}}\) from both sides (Chapter 8). At zero friction the energy neither rises nor falls, which is Noether's theorem for symmetry in time (Chapter 7).

9.5Figures

Figure 9.2Each gradient step lowers f by a guaranteed amount

On an L-smooth function each gradient step with η below 2/L lowers f by at least η(1 − Lη/2)|∇f|², so the drops add up to at most f(x₀) − f*, which bounds how many steps can have a large gradient.

Here f(x, y) = 2(1 − cos x) + 5y² has L = 10, and its Hessian entry 2 cos x is −1.884 at the start (2.8, 1), so descent begins where f is nonconvex. At the default ηL = 1, f falls on all 60 steps, the measured curve stays under the guaranteed one, and min |∇f|² over the 60 steps is 4.5e−9 against the bound 2.96. The bound holds for every L-smooth function, so on this easy one it is loose. Slide ηL to 1.8: the path zigzags across the valley, and f still falls on every step. At ηL = 2 the y-coordinate flips sign forever, |∇f|² stays at 100, and f stalls at 5. At 2.05, f rises on 59 of the 60 steps and reaches 1.7e3.

Figure 9.3Best responses stop when a potential exists

In a congestion game every improving move lowers Rosenthal's potential by exactly the mover's gain, so best responses stop at an equilibrium, while rock-paper-scissors has no such number and its best responses cycle forever.

Road 1 takes 2n minutes for n drivers, road 2 takes n + 6, and road 3 takes 3n + 2. All 10 drivers start on road 1 and take turns switching to a faster road. Five switches reach the equilibrium (5, 3, 2), where the roads take 10, 9, and 8 minutes, and Φ falls from 110 to 67, the smallest value it takes over every split of the drivers. On each switch the mover saves 15, 11, 8, 6, and then 3 minutes, and Φ drops by the same amount, so the largest gap is 0. Slide the drivers from 8 to 12: equilibrium takes 4 to 7 switches. Switch to Rock-paper-scissors: the players alternate best responses, the state repeats after 6 moves, and the movers' changes around that cycle sum to −12, where a potential would need 0. Press Play to step through the moves.

9.6Four ways to see it

The same telescoping sum is a stability proof, a convergence rate, a martingale argument, and an accounting trick.

  1. 1A Lyapunov functiondynamics and control

    For a flow, a function that never increases along trajectories fences them in: its level sets are crossed only inward (Figure 9.1). Control theory turns this around and picks the input that makes a chosen \(\dot V\) most negative, the same minimization over \(u\) as the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation of Chapter 3.

  2. 1 → 2Take the gradient flow \(\dot x = -\nabla f(x)\) and \(V = f\). Then \(\dot V = -|\nabla f|^2\), so \(\int_0^\infty |\nabla f(x(t))|^2\, dt \le f(x_0) - f^*\). An Euler step of size \(\eta\) keeps the first-order drop \(\eta|\nabla f|^2\) and loses at most \(\tfrac L2 \eta^2 |\nabla f|^2\) to curvature, which is (9.3). The discrete potential survives exactly while \(\eta \lt 2/L\).

  3. 2A descent lemmaoptimization

    Every rate for gradient methods comes from a potential: \(f\) itself for nonconvex problems (Figure 9.2), \(f + \tfrac{\mu}{2}|x - x^*|^2\)-type sums for accelerated methods, and the Bregman distance to the optimum for mirror descent (Chapter 6).

  4. 2 → 3With a noisy gradient \(g\), \(\mathbb E[g] = \nabla f\) and \(\mathbb E|g - \nabla f|^2 \le \sigma^2\), the same expansion and an expectation over the noise give

    \[ \mathbb E\big[f(x_{k+1}) \mid x_k\big] \le f(x_k) - \eta\Big(1 - \frac{L\eta}{2}\Big)|\nabla f(x_k)|^2 + \frac{L \eta^2 \sigma^2}{2}. \]

    So \(f(x_k) + (K - k)\tfrac{L\eta^2\sigma^2}{2}\) only goes down in expectation: it is a supermartingale.

  5. 3A supermartingaleprobability

    A process that goes down on average and is bounded below converges almost surely (Doob). Stochastic gradient methods, stochastic approximation, and the gambler's ruin are analyzed this way, and optional stopping turns a martingale potential into exact probabilities.

  6. 1 → 4Charge each operation an amortized cost \(\hat c_k = c_k + \Phi_k - \Phi_{k-1}\). Summing telescopes again:

    \[ \sum_{k \le n} c_k = \sum_{k \le n} \hat c_k - \big(\Phi_n - \Phi_0\big) \le \sum_{k \le n} \hat c_k + \Phi_0 - \Phi_{\min}. \]

    For an array that doubles when full, \(\Phi = 2 \cdot \text{size} - \text{capacity}\) makes every append cost at most 3, copies included. A potential game is the same bookkeeping with the players' costs.

  7. 4Amortized analysis and potential gamesalgorithms and economics

    Expensive steps are paid for by a potential that cheap steps built up. Union-find, splay trees, and dynamic arrays are analyzed this way, and in a congestion game every selfish improvement lowers one global number, so selfish routing settles (Figure 9.3).

9.7Where it breaks and what is open

Two things break the method. Some processes have no potential at all: best responses in rock-paper-scissors cycle forever, and Chapter 8's last iterates spiral, because a quantity that only went down would forbid a cycle. And a potential for a flow can fail for its discretization. Past \(\eta = 2/L\) the descent lemma promises nothing, and gradient descent on a sharp start either diverges or catapults: the loss spikes, the weights fly to a flatter region, and training settles where the sharpness is below \(2/\eta\) (Figure 9.4). Neural networks trained with full-batch gradient descent reach this regime routinely. Their sharpness rises until it reaches about \(2/\eta\), and the loss keeps falling over long windows while it rises over short ones (Cohen et al.).

Figure 9.4Past 2/sharpness the loss catapults

Past η = 2/sharpness the descent lemma's potential stops going down, and gradient descent on a two-layer toy either diverges or catapults: the loss spikes, the weights fly to a flatter region, and training settles with sharpness below 2/η.

The loss ½(uv − 1)² belongs to a linear network with one hidden unit and one training point, and on the minimum set uv = 1 the sharpness is u² + v². The start (2.8, 0.1) has sharpness 7.865, so the descent lemma's condition η < 2/sharpness fails there for every η above 0.254. At the default η = 0.4, 2/η = 5: the loss rises on steps 1 and 2 to a peak of 4.359, the weights cross to (0.750, 1.333) on the flat side of uv = 1, and the run settles at sharpness 2.340, below 2/η. Slide η to 0.2: the loss falls on every step and the sharpness ends at 7.845. On the slider, every η from 0.26 to 0.48 sends the loss above its start and still ends below 2/η, and from η = 0.49 the run diverges.

  1. A potential for the edge of stability. At the edge of stability \(f\) is no longer a potential, and something else must be going down. Self-stabilization arguments propose one for simple models (Damian, Nichani, and Lee). A potential that held for real networks would let step sizes be computed from it instead of from \(L\).
  2. Lyapunov stability for samplers and bridges. When \(p_t\) is \(\alpha\)-strongly log-concave, the probability-flow ODE run backward contracts nearby paths at rate \(\tfrac12 g^2 \alpha\), which bounds how score errors accumulate. Designing the forward process or the bridge so that such a certificate holds at every \(t\), and with several basins on purpose, is open.
  3. Reward hacking as instability. One definition of reward hacking treats it as an unstable state with high reward and penalizes the value's Laplacian. A Lyapunov function for the closed loop, decreasing under the policy everywhere except in hacked states, would make that definition testable on environments with known hacks.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 9.1The descent lemma and its rate

    From the Lipschitz bound on \(\nabla f\) alone, derive the quadratic upper bound \(f(y) \le f(x) + \nabla f(x)\cdot(y - x) + \tfrac L2|y - x|^2\), then (9.3), the best fixed \(\eta\), and (9.4).

    Solution

    By the fundamental theorem of calculus and the Lipschitz bound,

    \[ \begin{aligned} f(y) - f(x) - \nabla f(x)\cdot(y - x) &= \int_0^1 \big(\nabla f(x + s(y - x)) - \nabla f(x)\big)\cdot(y - x)\, ds \\ &\le \int_0^1 L s\, |y - x|^2\, ds = \tfrac L2 |y - x|^2. \end{aligned} \]

    With \(y = x - \eta\nabla f(x)\) the bound reads \(f(y) \le f(x) - \eta|\nabla f|^2 + \tfrac L2 \eta^2 |\nabla f|^2\), which is (9.3). The guaranteed drop \(\eta(1 - L\eta/2)\) is largest at \(\eta = 1/L\), where it is \(1/(2L)\). Summing \(f(x_k) - f(x_{k+1}) \ge |\nabla f(x_k)|^2/2L\) over \(k \lt K\) gives \(K \min_k |\nabla f(x_k)|^2 / 2L \le f(x_0) - f^*\).

  2. Derivation 9.2Exponential convergence from a Lyapunov inequality

    Suppose \(f\) satisfies the Polyak-Łojasiewicz inequality \(\tfrac12 |\nabla f(x)|^2 \ge \mu\, (f(x) - f^*)\). Show that the gradient flow \(\dot x = -\nabla f(x)\) has \(f(x(t)) - f^* \le e^{-2\mu t}\,(f(x_0) - f^*)\), and that gradient descent with \(\eta = 1/L\) has \(f(x_k) - f^* \le (1 - \mu/L)^k (f(x_0) - f^*)\).

    Solution

    Let \(V = f - f^*\). Along the flow \(\dot V = -|\nabla f|^2 \le -2\mu V\), so \(\frac{d}{dt}\big(e^{2\mu t} V\big) \le 0\) and \(V(t) \le e^{-2\mu t} V(0)\).

    For gradient descent, (9.3) at \(\eta = 1/L\) gives \(V_{k+1} \le V_k - |\nabla f(x_k)|^2/2L \le V_k - \tfrac{\mu}{L} V_k\), so \(V_k \le (1 - \mu/L)^k V_0\). The inequality needs no convexity. It holds for least squares, including underdetermined systems whose minimizers fill an affine subspace, where \(f\) is not strongly convex.

Project. On a small MLP trained with full-batch gradient descent at several step sizes around \(2/\lambda_{\max}\), log the loss and the top Hessian eigenvalue every step. Propose a quantity built from them that falls monotonically through the phase at the edge of stability, and report the fraction of steps on which it rises, against the loss's own fraction.

Chapter 10

Entropy is a code length

Information theory, from communication

Describe an outcome \(x\) with \(-\log_2 p(x)\) bits, and no code does better on average. Prediction and compression are then one task: a model that predicts well is a short code, and a language model's loss in bits per token is the size of the file it would compress its text to.

Uses Chapter 2 and Appendix A.5.

10.1Motivation

Before 1948, engineers designed codes and modulation schemes case by case, and the measures of capacity they had, from Nyquist and Hartley, counted symbols and signal levels rather than probabilities. Shannon asked how many bits a source needs on average and found one number, the entropy, that bounds every code at once and is reached by long ones. The same number measures how well a model predicts, so compression, prediction, and, through Kelly, betting became one problem.

PAPERA document that moved capital

A Mathematical Theory of Communication

Information is measured in bits, and a noisy channel carries it reliably up to a fixed capacity.

Claude E. Shannon, 1948 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

It founded information theory, and with it the digital communication, storage, and compression that followed.

The link to this chapter: Theorem 2 derives \(H = -K \sum_i p_i \log p_i\) from three requirements, and the fundamental theorem for a noiseless channel (Theorem 9) proves that a source can be sent at \(C/H - \varepsilon\) symbols per second and no faster, with codewords between \(\log_2(1/p)\) and \(1 + \log_2(1/p)\) bits long, which is (10.2). Section 28 defines the rate at a given fidelity as a minimized mutual information, the rate-distortion function of Chapter 11.

PAPERA document that moved capital

Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

A language model's loss falls as a power law in parameters, data, and compute, so capability can be planned.

Jared Kaplan et al., 2020 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

It turned model training into a planned investment and helped justify the compute buildout that followed. Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022, also on the site) revised the split toward more data.

The link to this chapter: the loss is "the cross entropy loss in nats" per token (Section 1.3), a code length by (10.3). Kaplan's power laws have no constant term, and they contradict each other near 1.7 nats per token (Section 6.3), which the paper offers as a rough estimate of the entropy of the text. Chinchilla's fit has one, \(E = 1.69\) nats per token, read the same way: the code length no model can beat.

10.2Intuition

Almost all the probability of a long sequence of draws sits on about \(2^{nH}\) nearly equally likely sequences, so naming one takes \(nH\) bits.

Figure 10.1Long runs are typical, and the likeliest run is not

For long runs of coin flips, −(1/n) log₂ p of the run actually drawn concentrates on the entropy H, so about 2ⁿᴴ typical runs carry almost all the probability while the single most likely run sits far below them.

Every run with k ones has the same probability, so the binomial mass over k gives the exact distribution of bits per flip, with no sampling. At the defaults, n = 200 flips with p(1) = 0.1 and ε = 0.05, the entropy is H = 0.469 bits. The band H ± ε holds probability 0.591 and 2^99.7 of the 2^200 runs, so (1/n) log₂ of its size is 0.498, inside [0.419, 0.519]. The all-zeros run is the most likely single run, at 0.152 bits per flip and probability 7.1e−10. Slide n to 2000: the band holds 0.981 of the probability, (1/n) log₂ of its size is 0.514, and all zeros has probability 3.1e−92. Shrink ε to 0.01 there: the size exponent falls to 0.476, nearer H, and the band holds 0.372. At p = 0.5 every run has probability 2^−n and all of them are typical.

10.3Statement

Theorem 10.1 (Kraft and the source coding theorem)

The codeword lengths \(\ell(x)\) of a prefix code, in which no codeword begins another, satisfy

\[ \sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)} \le 1, \tag{10.1} \]

and any lengths that satisfy (10.1) belong to some prefix code. For a source \(p\), every prefix code has expected length at least the entropy, and the lengths \(\lceil -\log_2 p(x) \rceil\) come within one bit of it:

\[ H(p) = -\sum_x p(x) \log_2 p(x) \;\le\; \mathbb E_p\, \ell(X) \;\lt\; H(p) + 1. \tag{10.2} \]

Proposition 10.2 (the wrong model costs KL)

Coding a source \(p\) with lengths \(-\log_2 q(x)\) built for a model \(q\) costs the cross-entropy, and the extra bits are the KL:

\[ \mathbb E_p\big[-\log_2 q(X)\big] = H(p) + \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q). \tag{10.3} \]

Theorem 10.3 (asymptotic equipartition)

For \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) drawn independently from \(p\), \(-\frac1n \log_2 p(X_1, \dots, X_n) \to H(p)\) in probability. For \(\varepsilon \gt 0\) and \(n\) large, the typical set \(A_\varepsilon^{(n)}\) of sequences whose surprisal per symbol is within \(\varepsilon\) of \(H\) has probability above \(1 - \varepsilon\), and

\[ (1 - \varepsilon)\, 2^{n(H - \varepsilon)} \le \big|A_\varepsilon^{(n)}\big| \le 2^{n(H + \varepsilon)}. \tag{10.4} \]

Theorem 10.4 (Kelly)

In a race with odds \(o_i\), betting the fractions \(b_i\) of wealth on outcome \(i\), with \(\sum_i b_i = 1\), grows \(\log_2\) wealth at the rate \(W(b) = \sum_i p_i \log_2 (b_i o_i)\) per race. The rate is largest at \(b = p\), and

\[ W(p) - W(b) = \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, b). \tag{10.5} \]

10.4Derivation

(10.1). For a finite alphabet, put the codewords on a binary tree, and let \(L\) be the longest length. A codeword of length \(\ell\) is a node whose descendants at depth \(L\) number \(2^{L - \ell}\), and in a prefix code these sets of descendants are disjoint, so \(\sum_x 2^{L - \ell(x)} \le 2^L\). Conversely, assign codewords in order of increasing length, each the leftmost free node at its depth. Inequality (10.1) guarantees one is always free.

(10.2). Let \(r(x) = 2^{-\ell(x)} / \sum_y 2^{-\ell(y)}\). Then

\[ \mathbb E_p\,\ell(X) - H(p) = \sum_x p(x) \log_2 \frac{p(x)}{2^{-\ell(x)}} = \mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, r) - \log_2 \sum_y 2^{-\ell(y)} \;\ge\; 0, \]

since both terms are nonnegative. The lengths \(\lceil -\log_2 p(x)\rceil\) satisfy (10.1), because \(2^{-\ell(x)} \le p(x)\), and each is less than \(-\log_2 p(x) + 1\).

(10.3).

\[ -\sum_x p \log_2 q = -\sum_x p \log_2 p + \sum_x p \log_2 (p/q). \]

(10.4). The surprisal per symbol \(\frac1n \sum_i -\log_2 p(X_i)\) is an average of independent terms with mean \(H\), so the law of large numbers gives the limit. Each typical sequence has probability between \(2^{-n(H + \varepsilon)}\) and \(2^{-n(H - \varepsilon)}\), so \(1 \ge P(A) \ge |A|\, 2^{-n(H+\varepsilon)}\) and \(1 - \varepsilon \le P(A) \le |A|\, 2^{-n(H - \varepsilon)}\).

(10.5).

\[ W(b) = \sum_i p_i \log_2 o_i + \sum_i p_i \log_2 p_i - \sum_i p_i \log_2 (p_i / b_i), \]

and only the last term, \(-\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, b)\), depends on \(b\). ∎

Whole sequences. Arithmetic coding turns any predictive model \(p(x_t \mid x_{\lt t})\) into a code for a whole sequence. It narrows an interval in \([0, 1)\) by each symbol's probability, so the final interval has width \(p(x_1, \dots, x_n)\), and naming a point inside it takes at most \(-\log_2 p(x_1, \dots, x_n) + 2\) bits, for a decoder that knows the length \(n\) or reads an end symbol. The code length of a text is at most the model's summed loss in bits, plus two.

10.5Figures

Figure 10.2Arithmetic coding spends −log₂ p bits, plus under 2

Arithmetic coding narrows an interval by each symbol's model probability, so a string costs −log₂ p(string) bits plus under 2, and a worse model costs its cross-entropy.

The string aabaaaadcabaadcabaab was drawn with seed 23 from the letter probabilities 0.6, 0.2, 0.1, and 0.1, and holds 12 a, 4 b, 2 c, and 2 d. The intervals are exact fractions, and the decoder knows the length. With Adaptive counts, which give each letter its count so far plus one, the final interval has width 2^−36.45, and the code length ⌈36.45⌉ + 1 is 38 bits, 1.55 over. The 38-bit codeword under the rows is the shortest dyadic interval inside the final one, and it decodes back to the string. Switch to Own frequencies, whose counts the decoder would also need: the string costs 31.42 bits, 20 times its empirical entropy of 1.571. Uniform costs 40.00, and its extra 8.58 bits equal 20 KL(empirical ‖ uniform). Adaptive counts pay 5.03 bits over own frequencies to learn the counts as they go. Step through the symbols or press Play: over every prefix and model the codeword stays at most 1.82 bits above −log₂ p.

Figure 10.3A bettor with the wrong belief loses KL(p‖q) bits per bet

Betting on a coin at even odds grows wealth by log₂(1 + f) bits per win and log₂(1 − f) per loss, so the best fraction f* = 2p − 1 earns 1 − H(p) bits per bet, and a bettor who believes q earns exactly KL(p‖q) less.

At the defaults the coin lands heads with p = 0.6, and the bettor believes q = 0.7 and stakes f = 0.4 of wealth on heads at even odds. Kelly's fraction f* = 0.2, found by a search over f, grows wealth at G(f*) = 0.0290 bits per bet, which equals 1 − H(0.6). The bettor's rate is G(0.4) = −0.0035, so a coin tilted in the bettor's favor still loses money, and the drop of 0.0326 bits equals KL(0.6 ‖ 0.7). Every f above 0.389 loses at this p. Over 2000 seeded paths of 500 bets the median final log₂ wealth is −1.77 against 500 G(f) = −1.77, and 54.5% of the bettor's paths end below the start against 1.6% of Kelly's. Slide q to 0.6: the gap closes to 0. Slide q to 0.95: f = 0.9, the rate falls to −0.773 bits per bet, and the median path ends at −386.59 bits.

10.6Four ways to see it

Entropy counts possibilities, sets the length of a code, measures how well a model predicts, and prices a bet. Each picture follows from the one before it.

  1. 1Countingcombinatorics and physics

    By Stirling's formula, the number of binary sequences of length \(n\) with \(k\) ones is \(\binom{n}{k} = 2^{n H(k/n) + O(\log n)}\). Entropy is the logarithm of the number of equally likely possibilities, which is Boltzmann's \(S = k_B \ln W\) for the microstates of a gas (Figure 10.1).

  2. 1 → 2Number the roughly \(2^{nH}\) typical sequences, so naming one takes about \(nH\) bits, and give each atypical sequence its own index of \(n \log_2 |\mathcal X| + 1\) bits behind a flag. The atypical ones carry probability below \(\varepsilon\), so the expected length per symbol tends to \(H\): the source coding theorem by counting.

  3. 2Codingengineering

    Kraft's inequality (10.1) is a budget: a codeword of length \(\ell\) spends \(2^{-\ell}\) of a unit of space. Huffman's algorithm spends it optimally symbol by symbol, and arithmetic coding spends it on whole sequences, within two bits of \(-\log_2 p\) (Figure 10.2).

  4. 2 → 3Feed arithmetic coding a model's predictions \(p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{\lt t})\). The code for a text has length at most \(\sum_t -\log_2 p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{\lt t}) + 2\), and its average over text from the true source is the cross-entropy, \(H\) plus the KL of (10.3). Lowering a model's loss and shortening its code are the same act.

  5. 3Predictionmachine learning and statistics

    A language model's cross-entropy loss, in bits per token, is the size of its compressed text. Minimum description length picks the model that makes the total, the model's own length plus the data's code length under it, shortest. Kolmogorov complexity, the length of the shortest program that prints \(x\), is the limit: no algorithm computes it, and for \(n\) draws from a computable source its expected value is \(nH\) up to the length of a program for the source plus \(O(\log n)\).

  6. 3 → 4Let the odds be fair for some distribution \(r\), so \(o_i = 1/r_i\). Then

    \[ W(b) = \sum_i p_i \log_2 \frac{b_i}{r_i} = \mathbb E_p\big[-\log_2 r(X)\big] - \mathbb E_p\big[-\log_2 b(X)\big], \]

    the bookmaker's log loss on the outcomes minus the bettor's, so wealth grows by the number of bits per race by which the bettor predicts better than the bookmaker.

  7. 4Bettingfinance

    At even odds on a coin with \(p \gt \tfrac12\), the Kelly bettor stakes \(f^* = 2p - 1\) of wealth and grows it by \(1 - H(p)\) bits per bet. Betting about twice that fraction drives the growth rate to zero when the edge is small, and a bettor who believes \(q\) gives up \(\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q)\) bits per bet (Figure 10.3).

10.7Where it breaks and what is open

The most probable sequence is atypical. For a coin with \(p(1) = 0.1\), the all-zeros sequence is the single most likely sequence of every length, yet its surprisal per flip is \(-\log_2 0.9 = 0.152\) bits against \(H = 0.469\), so it lies outside the typical set, and the chance of drawing it, \(0.9^n\), vanishes. A language model behaves the same way: the highest-probability continuation, which beam search approximates, carries little surprisal per token and often repeats itself, while samples land at the model's entropy rate (Figure 10.4). Differential entropy fails in another way. For continuous \(X\), \(h(X) = -\int p \log p\) changes under a change of variables, \(h(aX) = h(X) + \log |a|\), and can be negative, so only differences such as KL and mutual information carry meaning, and a code for continuous data must first quantize it.

Figure 10.4The most probable sequence looks nothing like a sample

The most probable sequence of a language model is atypical: its surprisal per token sits far below the entropy rate, it repeats itself, and samples never come near it.

The chain has eight tokens a to h. Token a repeats with probability 0.5, b → c → d → b runs at 0.4 per step, and the entropy rate is 2.704 bits per token. At the default n = 20 the 2000 samples average 2.712 bits per token, against an exact mean of 2.717 that counts the first token's 2.966 bits. The most probable sequence, found exactly by Viterbi and by beam search of width 4, is twenty a's at 1.088 bits per token, with probability 2.8e−7. It uses 1 token where samples use 7.22 on average, and no sample is as probable: the lowest sample sits at 1.757. Set the width to 1 (greedy): decoding falls into the cycle c d b at 1.387 bits per token. Slide n down to 4: the mode aaaa has probability 0.019, and 1.60% of samples equal it. From n = 8 on none of the 2000 samples reaches the mode, and at n = 40 its probability is 2.7e−13.

  1. The mode or the typical set. One can ask whether the sequence with the lowest entropy per token is the most probable one. Equipartition answers that the most probable sequence is atypical and that each typical sequence is improbable. Which of the two a decoder should aim at is open for tasks with checkable answers, where the mode is sometimes right, and branch-and-bound decoding for diffusion language models needs an answer to choose its objective.
  2. Compression as a measure of capability. Language models compress text far better than general-purpose compressors when their own size is not counted (Delétang et al.), and loss in bits tracks downstream ability in many settings. When fewer bits per token stops predicting capability, as with memorized or contaminated data, is open.
  3. Kolmogorov complexity in practice. It cannot be computed. A trained model's code length, plus the length of the model, bounds it from above. The prequential code length of a training run, the sum of the losses as the model learns, minus the final model's loss, measures the information the trained parameters hold about the data (Blier and Ollivier). Whether it ranks models and datasets usefully at scale is open.

    • Build the Huffman code for p: its lengths, and its mean length in bits. Then code the source with the Huffman code built for q. How many bits per symbol now, and where do the extra bits come from?

    huffman_lengths([0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125])                        # [1, 2, 3, 3]
mean_bits([0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125], [0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125])   # 1.75
mean_bits([0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125], [0.125, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5])   # 2.625

  2. Exercise 10.2 A language model's loss is its file size

    • Arithmetic-code the 20 characters "abcabcabcabcabacabca". What is −log₂ p of the string, how many bits does the coder send, and what is the model's loss in bits per character?

    ideal_bits("abcabcabcabcabacabca")      # 14.9766
coded_bits("abcabcabcabcabacabca")      # 16
bits_per_char("abcabcabcabcabacabca")   # 0.7488

    • Which f grows wealth fastest, and at how many bits per bet? A bettor who believes heads has probability 0.7 picks f by the same rule. How many bits per bet does the wrong belief cost?

growth_bits(0.6, 0.2)        # 0.02905
belief_cost_bits(0.6, 0.7)   # 0.03258

  4. Exercise 10.4 The most likely sequence is rare

    • How likely is that sequence, and what is its surprisal per flip against H? How likely is a sample to hold exactly 10 ones?

mode_bits_per_flip()         # 0.152

  5. Exercise 10.5 The typical set

    • A coin shows 1 with probability 0.1, so H = 0.469 bits. Flip it n times. A sequence is typical when its surprisal per flip, −(1/n)·log₂ p(sequence), is within ε = 0.05 of H.
    • For n = 100, what is the probability of the typical set, and how many sequences does it hold, in bits? What does the probability become at n = 1000?

log2_typical_size(100)      # 47.1926

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 10.1The best code lengths

    Minimize \(\sum_x p(x)\, \ell(x)\) over real lengths with \(\sum_x 2^{-\ell(x)} = 1\) by a Lagrange multiplier (Appendix A.5), and show that the minimum is \(H(p)\), reached at \(\ell(x) = -\log_2 p(x)\).

    Solution

    Differentiate \(\sum_x p\,\ell + \lambda (\sum_x 2^{-\ell} - 1)\) in \(\ell(x)\): \(p(x) - \lambda \ln 2\; 2^{-\ell(x)} = 0\), so \(2^{-\ell(x)} = p(x)/(\lambda \ln 2)\). Summing over \(x\) and using the constraint gives \(\lambda \ln 2 = 1\), so \(\ell(x) = -\log_2 p(x)\), and the objective is \(H(p)\).

    The objective is linear and the constraint set \(\{\sum 2^{-\ell} \le 1\}\) is convex, so this stationary point is the minimum. Integer lengths cost at most one more bit, which is (10.2).

  2. Derivation 10.2Kelly on a coin

    At even odds on a coin with \(P(\text{heads}) = p\), staking a fraction \(f\) of wealth on heads multiplies wealth by \(1 + f\) or \(1 - f\). Derive the growth rate \(G(f)\), the best \(f\), and \(G(f^*) = 1 - H(p)\) bits. Then show that \(G\) returns to about zero near \(f = 2f^*\) when the edge is small.

    Solution

    \(G(f) = p \log_2(1 + f) + (1 - p)\log_2(1 - f)\). Setting \(G'(f) = 0\) gives \(p/(1 + f) = (1-p)/(1 - f)\), so \(f^* = 2p - 1\). Then \(1 + f^* = 2p\) and \(1 - f^* = 2(1-p)\), so

    \[ G(f^*) = p\log_2 2p + (1-p)\log_2 2(1-p) = 1 - H(p). \]

    In nats, \(G(f) \approx (2p - 1) f - f^2/2\) for small \(f\), which is zero at \(f = 0\) and at \(f = 2(2p - 1) = 2 f^*\).
