Project. On a small open language model, take 200 prompts and compare the continuations of greedy decoding, beam search, plain sampling, and locally typical sampling by their surprisal per token against the model's conditional entropy at each step. Report the share of tokens each decoder keeps within 0.5 bits of the entropy.

Chapter 11

Information never grows downstream

Information theory, from estimation

The information \(Y\) carries about \(X\) is the KL between their joint law and the product of their marginals. Processing \(Y\) can only lose it, and in a Gaussian channel it grows at exactly half the error of the best denoiser, so information is integrated denoising error.

Uses Chapters 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, and 10, and Appendix A.1.

11.1Motivation

Every learning system processes data in stages: a sensor, a pipeline, an encoder, a decoder. Each stage can be engineered, and none can recover information about the source that an earlier stage discarded. Mutual information makes that precise. It gives the speed limit of a noisy channel, the fewest bits a lossy code needs, and, in a Gaussian channel, half the area under the best denoiser's error curve plotted against the signal-to-noise ratio, which ties it to the diffusion models of Chapter 1.

PAPERA document that moved capital

Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space

Train word vectors to predict their neighbors, and meaning becomes geometry.

Tomas Mikolov et al., 2013 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

Word embeddings became a standard way to represent words and set up the representation learning behind later language models.

The link to this chapter: the skip-gram model it introduced, trained with the negative sampling of its companion paper, implicitly factorizes the matrix of pointwise mutual information between words and contexts, shifted by \(\log k\) for \(k\) negative samples: \(w \cdot c = \mathrm{PMI}(w, c) - \log k\) when the vectors are wide enough (Levy and Goldberg, NeurIPS 2014). The average of the pointwise mutual information over pairs is the mutual information (11.1).

11.2Intuition

Information about a source is a quantity that each processing step can keep or lose but never create.

Figure 11.1Each noisy channel leaves less information about the bit

A bit sent through two noisy channels in a row keeps less information about its source after each one, and Fano's inequality turns the information left into a floor on how often any guess of the source is wrong.

At the defaults ε₁ = 0.10 and ε₂ = 0.15, the first channel keeps I(X; Y) = 0.531 bits of the 1 bit in X, the second channel alone would keep 0.390, and the pair keeps I(X; Z) = 0.240, under its ceiling of 0.390. The two channels act as one that flips with probability 0.220. The best guess of X from Z errs 0.220 of the time, and Fano's floor is also 0.220, because a fair bit through symmetric channels meets the bound with equality. Slide ε₂ to 0.5: I(X; Z) falls to 0 and the guess errs half the time. Switch to the biased bit: the best guess from Z errs 0.200 of the time, the rate of the rarer value, against a floor of 0.133. Over every setting of both sliders and both sources, I(X; Z) stays at or under its ceiling.

11.3Statement

Definition 11.1 (mutual information)

\[ I(X; Y) = \mathrm{KL}\big(p_{XY} \,\big\|\, p_X \otimes p_Y\big) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y), \qquad I(X; Y, Z) = I(X; Y) + I(X; Z \mid Y). \tag{11.1} \]

Theorem 11.2 (data processing and Fano)

If \(X \to Y \to Z\) is a Markov chain, then

\[ I(X; Z) \le I(X; Y). \tag{11.2} \]

If \(X\) and its estimate \(\hat X(Y)\) both take values in a finite set \(\mathcal X\), the estimate errs with a probability \(P_e\) that satisfies, with \(h\) the binary entropy,

\[ H(X \mid Y) \le h(P_e) + P_e \log\big(|\mathcal X| - 1\big). \tag{11.3} \]

Theorem 11.3 (I-MMSE and de Bruijn)

Let \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, I)\) be independent of \(X\), with \(\mathbb E|X|^2 \lt \infty\). For \(Y_{\mathrm{snr}} = \sqrt{\mathrm{snr}}\, X + Z\), in nats,

\[ \frac{d}{d\,\mathrm{snr}}\, I(X; Y_{\mathrm{snr}}) = \tfrac12\, \mathrm{mmse}(\mathrm{snr}), \qquad \mathrm{mmse}(\mathrm{snr}) = \mathbb E\, \big|X - \mathbb E[X \mid Y_{\mathrm{snr}}]\big|^2, \tag{11.4} \]

and the differential entropy of \(X_t = X + \sqrt t\, Z\) rises at half its Fisher information \(J(p) = \mathbb E\, |\nabla \log p|^2\):

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\, h(X_t) = \tfrac12\, J(X_t). \tag{11.5} \]

Proposition 11.4 (rate-distortion)

The least rate per symbol at which long sequences of independent copies of \(X\) can be described within expected distortion \(D\) per symbol is \(R(D) = \min I(X; \hat X)\) over channels \(p(\hat x \mid x)\) with \(\mathbb E\, d(X, \hat X) \le D\). At a multiplier \(\beta \ge 0\), the minimizing channel is a tilt of its own output marginal \(q\):

\[ p(\hat x \mid x) = \frac{q(\hat x)\, e^{-\beta\, d(x, \hat x)}}{\sum_{\hat x'} q(\hat x')\, e^{-\beta\, d(x, \hat x')}}, \qquad q(\hat x) = \sum_x p(x)\, p(\hat x \mid x). \tag{11.6} \]

For a Gaussian source \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) with squared error, \(R(D) = \tfrac12 \log(\sigma^2 / D)\) for \(D \le \sigma^2\).

11.4Derivation

(11.1).

\[ \mathbb E \log \frac{p(x, y)}{p(x) p(y)} = \mathbb E \log \frac{p(x \mid y)}{p(x)} = H(X) - H(X \mid Y). \]

For the chain rule, split \(\frac{p(x \mid y, z)}{p(x)} = \frac{p(x \mid y)}{p(x)} \cdot \frac{p(x \mid y, z)}{p(x \mid y)}\) and take expectations of the logarithm.

(11.2). Expand \(I(X; Y, Z)\) by the chain rule both ways:

\[ I(X; Z) + I(X; Y \mid Z) = I(X; Y) + I(X; Z \mid Y). \]

The Markov property makes \(I(X; Z \mid Y) = 0\), and \(I(X; Y \mid Z) \ge 0\).

(11.3). Let \(E\) indicate an error. \(E\) is a function of \(X\) and \(Y\), so

\[ H(X \mid Y) = H(X, E \mid Y) = H(E \mid Y) + H(X \mid E, Y). \]

The first term is at most \(h(P_e)\). Given no error, \(X = \hat X(Y)\) is known, and given an error, \(X\) has at most \(|\mathcal X| - 1\) values left, so the second term is at most \(P_e \log(|\mathcal X| - 1)\).

(11.5). The density \(p_t\) of \(X_t\) solves the heat equation \(\partial_t p = \tfrac12 \Delta p\) (Chapter 1, with \(g = 1\)). Integrating by parts,

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\Big(-\int p_t \log p_t\Big) = -\tfrac12 \int \Delta p_t\, \log p_t = \tfrac12 \int \frac{|\nabla p_t|^2}{p_t} = \tfrac12\, J(X_t). \]

(11.4). Write \(\mathrm{snr} = 1/t\). Scaling by \(\sqrt t\) does not change information, so \(I(X; Y_{\mathrm{snr}}) = I(X; X_t) = h(X_t) - \tfrac{d}{2}\log(2\pi e t)\). By Tweedie's formula (Chapter 1) the score of \(X_t\) is \((\mathbb E[X \mid X_t] - X_t)/t\), and the orthogonality of the estimation error to functions of \(X_t\) gives \(J(X_t) = (d\,t - \mathrm{mmse})/t^2\). Then \(\frac{d}{dt} I = \tfrac12 J - \frac{d}{2t} = -\frac{\mathrm{mmse}}{2t^2}\), and \(\frac{dt}{d\,\mathrm{snr}} = -t^2\) gives (11.4).

(11.6). Minimize \(I(X; \hat X) + \beta\, \mathbb E\, d\) over channels, with a multiplier \(\nu(x)\) for each normalization. Stationarity in \(p(\hat x \mid x)\) reads \(\log \frac{p(\hat x \mid x)}{q(\hat x)} + \beta\, d(x, \hat x) + \nu(x) = 0\), which is (11.6). For the Gaussian,

\[ I(X; \hat X) = h(X) - h(X \mid \hat X) \ge h(X) - h(X - \hat X) \ge \tfrac12 \log(2\pi e \sigma^2) - \tfrac12 \log(2 \pi e D), \]

because a Gaussian has the largest entropy at a given variance. Taking \(X = \hat X + N\) with independent \(\hat X \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 - D)\) and \(N \sim \mathcal N(0, D)\) reaches the bound. ∎

Blahut-Arimoto. Alternate the two halves of (11.6): fix \(q\) and tilt the channel, then fix the channel and recompute \(q\). Each half minimizes the joint objective \(\sum_x p(x)\, \mathrm{KL}\big(p(\cdot \mid x) \,\|\, q\big) + \beta\, \mathbb E\, d\) in one block of variables, so the objective is a potential that never rises (Chapter 9), and the iteration is a fixed-point method (Chapter 4) whose fixed points are the tilts of Chapter 2. The information bottleneck replaces the distortion by the information lost about a target \(Y\) and has a tilted solution of a similar form, though its distortion depends on the encoder, so three equations are iterated and the solution need not be unique, and a \(\beta\)-VAE's loss is a distortion plus \(\beta\) times a rate (the encoder's KL from its prior, an upper bound on \(I(X; Z)\)), which is the objective above with multiplier \(1/\beta\). Under squared error, uniform scalar quantization of a smooth source at high resolution, followed by an ideal entropy code, pays \(\tfrac12 \log_2(\pi e / 6) \approx 0.254\) bits per sample above \(R(D)\).

11.5Figures

Figure 11.2Information is integrated denoising error

In a Gaussian channel the information that Y = √snr·X + Z carries about X grows at exactly half the error of the best denoiser, so I(snr) is half the integral of mmse(γ) from 0 to snr.

Every input has mean 0 and variance 1, and I and mmse are computed separately. At the default ±1 input and snr = 1, the finite difference of I gives dI/dsnr = 0.22480, and the best denoiser's error is mmse = 0.44960, half of which is also 0.22480. The information is I = 0.33683 nats, and half the area under the mmse curve up to snr = 1 is 0.33683. A Gaussian input of the same power carries more, 0.34657 nats, and is harder to denoise, with mmse 0.50000. Slide snr to 100: I reaches 0.69315 = ln 2, all that one sign can carry, the error falls to 2.3884e−23, and the finite difference still matches half of it. Switch to the Chapter 1 mixture, the three-bump density of the first figures standardized: from snr 0.01 to 100 the two sides of the integral identity differ by at most 7.3e−10 nats.

Figure 11.3Blahut-Arimoto finds the best lossy code

Blahut-Arimoto finds the least rate at each distortion by alternating two updates, the tilted channel p(x̂ | x) ∝ q(x̂)·exp(−β d(x, x̂)) and its output marginal q, and on a Gaussian source its curve meets ½ log₂(σ²/D).

The source is N(0, 1) on 201 grid points from −5 to 5, with variance σ² = 0.99999 on the grid, and the reproductions use the same grid with squared error. Each run starts from a uniform q and stops when an iteration lowers the potential F = −Σ p(x) log₂ Z(x) by less than 1e−9 bits. At the default β = 1.995, Blahut-Arimoto stops after 36 iterations at D = 0.2506 and R = 0.99828 bits, and ½ log₂(σ²/D) gives 0.99828. The measured slope dR/dD is −2.879, equal to −β/ln 2, so β prices distortion in bits. At x = 1 the optimal channel has mean 0.7494 and standard deviation 0.4334, which are (1 − D/σ²)x and √(D(1 − D)) for the Gaussian test channel. Slide β down to 0.631, where R falls to 0.168 and nears 0: the run needs 147 iterations. Over all 23 points of the curve, R stays within 6.4e−7 bits of the closed form.

Figure 11.4Unmasking tokens together costs their total correlation

Unmasking several tokens at once, each from its own conditional, costs exactly their total correlation given the tokens already seen, so the sampler's KL from the true model is the sum of these costs over the steps, and the grouping decides how large they are.

The chain has three tokens over eight positions, all 6,561 sequences are enumerated, and positions 1 and 2 share 0.347 nats. At the default two tokens per step in adjacent pairs, the steps pay 0.347, 0.214, 0.212, and 0.211 nats of total correlation, and their sum, 0.984, equals KL(true ‖ sampler) = 0.984. Neighbours in its samples agree 0.578 of the time against 0.742 in the chain. Switch to spread, pairs 1 and 5, 2 and 6, and so on: only the first step pays, 0.0185 nats, because given the tokens already seen each later pair is independent in a Markov chain. Greedy by MI takes the least informative pair at each step, opens with positions 1 and 8, and must close with neighbours 4 and 5, which cost 0.134 of its 0.156. Over all 105 ways to pair the positions, spread has the least summed pairwise information. At four tokens per step the pairwise sum double counts: adjacent groups pay 1.857 nats of total correlation while their pairwise informations add to 2.382. One token per step pays nothing.

11.6Four ways to see it

Mutual information is a distance from independence, the capacity of a channel, the area under a denoising curve, and the score of a contrastive classifier.

  1. 1Distance from independenceprobability

    By (11.1), \(I(X; Y)\) is the KL between the joint law and the product of the marginals: the extra bits per pair that a code assuming independence pays (Chapter 10), and the evidence per sample against independence (Figure 11.1).

  2. 1 → 2Fix the channel \(p(y \mid x)\) and choose the input law. The largest information, \(C = \max_{p(x)} I(X; Y)\), is the capacity, and Shannon's channel coding theorem says it is the largest rate of reliable communication. For a Gaussian channel \(Y = X + W\) with signal power \(P\) and noise power \(N\),

    \[ I = h(Y) - h(W) \le \tfrac12 \log 2\pi e(P + N) - \tfrac12 \log 2\pi e N, \]

    with equality for a Gaussian input, so \(C = \tfrac12 \log(1 + P/N)\).

  3. 2Channel capacitycommunication engineering

    Capacity is the speed limit of a noisy channel. Codes approach it by spreading each message over many uses of the channel, which is the equipartition of Chapter 10 applied to pairs of sequences.

  4. 1 → 3Integrate (11.4) from \(\mathrm{snr} = 0\), where \(Y\) is pure noise and carries no information:

    \[ I(X; Y_{\mathrm{snr}}) = \tfrac12 \int_0^{\mathrm{snr}} \mathrm{mmse}(\gamma)\, d\gamma. \]

    In a diffusion model \(Y_{\mathrm{snr}}\) is the data noised to level \(1/\mathrm{snr}\), and the best denoiser is Tweedie's posterior mean (Chapter 1), so the information the noisy data keeps is half the area under the denoising-error curve.

  5. 3Estimationstatistics and diffusion models

    Information and estimation are one quantity read two ways (Figure 11.2). Applied to each data point rather than on average, the same identity writes \(-\log p(x)\) exactly as an integral over noise levels of how far the best denoiser's error at \(x\) falls below the error for a Gaussian of the same scale, and a trained denoiser turns it into an upper bound on the model's own \(-\log p_\theta(x)\), and on \(\mathbb E_p[-\log p(X)]\) on average (Kong et al.).

  6. 1 → 4Apply Donsker-Varadhan (Chapter 2) to the KL in (11.1): every critic \(T(x, y)\) gives \(I \ge \mathbb E_{p_{XY}}[T] - \log \mathbb E_{p_X \otimes p_Y}[e^{T}]\). A multi-sample bound of the same family averages the critic over the \(N\) candidates in a batch, the true pair included, and is still a lower bound (Poole et al.). It is InfoNCE,

    \[ I(X; Y) \ge \mathbb E \Big[\log \frac{e^{T(x_1, y_1)}}{\frac1N \sum_{j=1}^N e^{T(x_1, y_j)}}\Big], \]

    whose value can never exceed \(\log N\), since the fraction is at most \(N\).

  7. 4Contrastive learningmachine learning

    CLIP and contrastive predictive coding train a critic to pick the true pair out of a batch, and the InfoNCE loss they minimize, a cross-entropy over the batch, equals \(\log N\) minus the bound above. The information the loss can certify is capped at \(\log N\) (Figure 11.5).

11.7Where it breaks and what is open

Mutual information is defined by distributions and measured from samples, and the measurement fails twice. Any distribution-free high-confidence lower bound from \(n\) samples stays below a quantity of order \(\log n\) (McAllester and Stratos, and the open problems of Chapter 2). InfoNCE with a batch of \(N\) cannot exceed \(\log N\) even with the perfect critic, and bounds without that cap, such as the NWJ bound, pay with a variance that, even with the optimal critic, is at least exponential in the information (Song and Ermon). A measured spread can hide that variance: the rare large terms go undrawn, so at high information the spread across batches shrinks while the mean drifts above the truth (Figure 11.5). And the data processing inequality ignores computation. Encrypting an image with a fixed secret key keeps every bit of its information, yet no efficient learner without the key can classify the ciphertext, and decrypting it is a downstream step that raises the information a model family can use, though the information itself cannot grow. Usable information makes this precise relative to a family of predictors (Xu et al.).

Figure 11.5InfoNCE cannot report more than log N

With a batch of N pairs, InfoNCE never reports more than log N nats, even with the perfect critic, while NWJ, which has no cap, pays with a spread across batches that grows with the information.

X and Y have five coordinates each, and each coordinate pair has correlation ρ, so the true information is −(5/2) log(1 − ρ²) nats. Both estimators use the optimal critic log p(y | x)/p(y). At the default ρ = 0.99 and N = 64, the truth is 9.793 nats. InfoNCE reads 4.151 over 200 batches, just under log 64 = 4.159, and no batch passes the cap. NWJ averages 9.669 with a standard deviation of 5.550, and one batch reads −57.1. Slide ρ down: InfoNCE first falls 0.5 nats short at a truth of 3.610, and at ρ = 0.684 NWJ reads 1.579 ± 0.197 against 1.576. Slide ρ up to 0.999: NWJ reads 16.510 ± 0.575 against 15.538, because the shuffled pairs' ratio, whose mean should be 1, averages 0.035 when its rare large values go undrawn. Raising N to 1024 lifts the cap only to 6.931, and InfoNCE reads 6.809 at the default ρ over 10 batches.

  1. Estimating large information. Predicting pairwise information between tokens works because the values are small. Estimating information of hundreds of nats, between a prompt and a long response or between two layers, is open, because the cap of \(\log N\) and the variance of uncapped bounds both stand in the way.
  2. How many tokens to unmask at once. If each token's distribution given the context is exact, a parallel unmasking step costs exactly the total correlation of the tokens it reveals, conditional on that context, and the sum of their pairwise informations approximates it, missing synergy and double-counting redundancy (Figure 11.4). Choosing the least informative group one step at a time is myopic: on a Markov chain it leaves neighbours for the last step and pays several times what a fixed spread schedule pays. Whether pairwise information is enough for long-range structure, and how to budget total correlation per step against the number of steps, is open.
  3. Likelihoods from denoisers. The I-MMSE likelihood of a diffusion model is exact for the best denoiser, and a trained denoiser gives an upper bound on its own \(-\log p_\theta\) and, on average, on the data's (Kong et al.). For masked discrete diffusion the cross-entropy of each revealed token plays the part of the denoising error, and with exact conditionals the negative ELBO equals \(-\log p(x)\), because every unmasking order is a chain rule. How tight these bounds are for trained models, and which noise schedule makes them tightest per unit of compute, are open.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 11.1 Information never grows downstream

    • X is a fair bit. Y is X sent through a binary symmetric channel that flips it with probability ε₁ = 0.1, and Z is Y sent through another with ε₂ = 0.2.
    • In bits, what are I(X; Y) and I(X; Z), and how often does the cascade flip X? Check the data processing inequality, and Fano's floor on the error of any guess of X from Z.
    Answer
    mutual_info_bits(0.1)        # 0.531
mutual_info_bits(0.1, 0.2)   # 0.1733
cascade_flip(0.1, 0.2)       # 0.26

  2. Exercise 11.2 Unmasking two tokens at once

    • A masked model fills the two blanks in "I flew in from _ _". It gives (New, York) 0.36, (San, Francisco) 0.26, (Los, Angeles) 0.26, and each of the six mixed pairs, such as (San, York), 0.02.
    • A parallel sampler unmasks both blanks in one step, each from its own marginal. In nats, what is the KL from the model's joint to the sampler's product of marginals? How often is its pair a city?
    Answer
    parallel_kl_nats()   # 0.6401
real_city_share()    # 0.34

  3. Exercise 11.3 Information is integrated denoising error

    • A fair ±1 bit X is sent as Y = √snr·X + Z with Z ~ N(0, 1). The best denoiser guesses E[X | Y], and its mean squared error is mmse(snr).
    • At snr = 1, compute I(X; Y) in nats from the densities, as h(Y) − h(Y | X), and separately ½∫₀¹ mmse(γ) dγ. What is mmse(1)?
    Answer

half_integrated_mmse(1.0)    # 0.3368

  4. Exercise 11.4 InfoNCE cannot see past log N

    • X and Y are standard normals with correlation ρ = 0.999, so I(X; Y) = −½ ln(1 − ρ²) nats. A batch holds N = 8 pairs, and InfoNCE scores each x against all 8 y's with the best critic, log p(y | x)/p(y).
    • What are the true information and the InfoNCE estimate in nats, averaged over 20,000 batches (seed 0)? How large must N be before log N even reaches the true value?

infonce_nats(0.999, 8)          # 1.8

  5. Exercise 11.5 Rate-distortion of a Gaussian by Blahut-Arimoto

    • X ~ N(0, 1) on a grid of 161 points over [−8, 8], reproduced on the same grid, with squared error. Blahut-Arimoto alternates p(x̂ | x) ∝ q(x̂)·e^{−β(x − x̂)²} and q(x̂) = Σ_x p(x)·p(x̂ | x), from q = p.
    • With β = 2, run it until q moves less than 1e-9. What distortion D and what rate R in bits does it reach? A 1-bit quantizer that sends sign(x) and decodes ±E|X| also spends 1 bit; what is its error?
    Answer
    distortion(2.0)            # 0.25
rate_bits(2.0)             # 1.0
one_bit_quantizer_mse()    # 0.3634

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 11.1From de Bruijn to I-MMSE

    Starting from the heat equation for \(X_t = X + \sqrt t\, Z\) in one dimension, derive de Bruijn's identity (11.5). Then use Tweedie's formula to show \(J(X_t) = (t - \mathrm{mmse}_t)/t^2\), and conclude (11.4). Check it on \(X \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\), where \(I = \tfrac12\log(1 + \mathrm{snr})\).

    Solution

    As in Section 11.4,

    \[ \frac{d}{dt} h = -\int \partial_t p\, (\log p + 1) = -\tfrac12 \int p'' \log p = \tfrac12 \int (p')^2/p = \tfrac12 J, \]

    with the boundary terms vanishing for a Gaussian-smoothed density.

    Tweedie gives the score \(s(y) = (m(y) - y)/t\) with \(m(y) = \mathbb E[X \mid X_t = y]\). Write \(e = X - m(X_t)\), so \(X_t - m = e + \sqrt t\, Z\). Since \(\sqrt t\, Z = X_t - X\), \(\mathbb E[e \sqrt t Z] = \mathbb E[e X_t] - \mathbb E[e X] = 0 - \mathbb E[e^2]\), using \(\mathbb E[e\, g(X_t)] = 0\) and \(\mathbb E[e X] = \mathbb E[e (e + m)] = \mathbb E e^2\). So

    \[ J = \mathbb E(e + \sqrt t Z)^2 / t^2 = (\mathrm{mmse} - 2\,\mathrm{mmse} + t)/t^2 = (t - \mathrm{mmse})/t^2. \]

    With \(I = h(X_t) - \tfrac12 \log(2\pi e t)\), \(\frac{dI}{dt} = -\mathrm{mmse}/(2t^2)\), and \(\mathrm{snr} = 1/t\) gives \(\frac{dI}{d\,\mathrm{snr}} = \tfrac12\,\mathrm{mmse}\). For \(X \sim \mathcal N(0,1)\), \(\mathrm{mmse} = 1/(1 + \mathrm{snr})\), and \(\frac{d}{d\,\mathrm{snr}} \tfrac12 \log(1 + \mathrm{snr}) = \tfrac12 \cdot \frac{1}{1 + \mathrm{snr}}\).

  2. Derivation 11.2The rate-distortion tilt, and why Blahut-Arimoto descends

    Show that \(I(X; \hat X) = \min_q \sum_x p(x)\, \mathrm{KL}\big(p(\cdot \mid x) \,\|\, q\big)\), with the minimum at the output marginal. Then derive the channel update (11.6) for fixed \(q\), and explain why alternating the two updates never raises \(I + \beta\, \mathbb E\, d\).

    Solution
    \[ \sum_x p(x)\, \mathrm{KL}(p(\cdot \mid x) \,\|\, q) = I(X; \hat X) + \mathrm{KL}(q^\circ \,\|\, q), \]

    where \(q^\circ\) is the output marginal, because the log ratio splits as \(\log \frac{p(\hat x \mid x)}{q^\circ(\hat x)} + \log \frac{q^\circ(\hat x)}{q(\hat x)}\). The second term is nonnegative and zero at \(q = q^\circ\).

    For fixed \(q\), minimizing \(\sum_{\hat x} p(\hat x \mid x) \big[\log \frac{p(\hat x \mid x)}{q(\hat x)} + \beta d(x, \hat x)\big]\) for each \(x\) is Theorem 2.1 with \(f = -\beta d(x, \cdot)\) and base \(q\), so the minimizer is the tilt \(q\, e^{-\beta d}/Z\).

    The joint objective

    \[ F(\text{channel}, q) = \sum_x p(x)\,\mathrm{KL}(p(\cdot \mid x) \,\|\, q) + \beta\, \mathbb E\, d \]

    is minimized exactly in each block by each update, so \(F\) never rises. After each update of \(q\), \(F\) equals \(I + \beta\, \mathbb E\, d\) of the current channel, so that quantity never rises either.

On a masked diffusion model for Sudoku or short text, estimate the total correlation of the tokens revealed at each parallel step, exactly on a small vocabulary and with a learned pairwise-information estimator, and report the correlation between the estimated total correlation and the drop in sample quality per step.

Chapter 12

The adjoint method

Optimal control and automatic differentiation

To differentiate one number computed by a long chain of steps with respect to every input of every step, run the chain forward once and a chain of costates backward once. The backward chain is backpropagation for networks, the adjoint equation for differential equations, and the costate of optimal control.

Uses Chapters 3 and 4 and Appendix A.5.

12.1Motivation

Training a model with a billion parameters needs the gradient of one loss with respect to all of them at every step. Perturbing the parameters one at a time costs a billion forward passes, and carrying sensitivities forward through the computation costs one pass per parameter too. Control engineers met the same problem around 1960, designing flight trajectories in which the parameters are a whole control signal. The adjoint method computes every sensitivity at once by running one linear recursion backward, at a cost close to one forward pass. Reverse-mode differentiation (Linnainmaa, 1970) and backpropagation, popularized for neural networks in 1986, are the same computation.

PAPERA document that moved capital

Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

Let each block learn a correction to its input instead of a new representation, and networks train hundreds of layers deep.

Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, and Jian Sun, 2015 · billiondollarpdf.com

What it changed

Residual networks took first place in the ImageNet and COCO competitions of 2015, and the residual connection has been part of nearly every deep architecture since, the Transformer included.

The link to this chapter: a residual block computes \(x_{l+1} = x_l + F(x_l)\), an explicit Euler step of \(\dot x = f(x)\) with unit step, a reading that Haber and Ruthotto made precise (Section 3, equations 2.1 and 3.5). Backpropagation through it is the discrete adjoint (12.1) with Jacobian \(I + \partial_x F\), so the costate passes back through the identity path intact, and as the steps shrink it becomes the continuous adjoint (12.2) that neural ODEs train with.

12.2Intuition

The costate at each step says how much the final loss would change if that step's state moved, and it can be handed backward one step at a time.

Figure 12.1Costates handed back through a 24-step chain

Each costate λₖ is the gradient of the final loss with respect to the state xₖ, each one comes from the next by a single vector-Jacobian product, and the same backward sweep gives the gradient for all 144 weights and biases.

Each step is xₖ₊₁ = xₖ + 0.2 tanh(Wₖxₖ + bₖ), with seeded weights that drift from step to step, and the loss is ½|x₂₄ − target|² = 1.802. The arrows are the costates. At the end λ₂₄ = x₂₄ − target has length 1.90, and passed back through 24 Jacobians it grows to length 13.66 at λ₀ = (11.635, 7.160), which finite differences in x₀ match to five decimals. The same sweep gives all 144 entries of the gradient, and central finite differences with step 10⁻⁴ agree with them to 3.8e−9 of the largest entry, at a cost of 288 forward passes against one forward and one backward. Slide the parameter count down to 6: finite differences cost 12 passes for those six entries, and the one backward sweep still covers all 144. Press Train 80 steps: gradient descent with step 0.2 on the adjoint's gradient bends the path onto the target and takes the loss to 3.6e−4.

12.3Statement

Theorem 12.1 (the discrete adjoint)

Let \(x_{k+1} = F_k(x_k; \theta)\) for \(k \lt N\) and \(L = \ell(x_N)\). Set \(\lambda_N = \nabla \ell(x_N)\) and \(\lambda_k = \big(\partial_x F_k(x_k)\big)^\top \lambda_{k+1}\). Then

\[ \nabla_{x_0} L = \lambda_0, \qquad \nabla_\theta L = \sum_{k \lt N} \big(\partial_\theta F_k(x_k)\big)^\top \lambda_{k+1}. \tag{12.1} \]

Each \(\lambda_k\) costs one vector-Jacobian product, so the whole gradient costs a small multiple of the forward pass, whatever the number of parameters.

Theorem 12.2 (the continuous adjoint)

Let \(\dot x = f(x, t; \theta)\) on \([0, T]\) and \(L = \ell(x(T))\). Solve \(\dot\lambda = -(\partial_x f)^\top \lambda\) backward from \(\lambda(T) = \nabla \ell(x(T))\). Then

\[ \nabla_{x(0)} L = \lambda(0), \qquad \nabla_\theta L = \int_0^T (\partial_\theta f)^\top \lambda\; dt. \tag{12.2} \]

Theorem 12.3 (Pontryagin's costate)

Minimize \(\int_0^T c(x, u)\, dt + \ell(x(T))\) subject to \(\dot x = f(x, u)\), and let \(H(x, u, \lambda) = c(x, u) + \lambda \cdot f(x, u)\). An optimal control minimizes \(H\) at each time, and along the optimal trajectory

\[ \dot x = \partial_\lambda H, \qquad \dot \lambda = -\partial_x H, \qquad \lambda(T) = \nabla \ell(x(T)). \tag{12.3} \]

Where the value function \(V\) is twice continuously differentiable, the costate is its gradient, \(\lambda(t) = \nabla_x V(t, x(t))\).

12.4Derivation

(12.1). Write \(\lambda_k = \nabla_{x_k} L\), the gradient of the loss with respect to the state at step \(k\) with all later steps held as functions. The chain rule through \(x_{k+1} = F_k(x_k)\) gives \(\lambda_k = (\partial_x F_k)^\top \lambda_{k+1}\), and at the end \(\lambda_N = \nabla \ell\). The parameters enter every step, and their effect at step \(k\) passes through \(x_{k+1}\), so their gradient is the sum of \((\partial_\theta F_k)^\top \lambda_{k+1}\) over \(k\). Read as Lagrange multipliers (Appendix A.5), \(\lambda_{k+1}\) prices the constraint \(x_{k+1} = F_k(x_k)\): stationarity of \(\ell(x_N) - \sum_k \lambda_{k+1} \cdot (x_{k+1} - F_k(x_k))\) in each \(x_k\) is the same recursion.

(12.2). Take Euler steps \(F_k(x) = x + h f(x, t_k)\). Then \(\lambda_k = \lambda_{k+1} + h (\partial_x f)^\top \lambda_{k+1}\), whose limit as \(h \to 0\) is \(\dot\lambda = -(\partial_x f)^\top \lambda\), and the sum \(\sum_k h (\partial_\theta f)^\top \lambda_{k+1}\) becomes the integral.

(12.3). The value function solves the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation \(-\partial_t V = \min_u \{c + \nabla V \cdot f\}\). Differentiate it in \(x\) at the minimizing \(u\), which the envelope theorem allows: \(-\partial_t \nabla V = \partial_x c + (\partial_x f)^\top \nabla V + \nabla^2 V\, f\). Along the trajectory,

\[ \frac{d}{dt} \nabla V(t, x(t)) = \partial_t \nabla V + \nabla^2 V\, f = -\partial_x c - (\partial_x f)^\top \nabla V = -\partial_x H, \]

with \(\nabla V(T, \cdot) = \nabla \ell\). So \(\nabla V\) along the path obeys the costate equation. This proof needs a smooth \(V\); the general principle is proved with needle variations of the control. ∎

Back to Chapter 3. In the control problem (3.3), \(V = -\log h\), so \(\nabla V = -\nabla \log h\) and the optimal control \(u^* = -\nabla V\) is the drift of the h-transform. Along a noisy path, \(\nabla V\) follows the costate equation in its drift plus a martingale term. Adjoint matching fine-tunes a diffusion model by regressing its control onto an adjoint computed backward along sampled trajectories, which is a pared-down (12.2), the lean adjoint, used as a training target. A fixed point \(x^* = F(x^*, \theta)\), as in deep equilibrium models (Chapter 4), has the adjoint \(\lambda = (I - \partial_x F)^{-\top} \nabla \ell\): one linear solve in place of a backward pass through the iterations, which is the implicit function theorem.

12.5Figures

Figure 12.2The pendulum's costate, run backward in time

Integrating the costate backward along a stored trajectory gives the gradient of a final loss with respect to the initial state, as λ(0), and with respect to a parameter, as the area under λᵀ∂f/∂c.

The pendulum is θ' = ω, ω' = −sin θ − cω, and the loss is the energy left at time T, L = ½ω(T)² + 1 − cos θ(T). The costate starts at λ(T) = ∇E(x(T)) and runs back along the stored path. At the defaults c = 0.3 and T = 8, L = 0.176968, the adjoint gives dL/dc = −1.246502 and λ(0) = (0.138295, 0.044966), and central finite differences agree to 6.6e−10 relative. Slide c to 0: energy is conserved, λ(0) equals ∇E(x(0)) = (sin 2, 0) = (0.909297, 0), and dL/dc = −10.0275 equals −∫ω² dt along the path. Slide T to 20 at c = 0.3: the pendulum has nearly stopped, L = 0.004114, and dL/dc shrinks to −0.080885. Press Run backward to watch the costate travel from x(T) back to x(0) and the area build up.

Figure 12.3The costate is the slope of the value function

Along an optimal path the costate, integrated backward from the end, equals ∂V/∂x from dynamic programming, so the adjoint and the Riccati equation compute the same slope from two ends.

The problem is ẋ = ax + u with cost ½∫₀³ (qx² + u²) dt + ½s·x(3)², from x(0) = 1. Dynamic programming integrates the Riccati equation −Ṗ = 2aP + q − P² back from P(3) = s, which gives V for every state. The adjoint integrates λ' = −(qx + aλ) back from λ(3) = s·x(3) along this one path. At the defaults a = 0.5, q = 1, and s = 0, the two agree to 2.6e−13, the cost J = 0.805455 equals V(0, x₀), and u*(0) = −λ(0) = −1.61091. In the slices, each tangent touches its slice at the path's point, and at t = 3 the slice is flat because s = 0. Slide s to 3: λ(3) = 0.0648, and the gap is 5.2e−13. Over the whole slider grid the largest gap is 3.6e−11.

12.6Four ways to see it

The adjoint is the chain rule run backward, a set of prices on constraints, a differential equation run in reverse time, and the momentum of optimal control.

  1. 1Backpropagationmachine learning

    A network is a chain of layers, and (12.1) is backpropagation: one backward sweep of vector-Jacobian products gives the gradient for every weight. Reverse-mode automatic differentiation applies the same sweep to any program.

  2. 1 → 2Treat each layer as a constraint \(x_{k+1} = F_k(x_k)\) with a multiplier \(\lambda_{k+1}\). Stationarity of the Lagrangian in \(x_k\) is the backward recursion, so the backpropagated gradient at a layer is the multiplier of that layer's equation, the rate at which the loss changes if the equation is relaxed.

  3. 2Shadow pricesoptimization and economics

    A Lagrange multiplier is the price of a constraint: how much the optimum improves per unit of slack. The costate prices the state at each step, which is why the same numbers appear as sensitivities in engineering design and as shadow prices in economics.

  4. 2 → 3Shrink the steps to an ODE. The recursion becomes \(\dot\lambda = -(\partial_x f)^\top \lambda\) run from \(T\) back to 0, and the gradient with respect to the parameters becomes an integral along the trajectory (12.2). Memory no longer grows with the number of steps if the state can be recomputed backward.

  5. 3The continuous adjointnumerical analysis

    Shape optimization of wings and the calibration of weather models solve one adjoint equation per loss instead of one forward solve per parameter, and neural ODEs train the same way (Figure 12.2).

  6. 3 → 4Let the parameters be a whole control signal \(u(t)\) and the loss the control objective. The gradient with respect to \(u(t)\) is \(\partial_u H\), so at an optimum \(\partial_u H = 0\), Pontryagin's principle strengthens this to \(u\) minimizing \(H\), and the costate equals the gradient of the value function (12.3).

  7. 4The costateoptimal control and mechanics

    Pontryagin's principle turns an optimal control problem into a two-point boundary problem for the state and the costate, with the costate playing the part of momentum in Hamiltonian mechanics. Dynamic programming computes \(\nabla V\) everywhere, and the adjoint computes it along one trajectory (Figure 12.3).

12.7Where it breaks and what is open

The costates are products of Jacobians, \(\lambda_0 = (\partial_x F_0)^\top (\partial_x F_1)^\top \cdots (\partial_x F_{N-1})^\top \lambda_N\), so their size grows or shrinks like \(e^{\Lambda N}\), with \(\Lambda\) the largest Lyapunov exponent of the dynamics. Through chaotic dynamics the gradient of a long-horizon loss explodes and stops describing how the expected loss changes, which is the trouble with differentiating through long rollouts and unrolled optimizers (Metz et al.; Figure 12.4). For contracting dynamics the same products vanish, so the loss stops depending on early states: the vanishing gradients of recurrent networks. Memory breaks next: the backward sweep needs the forward states, and recomputing them by running a dissipative ODE backward amplifies errors, so practical methods store checkpoints and recompute between them. And a step that samples a discrete token has no Jacobian, so the chain breaks there, and score-function estimators (Chapter 3) take over.

Figure 12.4Through chaos the gradient explodes

Through chaotic dynamics the adjoint of a long-horizon loss grows like exp(ΛN), with Λ the Lyapunov exponent, so the exact derivative soon says nothing about how the loss changes over any step one could take.

The loss is x_N for the logistic map xₖ₊₁ = r xₖ(1 − xₖ) from x₀ = 0.3, and one backward sweep gives dx_N/dr exactly. At the default r = 3.9 the Lyapunov exponent along 60 steps is Λ = 0.448 (0.496 over a million steps), and ln|dx_N/dr| grows at 0.459 per step. At N = 50 the adjoint gives −3.675e10 and a difference quotient with step 10⁻⁸ gives −2.120e6. Within that step x₅₀ swings from 0.776 below its value to 0.104 above it, and no difference quotient can exceed 1/(2·10⁻⁸) = 5e7, a size the gradient passes at N = 36. Slide r to 3.2: Λ = −0.659, the orbit is periodic, and both give 0.2815. At r = 2.8 the gradient settles at 1/r² = 0.1276, the derivative of the fixed point 1 − 1/r. The first r on the slider where the two differ by more than 1% at N = 50 is 3.67, and above it they agree only in periodic windows such as r = 3.84.

  1. Adjoints for value-function samplers. A sampler trained with a learned value function as its energy has terminal cost \(-Q\), so the adjoint starts from \(\lambda(T) = -\nabla_a Q\), a learned and noisy gradient. How errors in \(\nabla Q\) propagate through the backward adjoint to the learned control, and whether the costate's own dynamics damp or amplify them, is open.
  2. Gradients through long rollouts. World models, differentiable simulators, and backpropagation through time all face exploding or vanishing costates at long horizons. Which remedy (shorter windows, multiple shooting, smoothing the dynamics with noise) gives gradients that still point downhill on the expected loss is open.

Exercises

  1. Exercise 12.1 The adjoint method

    • A 10-layer network shares one weight: x_{k+1} = tanh(w·x_k) from x_0 = 0.5, with w = 1.1, and the loss is L = ½(x_10 − 1)².
    • Run the forward pass once and the costate λ_k = ∂L/∂x_k backward once. What are dL/dw and dL/dx_0?

    gradients(1.1, 0.5, 10)   # (-0.903046, -0.070962)

  2. Exercise 12.2 The gradient of an ODE's endpoint

    • A population grows by ẋ = θx(1 − x) from x(0) = 0.1, with θ = 1. At T = 3 the loss is L = ½(x(T) − 0.9)².
    • Solve the adjoint (12.2) backward from T, recomputing x on the way back instead of storing it. What are dL/dθ and dL/dx(0)?
    Answer
    endpoint_gradients(1.0)   # (-0.134257, -0.497248)

  3. Exercise 12.3 A shadow price

    • A budget B = 18 is split between x at price 1 and y at price 3, to maximize log x + 2 log y subject to x + 3y = B.

multiplier(18)   # 0.166667

    • Find dL/dθ with one linear solve at x*, without backpropagating through the iterations. What does backpropagating through only the first 2 iterations from x = 0 give instead?
    Answer
    implicit_gradient()    # (-0.246939, 0.287067)
unrolled_gradient(2)   # (-0.390867, -0.061297)

  5. Exercise 12.5 Gradients through chaos

    • The logistic map x_{k+1} = 4x_k(1 − x_k) is chaotic on [0, 1]. The costate of a loss on x_N picks up a factor 4(1 − 2x_k) at each step, so dx_N/dx_0 is the product of those factors.
    • From x_0 = 0.3, what is the growth rate (1/N)·ln|dx_N/dx_0| over N = 100,000 steps, to two decimals? What is its exact value, the mean of ln|4(1 − 2x)| under the invariant density 1/(π√(x(1 − x)))?
    Answer
    growth_rate(0.3, 100_000)   # 0.69
exact_rate()                # 0.693147

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 12.1Backpropagation for two layers

    For \(L = \tfrac12 |W_2\, \sigma(W_1 x) - y|^2\) with \(\sigma\) applied entrywise, derive \(\nabla_{W_2} L\) and \(\nabla_{W_1} L\) from (12.1), naming each costate.

    Solution

    The steps are \(a = W_1 x\), \(z = \sigma(a)\), \(\hat y = W_2 z\). The costates run backward: \(\lambda_{\hat y} = \hat y - y\), then \(\lambda_z = W_2^\top \lambda_{\hat y}\), then \(\lambda_a = \sigma'(a) \odot \lambda_z\).

    Each weight enters one step, so \(\nabla_{W_2} L = \lambda_{\hat y}\, z^\top\) and \(\nabla_{W_1} L = \lambda_a\, x^\top\).

  2. Derivation 12.2The costate of a linear-quadratic problem

    For \(\dot x = u\) with cost \(\tfrac12 \int_0^T u^2\, dt + \tfrac s2\, x(T)^2\), solve the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation with \(V = \tfrac12 P(t)\, x^2\), find the optimal control, and check that \(\lambda = P x\) satisfies (12.3).

    Solution

    \(H = \tfrac12 u^2 + \lambda u\) is minimized at \(u = -\lambda\). The HJB equation \(-\partial_t V = \min_u \{\tfrac12 u^2 + V_x u\} = -\tfrac12 V_x^2\) gives \(\dot P = P^2\) with \(P(T) = s\), so \(P(t) = s/(1 + s(T - t))\) and \(u^* = -P(t)\, x(t)\).

    Along the optimal path, \(\frac{d}{dt}(P x) = P^2 x + P(-P x) = 0 = -\partial_x H\), since \(H\) does not depend on \(x\), and \(P(T)x(T) = s\, x(T) = \nabla \ell\).

Project. In a chaotic simulator such as the Lorenz system, fit the initial condition to a target trajectory by gradient descent, comparing the full adjoint gradient, adjoints truncated to windows of one, two, and five Lyapunov times, and a smoothed finite-difference estimate. Chapter 13

Concentration of measure

High-dimensional probability

A function of many independent pieces, none of which matters much, is nearly constant: its fluctuations are exponentially unlikely to exceed a few standard deviations. In high dimension this makes Gaussians into thin shells, random directions orthogonal, random projections faithful, and empirical risks honest.

Uses Chapters 2 and 10 and Appendix A.6.

13.1Motivation

Statistics and learning promise that an average over data reflects the truth. The central limit theorem says how, but only in the limit and only near the center of the distribution. Learning theory needs bounds that hold at a finite sample size and far into the tail, because a union over many hypotheses or many pairs of points lives there. High-dimensional geometry also defies intuition from two and three dimensions: almost all of a ball's volume sits near its surface, and almost all of a Gaussian's mass sits far from its mode. Concentration inequalities answer both with one mechanism, exponential moments, which is the tilt of Chapter 2.

13.2Intuition

A function of many independent coordinates that depends little on each one barely varies, so in high dimension random objects look alike: almost every Gaussian vector has nearly the same length.

Figure 13.1A Gaussian vector in high dimension sits on a thin shell

A Gaussian vector in d dimensions has length about √d with a spread that stays near 1/√2 at every d, so in high dimension almost every vector has nearly the same length, and two independent vectors are nearly orthogonal.

At the default d = 200 the 4000 vectors have mean length 14.135 against √d = 14.142, and 90% of them lie between 12.99 and 15.30, a shell whose width is 16% of its radius. Their lengths have standard deviation 0.708 against the exact 0.707. The cosine between two independent vectors has standard deviation 0.0704 against 1/√d = 0.0707. Slide d to 2000: the radius grows to 44.7, the shell's width stays at 2.30, now 5.1% of the radius, and the cosine's spread falls to 0.0225. At d = 1 the length is |Z₁|, its middle 90% runs from 0.065 to 1.938, and every cosine is ±1. Press Play to sweep d from 1 to 2000.

13.3Statement

Theorem 13.1 (Chernoff and Hoeffding)

Let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) be independent copies of \(X\) with mean \(\mu\), and \(\bar X\) their average. For \(t \gt 0\),

\[ P\big(\bar X - \mu \ge t\big) \le e^{-n\, I(\mu + t)}, \qquad I(x) = \sup_{\lambda \ge 0}\, \big\{ \lambda x - \log \mathbb E\, e^{\lambda X} \big\}, \tag{13.1} \]

and if \(X \in [a, b]\) almost surely,

\[ P\big(\bar X - \mu \ge t\big) \le \exp\Big(-\frac{2 n t^2}{(b - a)^2}\Big). \tag{13.2} \]

Theorem 13.2 (Gaussian concentration)

If \(f: \mathbb R^d \to \mathbb R\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, I_d)\), then for \(t \gt 0\)

\[ P\big(f(Z) - \mathbb E f(Z) \ge t\big) \le e^{-t^2/(2L^2)}. \tag{13.3} \]

The length \(|Z|\) is 1-Lipschitz, so it stays within a constant of its mean, which is close to \(\sqrt d\), whatever \(d\) is.

Theorem 13.3 (Johnson-Lindenstrauss)

Let \(G\) be a \(k \times D\) matrix of independent standard Gaussians and \(f(x) = Gx/\sqrt k\). For \(n\) points, \(0 \lt \varepsilon \lt 1\), and

\[ k \ge \frac{6 \ln n}{\varepsilon^2/2 - \varepsilon^3/3}, \tag{13.4} \]

with probability at least \(1 - 1/n\) every pair satisfies

\[ (1 - \varepsilon)|x - y|^2 \le |f(x) - f(y)|^2 \le (1 + \varepsilon)|x - y|^2. \]

The dimension \(D\) does not appear.

Proposition 13.4 (a finite-class generalization bound)

For a finite set \(\mathcal H\) of predictors, losses in \([0, 1]\), and \(n\) independent examples, with probability at least \(1 - \delta\) every \(h \in \mathcal H\) has true risk \(R(h)\) and empirical risk \(\hat R_n(h)\) with

\[ \big| R(h) - \hat R_n(h) \big| \le \sqrt{\frac{\ln |\mathcal H| + \ln(2/\delta)}{2n}}. \tag{13.5} \]

13.4Derivation

(13.1) and (13.2). For \(\lambda \ge 0\), Markov's inequality applied to \(e^{\lambda n \bar X}\) gives \(P(\bar X \ge x) \le e^{-n \lambda x}\, \big(\mathbb E\, e^{\lambda X}\big)^n = e^{-n(\lambda x - \log \mathbb E e^{\lambda X})}\), and the best \(\lambda\) gives (13.1). The bound is a Legendre transform of the log moment generating function, the function whose tangents Chapter 2 drew. For bounded \(X\), Hoeffding's lemma (Appendix A.6) gives \(\log \mathbb E\, e^{\lambda (X - \mu)} \le \lambda^2 (b - a)^2/8\), and \(\lambda = 4t/(b - a)^2\) gives (13.2).

(13.3), with a weaker constant. Take \(f\) differentiable (a general Lipschitz \(f\) follows by approximation). Let \(Z'\) be an independent copy and \(Z_\theta = Z \sin\theta + Z' \cos\theta\), so \(f(Z) - f(Z') = \int_0^{\pi/2} \nabla f(Z_\theta) \cdot Z_\theta'\, d\theta\) with \(Z_\theta' = Z \cos\theta - Z' \sin\theta\). For each \(\theta\), \(Z_\theta\) and \(Z_\theta'\) are independent standard Gaussians. Jensen's inequality over \(Z'\) and then over \(\theta\) gives

\[ \mathbb E\, e^{\lambda(f(Z) - \mathbb E f)} \le \mathbb E\, e^{\lambda(f(Z) - f(Z'))} \le \frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2} \mathbb E\, e^{\lambda \frac{\pi}{2} \nabla f(Z_\theta) \cdot Z'_\theta}\, d\theta \le e^{\lambda^2 \pi^2 L^2/8}, \]

since \(\nabla f(Z_\theta) \cdot Z_\theta'\) is Gaussian with variance at most \(L^2\) given \(Z_\theta\). Markov's inequality then gives the tail \(e^{-2t^2/(\pi^2 L^2)}\). The sharp constant in (13.3) needs the Gaussian log-Sobolev inequality.

(13.4). For a fixed vector \(u\), \(|Gu|^2/|u|^2\) is a chi-square variable with \(k\) degrees of freedom, and the Chernoff bound (13.1) for it gives

\[ P\big(\big||Gu|^2/k - |u|^2\big| \ge \varepsilon |u|^2\big) \le 2\, e^{-k(\varepsilon^2/2 - \varepsilon^3/3)/2}. \]

Summing over the fewer than \(n^2/2\) pairs makes the failure probability at most \(n^2 e^{-k(\varepsilon^2/2 - \varepsilon^3/3)/2}\), which is at most \(1/n\) under (13.4).

(13.5). For one predictor, \(\hat R_n(h)\) averages \(n\) independent losses in \([0, 1]\), so (13.2) on both sides bounds the chance of a deviation \(t\) by \(2e^{-2nt^2}\). A union bound over \(\mathcal H\) gives \(2|\mathcal H| e^{-2nt^2} = \delta\), and solving for \(t\) gives (13.5). ∎

The tilt again. The rate in (13.1) for a coin with bias \(p\) is \(I(p + t) = \mathrm{KL}(p + t \,\|\, p)\), and (13.1) applied to the surprisal \(-\log p(X_i)\) gives the equipartition of Chapter 10 an exponential rate. For an infinite class, \(\ln |\mathcal H|\) in (13.5) is replaced by a capacity such as the VC dimension or a Rademacher complexity.

13.5Figures

Figure 13.2A coin's average deviates with probability about e^(−n·KL)

The chance that the average of n coin flips exceeds its mean by t falls exponentially in n at the rate KL(p + t ‖ p), the Legendre transform of the log moment generating function, and Hoeffding's e^(−2nt²) has a slower rate that holds for every variable in [0, 1].

At the defaults, n = 200 flips with bias p = 0.1 and excess t = 0.1, the exact chance that the mean reaches 0.2 is 1.70e−5. Chernoff's bound gives 1.39e−4 and Hoeffding's 1.83e−2, so exact ≤ Chernoff ≤ Hoeffding, as at every p and t on the sliders. The normal approximation gives 1.21e−6, too small by a factor of 14, because its rate t²/(2p(1 − p)) = 0.0556 overshoots KL(0.2 ‖ 0.1) = 0.0444. On the right the exact rate −(1/n) ln P is 0.0549 at n = 200 and 0.0451 at n = 5000, settling onto KL, while Hoeffding's rate stays at 2t² = 0.0200. Slide p to 0.5: KL = 0.0201 and 2t² = 0.0200 nearly agree, so Hoeffding's rate is close to exact for a fair coin.

Figure 13.3A random projection keeps every distance

A Gaussian random projection to k = O(log n/ε²) dimensions keeps the squared distance of every pair among n points within a factor 1 ± ε, and the dimension D the points start in never enters.

The 100 seeded points live in D = 1000 and give 4950 pairs. At the default k = 200 the worst pair's squared distance grows by a factor 1.359, a distortion of 0.359, inside the ε = 0.737 that Theorem 13.3 allows at this k for n = 100, and 36.9% of pairs keep their squared distance within 5%. The ratios have standard deviation 0.105 against √(2/k) = 0.100, the chi-square law each pair follows whatever D is. Slide k down: below k = 166 the bound gives no ε under 1, though the worst distortion at k = 100 is 0.593. Slide k to 500: the worst falls to 0.260 against ε = 0.386. At every k from 170 to 500 the worst stays below the bound, by at least 0.123. For ε = 0.1 the bound asks for k = 5921, more than the D = 1000 the points start in, so at that accuracy it compresses only data of higher dimension.

13.6Four ways to see it

Concentration is a tail bound, a fact about high-dimensional shapes, a license to compress dimension, and the reason a model's training error predicts its test error.

  1. 1Tail boundsprobability

    An average of \(n\) independent pieces in \([0, 1]\) deviates by \(t\) with probability at most \(e^{-2nt^2}\), and the exact exponential rate is the Legendre transform of the log moment generating function (Figure 13.2).

  2. 1 → 2Apply it to \(|Z|^2 = \sum_i Z_i^2\), a sum of \(d\) independent terms with mean 1 and variance 2. It sits at \(d \pm O(\sqrt d)\), so \(|Z| = \sqrt{|Z|^2}\) sits at \(\sqrt d \pm O(1)\). For two independent vectors, \(Z \cdot Z'/d\) is an average with variance \(1/d\), so their cosine is of order \(1/\sqrt d\).

  3. 2High-dimensional geometrygeometry

    A Gaussian in high dimension is a thin shell of radius \(\sqrt d\), and random directions are nearly orthogonal. Noise at level \(\sigma\) moves a \(d\)-dimensional point by about \(\sigma \sqrt d\), but almost orthogonally to the gap between any two data points, so it confuses them only once \(\sigma\) reaches their distance, about \(s\sqrt d\) for points that differ by \(s\) per pixel. That is why the noise schedules of Chapter 1 must reach far beyond the data's per-pixel scale.

  4. 2 → 3For a fixed vector \(u\), each coordinate of \(Gu\) is Gaussian with variance \(|u|^2\), so \(|Gu|^2/k\) is an average of \(k\) independent terms and concentrates at \(|u|^2\). Paying for all pairs of \(n\) points with a union bound costs only a factor \(\log n\) in \(k\), which is (13.4).

  5. 3Dimension reductionalgorithms

    Random projections, sketches, and hashing keep the geometry of a dataset in a dimension set by the number of points instead of the original dimension (Figure 13.3). The constant is large: for 100 points the bound (13.4) says nothing below \(k = 166\) and asks for \(k = 5921\) at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), so the guarantee pays off when the original dimension is far larger than that, and real projections usually do better than the bound. Compressed sensing rests on the same concentration.

  6. 1 → 4The empirical risk of a fixed predictor is an average of \(n\) bounded losses, so Hoeffding bounds its deviation from the true risk. Choosing the predictor after seeing the data is covered by a union bound over the class, which adds \(\ln |\mathcal H|\), and gives (13.5).

  7. 4Generalizationlearning theory

    Probably approximately correct learning, VC theory, and PAC-Bayes are concentration plus a measure of how many effectively different predictors the learner could have chosen.

Names across fields

  • Chernoff bound
  • Hoeffding's inequality
  • large deviations
  • thin shell
  • Johnson-Lindenstrauss
  • sketching
  • PAC learning
  • VC dimension
  • equivalence of ensembles
  • diversification

13.7Where it breaks and what is open

Every bound above needs light tails and independence. The mean of \(n\) Cauchy draws has the same distribution as a single draw, so averaging buys nothing, and for a Student-t variable with \(\nu \lt 2\) degrees of freedom the variance is infinite, so the spread of the mean shrinks only like \(n^{1/\nu - 1}\), slower than \(1/\sqrt n\) (Figure 13.4). Dependence breaks the bounds just as fast: a factor shared by all the pieces never averages out. Benchmark questions drawn from a few sources or templates are correlated in this way, so an evaluation's effective sample size can be far smaller than its number of items. Robust estimators such as the median of means restore exponential concentration from a finite variance alone, at a confidence level chosen in advance.

Figure 13.4Heavy tails stop averages from settling

The mean of n Cauchy draws is as spread out as a single draw, and Student-t draws with few degrees of freedom concentrate more slowly than 1/√n, so averaging buys little when the tails are heavy.

At the default ν = 1 the draws are Cauchy. The middle 90% of 2000 sample means is 13.14 wide at n = 1000, where shrinking the n = 1 width of 12.85 by √1000 would give 0.41, and it matches the exact 12.63 within sampling error. Its fitted slope on log-log axes is −0.027, where light tails give −0.5. Click ν = 1.5: the width at n = 1000 is 0.962 and the slope is −0.305, near the stable-law slope 1/ν − 1 = −0.333. At ν = 2 the variance is still infinite and the slope is −0.445. From ν = 3 the variance is finite: the width at n = 1000 is 0.172 against the Gaussian rate 3.29σ/√n = 0.180, and the slope is −0.494.

  1. Why overparametrized networks generalize. Bounds like (13.5) and their VC versions are vacuous for networks with more parameters than examples, yet such networks generalize. Which complexity measure explains it (norms, compression, PAC-Bayes posteriors) is open, and compression-based bounds tie this chapter to Chapter 10.
  2. Honest error bars for evaluations. A model's score on a benchmark is an average over correlated items, and the right uncertainty depends on how the items cluster. How many items an evaluation needs, and how to report its uncertainty when items share sources, is open in practice.
  3. Noise schedules across resolutions. An image's content is shared by many correlated pixels, so averaging \(k\) neighbours cuts the noise by \(\sqrt k\) and keeps the signal, and the same \(\sigma\) destroys less information at higher resolution. A schedule tuned at one resolution is therefore wrong at another, and image models shift their schedules with resolution for this reason. A principled rule for schedules across resolutions and data types is open.

Derivations from a blank page

  1. Derivation 13.1Hoeffding from the tilt

    Derive (13.2) from Markov's inequality and Hoeffding's lemma, then find the smallest \(n\) that estimates a mean in \([0, 1]\) within \(t = 0.05\) on both sides with probability at least 0.99.

    Solution
    \[ P(\bar X - \mu \ge t) \le e^{-\lambda n t}\, \mathbb E\, e^{\lambda \sum_i (X_i - \mu)} \le e^{-\lambda n t + n\lambda^2 (b-a)^2/8}, \]

    minimized at \(\lambda = 4t/(b - a)^2\), which gives \(e^{-2nt^2/(b-a)^2}\).

    Both tails together give \(2e^{-2nt^2} \le 0.01\), so \(n \ge \ln(200)/(2 \cdot 0.0025) = 1059.7\), and \(n = 1060\) suffices.

  2. Derivation 13.2Johnson-Lindenstrauss from chi-square tails

    For \(Q = |Gu|^2/|u|^2\), a chi-square variable with \(k\) degrees of freedom, use the Chernoff method to show \(P(Q \ge (1 + \varepsilon)k) \le e^{-\frac k2 (\varepsilon - \ln(1 + \varepsilon))}\), bound the exponent below by \(\frac k2 (\varepsilon^2/2 - \varepsilon^3/3)\), and finish (13.4). Evaluate \(k\) for \(n = 1000\) and \(\varepsilon = 0.1\).

    Solution

    \(\mathbb E\, e^{\lambda Q} = (1 - 2\lambda)^{-k/2}\) for \(\lambda \lt \tfrac12\), so \(P(Q \ge (1+\varepsilon)k) \le e^{-\lambda (1+\varepsilon) k}(1 - 2\lambda)^{-k/2}\). The best \(\lambda = \frac{\varepsilon}{2(1 + \varepsilon)}\) gives \(e^{-\frac k2(\varepsilon - \ln(1+\varepsilon))}\), and \(\ln(1 + \varepsilon) \le \varepsilon - \varepsilon^2/2 + \varepsilon^3/3\) gives the stated exponent. The lower tail is bounded the same way, with a larger exponent.

    Over fewer than \(n^2/2\) pairs, two tails each, a union bound gives failure probability below \(n^2 e^{-k(\varepsilon^2/2 - \varepsilon^3/3)/2}\), which is at most \(1/n\) when \(k \ge 6 \ln n/(\varepsilon^2/2 - \varepsilon^3/3)\). For \(n = 1000\) and \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), that is \(6 \cdot 6.908/0.004667 = 8881.4\), so \(k = 8882\), whatever the original dimension.

Project. Take a public language-model benchmark, group its items by source or template, and compute a cluster-robust standard error for a model's accuracy. Report the ratio of the clustered to the naive standard error, which tells how many independent questions the benchmark is really worth.

Chapter 14

Kernels

Statistics and functional analysis

A kernel measures the similarity of two inputs as an inner product in a feature space that is never built. Any method that touches the data only through inner products then runs in that space, which can be infinite-dimensional, and the function it fits is a weighted sum of kernels centered on the data. Kernel ridge regression, Gaussian processes, support vector machines, random features, and attention are this one construction.

Uses Chapters 2, 7, and 13.

14.1Motivation

Linear models are solved: least squares has a closed form, and its statistics are complete. Data rarely lie on a plane, though, and mapping each input through features \(\varphi(x)\), such as all monomials up to degree \(p\), lets a linear method fit curves at the price of a feature count that grows like \(d^p\). Aizerman, Braverman, and Rozonoer (1964) noticed that a method which uses the data only through inner products never needs \(\varphi\) itself, only \(k(x, x') = \varphi(x) \cdot \varphi(x')\). The kernel \((x \cdot x' + 1)^p\), for example, computes the inner product of a weighted set of all monomials up to degree \(p\) in \(O(d)\) time. Boser, Guyon, and Vapnik (1992) applied the idea to maximum-margin classifiers, which became support vector machines.

14.2Intuition

A kernel method fits the data with one bump per data point, and the kernel decides the bump's shape.

Figure 14.1Kernel ridge regression and the GP mean are one curve

Kernel ridge regression and the Gaussian-process posterior mean are the same weighted sum of bumps centered on the data, and the process adds a band of uncertainty that widens away from the data.

The kernel is k(x, x′) = exp(−(x − x′)²/2ℓ²). The GP mean comes from a Cholesky factor of K + σ²I, and kernel ridge comes from a pivoted solve of (K + λI)α = y with λ = σ². At the defaults ℓ = 0.6 and σ = 0.15, the two curves differ by less than 1e−14, and over every setting of the sliders by at most 1.4e−11, which is round-off. At x = 1, in the gap, both give 0.0833, and the band reaches ±1.709 there against at most ±0.280 at a data point. The fit spends 9.14 of its 16 degrees of freedom. Slide ℓ down to 0.2: each bump is too narrow to reach into the gap, the mean falls to 0 there inside ±2.000, which is the prior, and the degrees of freedom rise to 15.32. Set ℓ = 1.1 and σ = 0.1: the log marginal likelihood reaches 0.17, its highest value on the sliders, against −3.81 at the defaults.

14.3Statement

Definition 14.1 (positive definite kernels)

A symmetric function \(k: \mathcal X \times \mathcal X \to \mathbb R\) is a positive definite kernel if \(\sum_{i,j} c_i c_j\, k(x_i, x_j) \ge 0\) for every finite set of points and coefficients. By the Moore-Aronszajn theorem, each such \(k\) has a unique Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\) of functions on \(\mathcal X\), its reproducing kernel Hilbert space, in which \(k(x, \cdot) \in \mathcal H\) and

\[ f(x) = \langle f, k(x, \cdot) \rangle_{\mathcal H} \quad \text{for every } f \in \mathcal H, \qquad k(x, x') = \langle k(x, \cdot), k(x', \cdot) \rangle_{\mathcal H}. \tag{14.1} \]

So \(\varphi(x) = k(x, \cdot)\) is a feature map for \(k\), and evaluating a function is an inner product.

Theorem 14.2 (the representer theorem)

For any loss \(\ell\) and \(\lambda \gt 0\), every minimizer of \(\sum_{i=1}^n \ell\big(y_i, f(x_i)\big) + \lambda \|f\|_{\mathcal H}^2\) over \(f \in \mathcal H\) has the form \(f = \sum_i \alpha_i\, k(x_i, \cdot)\). For the squared loss, with \(K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)\) and \(k(x, X)\) the row of values \(k(x, x_i)\),

\[ \alpha = (K + \lambda I)^{-1} y, \qquad f(x) = k(x, X)\,(K + \lambda I)^{-1} y. \tag{14.2} \]

Theorem 14.3 (Gaussian processes)

Let \(f\) be a Gaussian process with mean 0 and covariance \(k\), and \(y_i = f(x_i) + \varepsilon_i\) with independent \(\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\). Given the data, \(f(x)\) is Gaussian with

\[ \mathbb E\big[f(x) \mid y\big] = k(x, X)(K + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} y, \qquad \mathrm{Var}\big[f(x) \mid y\big] = k(x, x) - k(x, X)(K + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} k(X, x). \tag{14.3} \]

The posterior mean is the kernel ridge fit (14.2) with \(\lambda = \sigma^2\).

Theorem 14.4 (Bochner, and random Fourier features)

A continuous function \(k(x - x')\) on \(\mathbb R^d\) is a positive definite kernel exactly when \(k(\delta) = \int e^{i \omega \cdot \delta}\, d\mu(\omega)\) for a finite nonnegative measure \(\mu\). If \(k(0) = 1\), \(\mu\) is a probability distribution, and with \(\omega_j \sim \mu\) and \(b_j\) uniform on \([0, 2\pi]\), all independent,

\[ z(x) = \sqrt{2/D}\,\big(\cos(\omega_j \cdot x + b_j)\big)_{j \le D} \quad \text{satisfies} \quad \mathbb E\; z(x) \cdot z(x') = k(x - x'). \tag{14.4} \]

For the Gaussian kernel \(e^{-|\delta|^2/(2\ell^2)}\), \(\mu\) is \(\mathcal N(0, \ell^{-2} I)\).

Proposition 14.5 (attention is a kernel smoother)

Softmax attention with a query \(q\), keys \(k_j\), and values \(v_j\) in dimension \(d\) outputs

\[ \frac{\sum_j \kappa(q, k_j)\, v_j}{\sum_j \kappa(q, k_j)}, \qquad \kappa(q, k) = e^{q \cdot k/\sqrt d}, \tag{14.5} \]

a Nadaraya-Watson estimator with the positive definite kernel \(\kappa\). If \(\kappa(q, k) \approx \phi(q) \cdot \phi(k)\) with \(\phi: \mathbb R^d \to \mathbb R^m\), the output is approximately \(\phi(q)^\top S / \phi(q)^\top s\) with \(S = \sum_j \phi(k_j) v_j^\top\) and \(s = \sum_j \phi(k_j)\). Both sums are shared by every query, so \(N\) queries cost \(O(Nmd)\) instead of \(O(N^2 d)\).

14.4Derivation

(14.1). On finite combinations \(f = \sum_i a_i k(x_i, \cdot)\) and \(g = \sum_j b_j k(x'_j, \cdot)\), define \(\langle f, g \rangle = \sum_{i,j} a_i b_j\, k(x_i, x'_j)\). Positive definiteness makes \(\langle f, f \rangle \ge 0\), and \(\langle f, k(x, \cdot)\rangle = \sum_i a_i k(x_i, x) = f(x)\) holds by construction. Completing this space gives \(\mathcal H\), and the reproducing property passes to the limit because evaluation is continuous: \(|f(x)| \le \|f\|\sqrt{k(x, x)}\) by Cauchy-Schwarz.

(14.2). Split any \(f \in \mathcal H\) as \(f_\parallel + f_\perp\), with \(f_\parallel\) in the span of the \(k(x_i, \cdot)\) and \(f_\perp\) orthogonal to it. By (14.1), \(f(x_i) = \langle f, k(x_i, \cdot)\rangle = f_\parallel(x_i)\), so the loss sees only \(f_\parallel\), while \(\|f\|^2 = \|f_\parallel\|^2 + \|f_\perp\|^2\) is smallest at \(f_\perp = 0\). With \(f = \sum_i \alpha_i k(x_i, \cdot)\) and squared loss, the objective is \(|y - K\alpha|^2 + \lambda\, \alpha^\top K \alpha\), whose gradient vanishes when \(K\big((K + \lambda I)\alpha - y\big) = 0\), which \(\alpha = (K + \lambda I)^{-1} y\) satisfies. Any other solution differs by a vector \(c\) with \(Kc = 0\), which leaves \(f\) unchanged since \(\|\sum_i c_i k(x_i, \cdot)\|^2 = c^\top K c = 0\).

(14.3). The pair \(\big(f(x), y\big)\) is jointly Gaussian with covariance blocks \(k(x, x)\), \(k(x, X)\), and \(K + \sigma^2 I\), and conditioning a Gaussian on a block gives (14.3). The posterior is the tilt of Chapter 2: the prior times the likelihood \(e^{-|y - f(X)|^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), and its mode, which is also its mean, minimizes, formally (the process's samples are not in \(\mathcal H\)), \(\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}|y - f(X)|^2 + \frac12 \|f\|_{\mathcal H}^2\), the objective of (14.2) with \(\lambda = \sigma^2\).

(14.4). If \(k(\delta) = \int e^{i\omega \cdot \delta} d\mu\), then

\[ \sum_{i,j} c_i c_j\, k(x_i - x_j) = \int \big|\sum_i c_i e^{i\omega \cdot x_i}\big|^2 d\mu(\omega) \ge 0. \]

The converse, that every continuous positive definite \(k\) arises this way, is Bochner's theorem. For the features,

\[ 2\cos(a + b)\cos(a' + b) = \cos(a - a') + \cos(a + a' + 2b), \]

and the second term averages to zero over \(b\), so each coordinate pair contributes \(\mathbb E\, \cos(\omega \cdot (x - x')) = k(x - x')\), since \(k\) is real.

(14.5). The softmax weights are \(\kappa(q, k_j)/\sum_l \kappa(q, k_l)\), which gives the first form. The kernel \(e^{q \cdot k/\sqrt d} = \sum_n (q \cdot k)^n/(n!\, d^{n/2})\) is a sum of products of positive definite kernels with nonnegative weights, so it is positive definite. Substituting \(\phi(q) \cdot \phi(k_j)\) and pulling \(\phi(q)\) out of both sums gives the linear form. ∎

Two kernels from learning theory. A network \(f_\theta\) defines the neural tangent kernel \(\Theta(x, x') = \nabla_\theta f_\theta(x) \cdot \nabla_\theta f_\theta(x')\). As the width grows, in the parametrization of Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler, \(\Theta\) stays at its value at initialization during training, and gradient flow on the squared loss becomes kernel gradient flow with \(\Theta\), which converges to \(f_0(x) + \Theta(x, X)\Theta(X, X)^{-1}(y - f_0(X))\), with \(f_0\) the network at initialization. The maximum mean discrepancy compares two distributions through their average features,

\[ \mathrm{MMD}^2(P, Q) = \mathbb E\, k(X, X') + \mathbb E\, k(Y, Y') - 2\,\mathbb E\, k(X, Y) \]

with \(X, X' \sim P\) and \(Y, Y' \sim Q\). For a Gaussian kernel it is zero only when \(P = Q\), which gives a two-sample test (Gretton et al.) and a distance between distributions to set beside the transport distances of Chapter 5.

14.5Figures

Figure 14.2Random Fourier features estimate the kernel

Sampling frequencies from the Fourier transform of a shift-invariant kernel gives finite features whose inner products estimate the kernel, with an error that shrinks like 1/√D.

The RBF kernel with ℓ = 0.6 is the Fourier transform of a Gaussian with variance 1/ℓ², so frequencies w drawn from it and phases b uniform on [0, 2π] give z(x) = √(2/D) cos(wx + b). Each draw holds 4096 frequencies, and D uses the first D of them. For the default D = 64, the largest error of z(x)·z(x′) over a 31 by 31 grid of pairs in [−3, 3]² is 0.227 for draw 1 and 0.268 averaged over 8 draws, against 1/√D = 0.125. From D = 4 to 4096 the mean error times √D stays between 2.09 and 2.60, and the fitted slope is −0.488, where a 1/√D rate gives −0.5. Ridge regression on the features, on the same sixteen points with λ = σ² = 0.0225, differs from exact kernel ridge by 0.351 at D = 64 and 0.047 at D = 4096 on average, a slope of −0.543. Slide D down to 4: the estimate is a sum of four cosines, and the mean error reaches 1.274.

Figure 14.3Attention is a kernel smoother

Softmax attention is a kernel smoother with the exponential kernel, and positive random features turn it into linear attention whose error falls as the number of features grows.

Queries and keys have entries N(0, s²) in d = 8, values are N(0, 1), and N = 64. Softmax attention, computed by subtracting the largest score before exponentiating, and the explicit kernel smoother, which averages the values with weights k(q, key) = exp(q·key/√8), differ only by round-off, below 1e−15, at every scale. Positive features φ(x) = exp(Wx − |x|²/2)/√m with x = q/8^¼ estimate that kernel without bias: with m = 200,000 they give 0.4585 against 0.4589. With the default m = 64 features, the relative output error is 0.473 for draw 1 and 0.625 over 8 draws, and the mean falls to 0.248 at m = 1024, a fitted slope of −0.278. The slope stays above −0.5 because one feature's estimate for the query's top key has relative variance exp(|x + y|²) − 1 = 89.2, and the 1/√m rate shows only once m is well past it. Switch to s = 0.5: that variance is 8.9, the slope is −0.409, and the error at m = 1024 is 0.090. At s = 1.0 the variance is 9774 and the slope is −0.127. At N = 64 and m = 64, linear attention costs 147,456 multiply-adds against 69,632 for softmax, and it becomes cheaper from N = 136.

14.6Four ways to see it

A kernel is a feature map, a space of smooth functions, a prior over functions, and the weighting inside attention.

  1. 1Feature mapsalgebra

    A kernel is an inner product of features, \(k(x, x') = \varphi(x) \cdot \varphi(x')\), and any algorithm written in inner products (ridge regression, support vector machines, principal components) runs on the Gram matrix \(K\) alone. The Gaussian kernel's features are infinitely many, one for each monomial in the expansion of \(e^{x \cdot x'/\ell^2}\).

  2. 1 → 2The feature \(\varphi(x) = k(x, \cdot)\) is itself a function, and the norm of the space it spans measures smoothness. For a shift-invariant kernel with spectral density \(s(\omega)\), \(\|f\|_{\mathcal H}^2\) is proportional to \(\int |\hat f(\omega)|^2/s(\omega)\, d\omega\), so a Gaussian kernel charges each frequency \(e^{\ell^2 |\omega|^2/2}\), Chapter 7's Fourier view applied to regularization.

  3. 2Function spacesfunctional analysis

    Fitting with a penalty \(\lambda\|f\|_{\mathcal H}^2\) prefers smooth functions, and the representer theorem reduces the search over an infinite-dimensional space to \(n\) coefficients. Cubic splines are the case where the norm is the energy \(\int (f'')^2\), with linear functions left unpenalized, and the reproducing kernel is the Green's function of \(d^4/dx^4\).

  4. 2 → 3Put a Gaussian prior with covariance \(k\) on \(f\). The negative log posterior is, formally, proportional to the objective of (14.2) with \(\lambda = \sigma^2\), so the posterior mean is the ridge fit, and the posterior adds a variance that grows away from the data (Figure 14.1).

  5. 3Gaussian processesstatistics

    Geostatistics calls (14.3) kriging, and Bayesian optimization uses its variance to decide where to evaluate an expensive function next. Bochner's theorem turns a kernel into a spectrum, and sampling that spectrum gives random features (Figure 14.2).

  6. 1 → 4The softmax weights \(e^{q \cdot k_j/\sqrt d}/\sum_l e^{q \cdot k_l/\sqrt d}\) are the Gibbs weights of Chapter 2's tilt with energy \(-q \cdot k_j/\sqrt d\), and as weights on values they make a kernel smoother. Swapping the kernel for a finite feature map lets the sums over keys be computed once.

  7. 4Attentiondeep learning

    Proposition 14.5 is linear attention. With positive random features \(\phi_w(x) = e^{w \cdot x - |x|^2/2}\), \(w \sim \mathcal N(0, I)\), the product \(\phi(q) \cdot \phi(k)\) is an unbiased estimate of \(e^{q \cdot k}\), the construction of Performer. The exponential kernel is not shift-invariant, so this comes from a Gaussian identity rather than from Bochner's theorem, and each feature's relative variance is \(e^{|q + k|^2} - 1\), so short queries and keys need few features and long ones need very many (Figure 14.3). A recurrence whose state is \(S\), with decay or gates, is the state-space view of Chapter 4.

14.7Where it breaks and what is open

A kernel fixes in advance which inputs count as similar. In high dimension that choice degrades: by Chapter 13 the distances between random points concentrate, so a Gaussian kernel gives nearly the same value to every pair, the Gram matrix approaches a constant plus a linear kernel plus a diagonal (El Karoui), and the fit can do little more than a linear model. With a small ridge it chases the noise in nearly equal kernel values and does worse than predicting the mean (Figure 14.4). The exact method also stores and inverts an \(n \times n\) matrix, at \(n^3\) time and \(n^2\) memory, which inducing points, random features, and the Nyström method cut by a low-rank approximation of \(K\). And the kernel stays fixed while a network learns its features: in the tangent-kernel limit the features never move, and trained networks beat their tangent kernels on image classification: the best convolutional tangent kernel reaches 77% on CIFAR-10, six points below the same architecture trained without batch normalization (Arora et al.), and standard training widens the gap.

Figure 14.4In high dimension the kernel sees every pair alike

In high dimension pairwise distances concentrate, so an RBF kernel matrix approaches a constant plus a diagonal, and kernel ridge regression on a fixed sample loses the signal: with a small ridge it fits noise, and with a large one it predicts the mean.

The target is y = sin(3x₁) + 0.1ε with x uniform in [0, 1]^d. The fit uses 200 training points, and test R² is measured on 500 test points against the noiseless sin(3x₁). The lengthscale ℓ is the median pairwise distance. Kernel ridge on x₁ alone, the one coordinate the target uses, reaches R² = 0.997. At the default d = 32 with λ = σ² = 0.01, R² is −0.144, the largest pairwise distance is 2.46 times the smallest (about 17,500 times at d = 1), and 98% of the off-diagonal kernel values lie between 0.465 and 0.753, around e^−½ = 0.607. Slide d: R² stays above 0.9 up to d = 8, crosses 0 near d = 27, and reaches −0.631 at d = 160, because the fit treats the small random differences between kernel values as signal. Switch to λ = 1: the fit starts at 0.993 on x₁ alone, drops to 0.733 by d = 4, and from d = 24 on settles on the mean, with R² between −0.081 and 0.021.

  1. Linear attention that matches softmax. Linear attention keeps a state of fixed size \(m \times d\), so it cannot recall an arbitrary earlier token the way softmax attention, whose state grows with the context, can. Which feature maps, gates, and hybrids of linear and softmax layers close the gap on recall at which state size is open, and a state that grows logarithmically with context would sit between the two.
  2. When learned features beat any kernel. For a target that depends on a few unknown directions of a high-dimensional input, a two-layer network that learns those directions needs far fewer samples than any rotation-invariant kernel. Which properties of real data make feature learning necessary, and how much of a trained network a kernel describes, are open.
  3. Choosing the kernel to compare distributions. A two-sample test with a Gaussian kernel loses power as the dimension grows, at a fixed bandwidth and at the median-heuristic bandwidth alike (Ramdas et al.), by the same concentration. How to choose or learn the kernel when comparing embeddings of different data types, and what a small MMD then guarantees, are open.

    • Fit kernel ridge regression with k(x, x′) = (x·x′ + 1)² and λ = 0.1, then ridge on the six features 1, √2x₁, √2x₂, x₁², x₂², √2x₁x₂, whose inner product that kernel is. What do they predict at (0.5, 0.5) and at (2, −1.5)?

predict((2, -1.5))    # -2.965538

  2. Exercise 14.2 Attention is a kernel smoother

  3. Exercise 14.3 Random features for the Laplace kernel

    • One random-feature term 2cos(ωx + b)cos(ωx′ + b), with b uniform on [0, 2π], has variance 1 + k(2δ)/2 − k(δ)². What is it at δ = 1, and how many features D bring the estimate's standard deviation down to 0.01?

    • At ℓ = 1, what is MMD² = E k(X, X′) + E k(Y, Y′) − 2E k(X, Y) against each Q? What does a linear kernel k = xy see for Q₂, and what happens to MMD²(P, Q₂) at ℓ = 5?

    mmd2((0, 1), (0.5, 1), 1)   # 0.047124
mmd2((0, 1), (0, 2), 1)     # 0.094187
mmd2((0, 1), (0, 2), 5)     # 0.006897

  5. Exercise 14.5 Distances concentrate

    • Draw x and x′ uniformly from the cube [0, 1]^d. Their squared distance S = Σ(xᵢ − x′ᵢ)² gets, from each coordinate, E(U − V)² = 1/6 and Var (U − V)² = 7/180.
    • What is the relative spread sd(S)/E(S) at d = 2 and at d = 1000? For a Gaussian kernel e^{−S/(2ℓ²)} with ℓ² = d/6, the mean squared distance, what are an entry's mean and relative spread at d = 1000?
    Answer
    relative_spread(2)      # 0.83666
